The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at the time of the luncheon recess I was putting forward
Supply-National Defence in a very general way certain principles which I thought should govern Canada's contribution to collective defence. We on this side of the house will discuss these principles in their more detailed application as this debate goes on. However, I wish to make it quite clear, as I tried to do earlier in my discussion, that in the circumstances I put forward I was not advocating a policy of neutralism or a policy of default on our obligations or international commitments to our allies, or indeed a policy of refusing to play our part in resistance to aggression when we have no other alternative than resistance, irrespective of the consequences, something which, of course, would be tragic beyond words.
When I say that no one can win a nuclear war, that no one can win a nuclear war in the old conventional sense, that is true. However, it should not be misunderstood-and I am sure it is not misunderstood by those who might wish to break the peace-that our understanding of this position in the western countries means that we would not attempt to defend ourselves because there was no possibility of victory in the old conventional sense. Free men will always defend themselves when attacked, I hope, irrespective of the consequences. However, we should be aware of the consequences, which are so far beyond those of previous wars that they must be taken into consideration when we discuss defence.
In Great Britain in 1940 it did not look as though there was much chance of a victorious result of the war. However, it came. Yet in a sense that fact proves the other side of the coin or the other phase of the question. The resulting victory which was achieved in 1944 and 1945, and the inability of the west to follow victory with the kind of peace which would endure has brought us, through no fault of our own, to the situation in which we find ourselves today of trying to defend ourselves against a nuclear war which, if it occurred, would mean planetary destruction.
Nor do I wish it to be understood by anyone-and this was made clear in the quotation I read from a speech by the premier of Manitoba in so far as his views were concerned-that when we take the position that nuclear arms are not required by Canada under Canadian control or indeed under joint control for the defence of peace and the discharge of our obligations, we take that position because of some feeling of smug moral superiority. Of course that is not the case because, as a country, we are committed to nuclear defence. Indeed, we supply the material that makes possible nuclear defence and nuclear deterrence, through the sale of

Supply-National Defence our uranium. It is therefore not because of any superior moral considerations of that kind that we take our stand.
Neither I nor the other members of the Liberal party who sit on this side of the chamber advocate the weakening of the strategic deterrent, let alone its unilateral abandonment. Indeed, I feel that the strategic deterrent in the hands of those who now possess it should be maintained strong and unimpaired. In the words of the phrase we now use, it should be credible so that in the minds of those who are tempted to break the peace there should exist no doubt that it can be used effectively.
I believe that western strategy-and that includes Canada-should be based on the credibility and on the invulnerability of the retaliatory forces not only on our side but perhaps even on the other side, strange as that may seem-the invulnerability of both sides through mobility-so that each side would be reasonably certain that the other side could destroy it. In that way the temptation would be removed to bring about victory through some kind of sneak attack with immunity from retaliation. That kind of mutual invulnerability, which may seem to be a strange idea to put forward on our side but which has been put forward by some fairly highly respected defence experts, would certainly discourage a surprise attack based on fear.
But while we take that view with regard to the strategic deterrent, we on this side are opposed to dispersal of the nuclear deterrent. We are opposed to purely national control of that deterrent, especially with regard to the North Atlantic alliance, just as we have great doubts-in fact our feelings are stronger than doubts-as to the advisability of national custody of the nuclear deterrent beyond the limits of those three countries which already possess that weapon.
That brings me to a subject which was dealt with by the minister and which has been discussed by other members in this chamber. I now leave the question of continental strategy and come to the question of what should be our NATO strategy in the present situation and what should be the attitude members should take to collective strategy and to the use of nuclear weapons in the implementation of that strategy.
So far as our own contribution to NATO is concerned, which contribution is to be strengthened, we are told, by the dispatch of additional troops overseas, we have a brigade group and we have an air division. I wish to refer the committee to Hansard of July 3,

1959 at page 5414. This was some time ago, and we were then told by the Minister of National Defence that this question of nuclear weapons for our forces overseas in NATO was being considered. General Pearkes said then:
-the Canadian brigade in Europe with short range nuclear weapons for NATO defence tasks are also being studied. These studies are continuing and are fast reaching a stage when there can be an exchange of notes of this matter.
He was referring, of course, to an exchange of notes with the United States. That was more than two years ago. I should like to know, and I am sure the committee would like to know, what exactly is the position now in that regard so far as our contribution to NATO forces is concerned. In the same debate, as reported at page 5415 of Hansard for July 3, 1959 the minister of national defence added:
I presume that eventually the Canadian forces will be equipped with atomic weapons under the same terms as the other NATO contingents under SACEUR-
What are these terms, and since that time has there in fact been a decision which covers the acquisition of nuclear weapons by Canadian forces in NATO? From what I have said it will be clear, I hope, that I do not object to the NATO alliance possessing in some form nuclear weapons for defence purposes; indeed, they have them now, but under national control. At present all these nuclear weapons which are available to certain NATO forces are, as far as I know-and the minister will correct me if I am wrong- in the custody of the United States or the United Kingdom.
I do not think that situation has been altered by what is referred to now as a sort of double key arrangement, or a joint control of such weapons. I believe it has been assumed by NATO, and NATO defence planning has been based on this assumption, that these nuclear weapons in the possession of certain NATO members will be used immediately against any aggressive move; that those forces in NATO which have these weapons have been trained for that purpose, and that there is equipment to discharge that purpose, though it is not in the hands of NATO; it is in the hands of the United States. Indeed, the minister said yesterday decisions were taken in this matter which made NATO, as he put it-I am not sure of the exact expression-a nuclear force back in 1954. That is quite true. The outspoken Field Marshal Montgomery-a man outspoken in this and other matters-said in 1954:
I want to make it absolutely clear-

He was the NATO commander at that time:
-that we at SHAPE are basing all our operational planning on using atomic and thermonuclear weapons in our defence. With us it is no longer: "They may possibly be used". It is very definitely: "They will be used if we are attacked."
That is clear enough. General Gruenther said the same thing, in different words, the same year when he confirmed that nuclear weapons would be used and agreed-and he is an expert in these matters-that once such weapons were used by NATO, that use would spread to all-out nuclear war, in what has been called the awful escalation of destruction. The minister and his predecessor have both said-I certainly remember General Pearkes saying this-that they saw no way by which you could limit the use of nuclear weapons; that if you started with a nuclear bullet-I am not quoting General Pearkes but I think this was his view-you would likely end with a nuclear bomb.
That is why we have been so anxious and so worried about nuclear weapons in the hands of NATO forces and not under NATO control, especially in circumstances like the present when NATO forces under United States immediate command are moving along or have been moving along the corridor leading to Berlin armed with weapons. In 1957 General Norstad-though he seems to have altered his views since-took the same view, that it was impossible to draw a line between the tactical use of atomic weapons against an attacker's forces-and I once hoped that line could be drawn

and their strategic use against the attacker's homeland.
Mr. Chairman, the minister said that NATO has now a nuclear strategy and in that sense is a nuclear force. We know that nuclear weapons are in the hands of certain NATO powers. Yet I do not know of any decision that has been made-and perhaps the minister will enlighten me on this point-notwithstanding the decision to which he referred, which I think was in December, 1958, and which dealt with the matter in broad principle, I do not know of any political decision that has been made by the NATO council or any other NATO body authorizing and laying down the conditions under which NATO nuclear weapons will be used, or laying down any rules governing the control of the use of such weapons in the hands of NATO members in Europe.
Surely the time has come to do something about that. In view of what General Gruenther, General Norstad and others have said about the inevitability of this escalation of destruction, to use the nuclear weapon even in its tactical form as a first strike weapon for NATO forces against an attack
Supply-National Defence surely might bring about the greatest danger of all, the danger of an atomic chain reaction, the kind of chain reaction which I have just mentioned, which begins with a bullet and ends with continent-destroying bombs.
This would result-and we have talked about this before in this house-in NATO becoming an agency, which it was never meant to become, for the conversion of what might after all be only an accidental or a limited incursion or attack, into a nuclear holocaust. That could be done either by immediate retaliation from strategic air forces which would not worry about the troops on the ground but would worry, in the language of General Gruenther, about the enemy's homeland; or it could be brought about by premature and unnecessary use of nuclear weapons in the hands of NATO front line forces or forces in reserve. Surely that is the most frightening aspect of this NATO strategic situation, and this NATO tactical situation also.
Henry Kissinger, who has written a great deal on this subject and I think is recognized as an authority, in an article called "The Necessity for Choice" had this to say:
If NATO can be defended only by all-out war, it will face a hopeless dilemma; to yield to pressure will set up a pattern of Soviet blackmail-
We know what that means. He went on to say:
-while to resist will involve catastrophic devastation.
That is the awful dilemma that those who are responsible for the political and military planning of NATO's strategy face at the present time. It seems to me that the answer, and perhaps the only way out of this dilemma, is not to do away with a NATO deterrent, even a NATO nuclear deterrent, as opposed to a United States or United Kingdom deterrent, but to bring that deterrent under some form of collective control and to build up enough conventional strength in NATO front line forces so that the nuclear deterrent will not have to be used until it is clear beyond doubt that a massive nuclear assault has been launched.
That does not mean leaving our front line forces defenceless. It does mean-and this seems to be a doctrine which is gaining more and more support-isolating the nuclear deterrent under NATO control from the conventional strength of its forces so there would not be this awful temptation to start a nuclear war when conventional defence might be sufficient to meet an attack. I have no doubt this is being looked into, and perhaps the minister will have a chance to tell us what progress is being made in NATO thinking in this regard.
I think these nuclear weapons, which NATO must have as a defence organization, must be

Supply-National Defence under some form of NATO and not national control. But I make a distinction in my mind, a distinction the full importance of which I did not realize some time ago, between custody and control. If these weapons are brought under control, and if the policy determining the use of these weapons is to be isolated from conventional weapons in some form and brought under NATO control, then it does not seem to me to matter nearly as much whether they are in United States custody or not.
The alternative-and perhaps this alternative would appeal to many people who are fundamentalists on this question-would be to have NATO not only in control but in custody of these weapons. This would mean that the United States, the United Kingdom and France would relinquish their nuclear weapons now in the possession of NATO forces to collective custody and control. I have no illusion about the difficulty of doing this, but if this were done and if weapons of this kind were in the hands of our forces as part of NATO it would not, in my view, be extending the area of membership in the nuclear club, because three members of that club would be giving up their own national control to a collective organization.
I think this would be a move in the right direction, and it would be limiting rather than expanding the extent of the nuclear club. If that is not possible, however, the only alternative which makes sense to me would be to bring about NATO control and have the nuclear weapons isolated from the conventional front line weapons and placed in reserve in the custody of those countries-I hope it would be only one-which now have that custody. In that case we might be able to resolve this awful dilemma of how to meet an attack, if there should be one, without converting the situation into nuclear war.
I am not now thinking about an all-out nuclear assault on this continent or on Europe. In that case it would not make any difference whether our weapons were under collective control or joint control or single control. Everyone would use everything he had; one would just hope for the best and pray for survival. But that is not the only kind of problem we have to face. The problem is also to deal with a limited assault which NATO perhaps could not meet without using nuclear weapons if the organization does not have sufficient conventional strength. Surely this makes it of fundamental importance to build up NATO's conventional strength so as to decrease the present reliance on nuclear retaliation. At present I think there is too much reliance on the trip wire function of the organi-

zation and on massive retaliation. The inadequate conventional strength means that the first strike in defence might be from nuclear weapons, weapons which, if we had sufficient conventional strength, would not have to be used.
This, I think and hope, is the basis upon which NATO is now developing its strategy. This position, as I understand it, requires a change in existing strategy and a change in the defence policies of its members with regard to the control and custody of atomic weapons possessed by NATO. There is certainly growing concern among NATO members about membership in an alliance where a decision to use nuclear weapons could be made without their participation and at very short notice. I read confirmation of this in the press this morning in a dispatch out of Norway. Collective control in the interests of strengthening the alliance, however difficult this may be, seems to me to be essential.
Someone is going to say, how can you have collective control in a council of 15 members? How can you have, to use the common phrase, 15 fingers on the trigger? That would be technically impossible, I think, except under the conditions I have just mentioned, which would provide for adequate conventional defence against an attack by conventional weapons in the case of anything but an all-out assault, with nuclear defence in reserve. If you could have that, if you had sufficient collective conventional defence to hold an attack, then it would be possible to call the members of the organization together and put the problem to the NATO council in the light of the conditions as they developed. I would hope this is the way in which it could be done rather than by setting up some directorate or committee.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I wonder where the deterrent would be in that situation. What would stop the Russians sending over their missiles and bombers?

I have been trying to deal with that situation. If we had sufficient conventional strength, and an attack was made by conventional forces, an attack which was not meant to be an all-out attack, we would have time to determine whether the NATO council would authorize nuclear weapons to be used. If there were to be a massive all-out nuclear assault by missiles across the continent and across the ocean, it would not make any difference what kind of mechanism we had set up.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The question is, what would deter the Russians from launching an attack of that kind if you could not retaliate?

There would be a more effective deterrent than we have now. We would have a threefold deterrent. They would know that we had adequate conventional forces available for front line defence. They would know that we had intermediate nuclear missiles in reserve, and they would also know that we had strategic nuclear deterrent strength across the ocean. This kind of control, which apparently does not appeal to the hon. member for Saskatoon, could avoid the frightening possibility of a national field commander acting on national orders using nuclear weapons in the front line when this might not be necessary, and might be fatal.
In this connection, and differing from what he said in 1957, at the annual conference of the NATO parliamentarians last November General Norstad had this to say:
I believe that our forces must have a substantial conventional capability. They must be able to operate, where the military situation permits, without using arms and weapons equipped with nuclear warheads. This will require shield forces of the general magnitude being provided under our present program, a program which I regret to say is not yet completed.
That is an understatement. General Norstad then went on to say:
This conventional strength requires an organization or a system under which the basic combat elements would react normally with conventional weapons-
I ask the hon. member for Saskatoon to listen to this.
-but it also requires that associated with these basic combat elements there are atomic weapon units which can be used if necessary.
And, I say, used under NATO control. General Norstad went on:
However, the threshold at which nuclear weapons are introduced into the battle should be a high one.
That is military jargon which means, do not use nuclear weapons until you are absolutely certain it is the only protection you have against destruction. Then he concluded-and this is the very core of my argument-by saying about nuclear weapons:
The use of these weapons should be the result of a specific, deliberate decision, made at a level consistent with the policies and plans of NATO.
That is a military way of saying it should be made by a NATO agency.
Then this final sentence:
In any case, this level must be higher than that of the commander of the basic combat elements to which I have made reference.
I have made reference to the lines along which NATO strategy should develop, and I hope it is developing along these lines. There may be some strengthening rather than weakening of the deterrent both politically and militarily along those lines. That can only
Supply-National Defence be done, of course, by strengthening political unity inside NATO itself by far greater political integration among the NATO countries, by greater defence integration among the NATO countries, and by using the NATO council as a council for strategy politically and militarily. If that is done; if the NATO council is given the kind of authority it should have and has not had, then with military advice and a re-examination of the military organizational set-up in NATO, we can make this organization a far stronger organization for military defence than it has been in the past. Perhaps part of what I call this diffusing strategy could be a disarmed zone right across Europe, which would avoid the difficulty of tactical nuclear weapons in the hands of opposing forces too close together.
This is a view that is not, of course, peculiar to me. A great deal of thinking has been going on along these lines. A group of the Conservative party in Great Britain called the Bow group, a rather radical young Conservative group, in a pamphlet called "Stability and Survival" issued not so long ago, at page 28 had this to say. This represents the views of some members of the Conservative party in the British House of Commons in regard to this very problem. The paragraph reads:
The British army is equipped with Honest Johns and Corporals, the warheads being under American control. The fundamental requirement for the relationship between tactical nuclear weapons and our armed forces is that the armed forces should always have a choice between using them and not using them and still be in a position to hold the line. In other words, they must be available, but not the only means of checking aggression. Thus, to quote Kissinger, "Forces in being are more important than at any previous time in our history!" It is important to understand that units once in battle cannot switch from one mode of warfare to another. To integrate nuclear weapons into every unit would make it virtually impossible to keep a war on a conventional basis. Far from being diffused throughout the army, tactical nuclear weapons must be kept in separate units, so that the temptation for a hard pressed junior officer to use them is avoided.
I say not only should they be kept in separate units in reserve, they should be kept under NATO as opposed to national control. If that can be done I think Canada could co-operate to the full in that kind of NATO strategy. But if we are being asked in NATO to accept nuclear weapons for our air division and for our infantry brigade under other than that kind of control, under national control, or under joint control which gives the United States an overpowering authority to use or not to use them, then I do not think we should accept them in Europe. I hope that choice will not have to be made, because I hope that NATO will develop along the lines which I have ventured to outline.

Supply-National Defence If it does it will mean far greater political unity as well as defence unity, and far from weakening the deterrent it will strengthen it.
This is the kind of continental defence and NATO strategy that I venture to put forward and which I hope we will be examining in detail as we go through the estimates. I should like to return to what I said at the beginning. There is only one sure defence, and that is peace. At the present time there is only one sure military way of maintaining peace-and I do not like to say this-and that is to preserve the balance of the terror by the maintenance of a strong and powerful nuclear deterrent force. I accept that in military strategy, but I see no reason-I see a great many arguments against it-for the extension of nuclear weapons from the countries which now have them to other countries thereby weakening their position in international affairs and in the United Nations and making it quite impossible, as I see it, for any Canadian secretary of state for external affairs to go down to the United States and argue against other countries accepting nuclear weapons.
It seems to me these are the advantages of adopting the kind of course I have put forward and the disadvantages of the alternative course by which we become a member of the nuclear club with nuclear weapons under national or joint control. If we are faced with that choice we should take the choice I have indicated, thereby strengthening our position in international affairs, and making our voice stronger in the only field which will save us, namely the maintenance and strengthening of international peace.

Mr. Chairman, a little while ago the Leader of the Opposition was talking about high levels and low levels, and I must say that the speech he has given since lunch was certainly on a much higher level than the one he gave before lunch. Before lunch what he was doing in effect was attempting to rationalize the irrational. It was a further attempt on his part to try and get out of the mess which the Liberal party got into at their January meeting as far as defence matters are concerned.
I indicated yesterday the comment of some well-qualified newspapermen with regard to the so-called position the Liberals took on defence at the January meeting. The Leader of the Opposition has been making a series of speeches across the country since then trying to explain this, and he complains that people do not understand what their position was. Well, certainly they do not understand it because it was not a position which is understandable. It was a matter of confusion. As I indicated yesterday, one of the reporters who was there said they decided to take

Canada out of NORAD, then they put Canada back into NORAD, then they finally ended up with it half in and half out, that is as far as interceptors are concerned, and it was much the same thing as far as nuclear weapons are concerned and so on all down the line. It resulted, as I say, in a mess and confusion.
I noted yesterday also what a very serious writer on defence subjects had to say in a serious magazine called the Canadian Commentator. John Gellner had this to say about the position the Liberal party is taking on interceptors in particular:
The policy which the Liberal party has adopted in this matter does not even make sense.
It does not make sense, and neither does a lot more of the so-called policy of the Liberal party on defence.
What did he say about your policy?
He said that at least our policy makes sense. He does not agree with all of it, but he said that at least there is some logic in it.
Where does he say that? He does not say it.
Paul, don't get too excited.

Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, the Minister of National Defence is a member of the government and he ought to know that it is contrary to our rules to refer to any member except as the hon. member for such and such constituency. Now, hon. gentlemen opposite do not like it, but it is about time ministers were taught that rudeness is no substitute for effective action in this house. There is no one who on occasion destroys his argument in that regard more effectively than does my genial friend the Minister of National Defence.
The hon. gentleman was in error. He does it to a greater extent than anybody else. I apologize for not mentioning the hon. member for Essex East. I realize I was in error.
According to the rules.

I am sorry. I was tempted to do that by the numerous remarks the hon. member for Essex East makes along the same line, and mostly from his seat. However, what I was saying, which the hon. member hoped I would forget but he has not succeeded in throwing me off the track, was that Mr. Gellner in dealing with this matter stated:
They-

The Liberals.
-want to leave all arrangements as they are except that Canadian forces in NORAD would not actually shoot. In other words, we would warn the Americans that the enemy was coming, we would tell him who he is, we would fix and track him, but then we would virtuously withdraw and let the Americans do the killing. This is a solution worthy of Pontius Pilate, not of a Lester B. Pearson and his associates.
That is not our solution at all.
I think truer words were never written.
It is not true.

It is a Pontius Pilate type of policy if there ever was one. It is an attempt to stand on both sides of the fence. It is an attempt to go in two opposite directions at the same time, and all the attempts of the Leader of the Opposition in various speeches across the country to try to rationalize this completely irrational position are just not going to succeed because it is impossible for them to succeed.
First of all the Leader of the Opposition today accused those in this party and myself in particular of refusing ever to change our minds. He was talking about the fact that he had changed his mind, and he said that we refused to change our minds, that we would not budge, that we were stubborn and so on. Yet about five or ten minutes later in his speech he was complaining bitterly because we did change our minds, as he said, in connection with interceptors. He cannot have it both ways. As a matter of fact, these two statements in his speech made only about five or ten minutes apart, are typical of the lack of logic in the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition on defence. He accuses us on the one hand of being absolutely unchanging and refusing to change and look at new conditions, and five minutes later he complains bitterly because, as he says, we did change.
What can the people of Canada make of such an attitude and statements of that kind? It is all right for the members of his party who sit behind him to applaud loudly when he makes a statement of that kind but when the general public or anybody who thinks seriously about these matters sits down and analyses what he has said it immediately becomes apparent that there is no validity in most of his remarks.
Let the public decide.
The public will certainly decide, and there is no question in my mind as to how they will decide.

Sooner or later?
Supply-National Defence

The Leader of the Opposition also went on to complain in his earlier remarks that this was the first debate we have had on defence this session, and that there had been none in the earlier part of the session. No one knows better than he does that the reason for that was his own absence and that of the hon. member for Trinity.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not so.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, that statement is untrue.
The defence estimates were announced for consideration by the leader of the house. They were to come up on a certain day. The Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Trinity-
That is not true.
-complained and requested that they be not brought up because they said they could not be here.
So we waited for six months.

As a result consideration of these estimates was delayed. He now complains that there was no debate on defence in the earlier part of the session, but the reason was the unwillingness of the Liberal party to go ahead with a debate at that time.
That is ridiculous nonsense.

The Leader of the Opposition went on to say that I should have made a statement on fundamental issues and questions, and that I had not done so. I submit that if he will read the speech I made he will see that it is a statement on the fundamental defence situation as far as this country is concerned, the position the government has taken in regard thereto, and what we have been doing and are doing. His chief complaint would seem to be that we have not said we are going to get nuclear weapons next week. That is really what it all boils down to.
From the statements of the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Essex East you would think that the acquisition or non-acquisition of nuclear weapons constituted the whole field of defence policy. They are one type of weapon, and they would be used in certain circumstances and not used in others. I think they have to be regarded as a certain type of weapon and not looked upon as the end-all and be-all of defence policy, which they are not.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to an editorial in this morning's Globe and Mail, a copy of which I have here, and quoted some portions of it with approval. I should

Supply-National Defence like to point out that it would appear impossible that the writer of the editorial had read the speech I made yesterday or any of my previous speeches on defence. Otherwise he could not possibly have written this editorial, because he states here, after quoting something I had said:
The picture this conjures up, intentionally or otherwise, is that of Canada facing single combat with Russia, and considering whether to become a full-fledged nuclear power to deter the prospective enemy. This is not the problem at all. Canada has no hope of becoming a nuclear power; to build long range rockets and the like as a deterrent is altogether beyond her resources.
That is exactly what I have been saying for months. The editorial goes on to say:
The main defence of the western world against nuclear war is its deterrent force and the most important components are the missiles and heavy bombers of the United States strategic air command-[DOT]
In speech after speech I have made those very statements, and for the writer of this editorial in the Globe and Mail to write as though these views are contrary to what I have been saying is, of course, simply an indication of the fact that the writer seems to have no knowledge whatsoever of what I have been saying for months past and what I said yesterday.
I have been insisting right along that Canada's defence depends on belonging to the NATO alliance, maintaining the NORAD agreement and our efforts toward peace in the United Nations. I have emphasized this time after time. I have emphasized the fact that the forces we maintain in Canada are not forces designed to meet every eventuality. We have no long range strategic bombers, we have no nuclear weapons, we have no missiles. We have no major naval vessels except one aircraft carrier. But within the NATO alliance as a whole we have all these components, and Canada's security is arrived at as a result of her membership in this alliance and the fact that we can depend on our allies to provide these various forces if they are required.
The editorial is completely ridiculous. The writer of the editorial and the Leader of the Opposition appear to dislike the fact that I used a somewhat homely analogy about a bear and a man with a rifle. Probably they do not like analogies of any kind, particularly rather homely ones.
The Leader of the Opposition went on to talk about NATO having a nuclear strategy. Later he said that he agrees that there is a nuclear strategy and believes that it must be maintained. I am glad to have him make that definite statement, because from some of the statements he has made through the country in past months you would think that he was against that idea. Having come to this position he, I hope, will remain with it.
[Mr. Harkness.l
I have said that every time I have spoken.

I hope he will not shift his position every month or so as he has done during the past several months. He asked me a question which I was not really able to catch, as to the basis on which I stated that there were several countries in NATO that have nuclear weapons on their soil and have entered into agreements with the United States in connection with those weapons, as I stated yesterday. I do not know exactly what he meant. I think he is aware of the fact that this is the case.
I asked you what countries, what members.

The only thing I would say about that would be to quote from a statement former President Eisenhower made on January 17, 1961 in a letter to congress which has been published. This letter contains a reference to an agreement with the government of Italy for co-operation in the use of atomic energy. I quote:
To facilitate the necessary co-operation on our part legislation amending the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 was enacted by the congress in 1958. Pursuant to that legislation agreements for co-operation were concluded with four of our NATO partners in May and June 1959. A similar agreement was also recently concluded with our NATO allies, the Republic of Italy. All of these agreements are designed to implement in important respects the agreed NATO program. This agreement with the government of Italy will enable the United States to co-operate effectively in mutual defence planning with Italy and in the training of Italian NATO forces in order that, if an attack on NATO should occur, Italian forces could, under the direction of the supreme allied commander for Europe, effectively use nuclear weapons in their defence.

May I ask the minister a question on this point, since I brought it up? Is he now telling us that these NATO members have bilateral agreements with the United States for the acquisition of nuclear weapons by their forces under national or joint control? If so, what members of NATO have made these agreements he has mentioned?
I think what I have read is self - explanatory.
That is another thing altogether; that is for the peaceful use of atomic energy.

Some people refuse to understand if it does not further their own purposes. This statement made by President Eisenhower contains this sentence to which I have already referred:
*-if an attack on NATO should occur, Italian forces could, under the direction of the supreme allied commander for Europe, effectively use nuclear weapons in their defence.

I think that is clear enough. As to the other countries, I have not seen any public statements in regard to which countries they are; therefore I have to consider that as security information.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Chairman, the Leader of the Opposition says "Oh, oh". He knows quite well that anything along this line is a matter of security until it is released by the people concerned. I have read the letter signed by President Eisenhower and sent to the congress of the United States, which is a matter of public record. I think it makes the situation quite clear. There is nothing to be gained by me spelling out the other four countries to which he referred. Once more, of course, as I pointed out yesterday, all this, which has been public information for some time, makes a complete sham of the position taken in connection with NATO by the New Democratic party at its convention.
Then the Leader of the Opposition went on to mention the weapons systems we have already secured, the Bomarc, the Honest John and the 104. He quoted at the time from a statement by General Foulkes in a pamphlet entitled "Canadian Defence Policy in a Nuclear Age", one of those behind the headlines booklets. He quoted what General Foulkes said as though it were government policy. The Leader of the Opposition knows that General Foulkes does not state government policy. He never did state government policy as chairman of the chiefs of staff. This was the prerogative of the members of the government under whom he served, both the government to which the hon. member belonged and the present government. From the way in which the Leader of the Opposition put this quotation on the record it would appear as though General Foulkes was stating government policy. I will not say he did so purposely, but it was designed to cause misapprehension on the part of the people listening to him or reading Hansard.
On that point, I should like to say I made it quite clear, as the record will show, that General Foulkes had no official responsibility when he made that statement.

This is fine, but I say that the way in which the quotation was put would lead most people reading Hansard to believe that General Foulkes was stating government policy. This is not the case. General Foulkes was a distinguished soldier. He is listened to with great respect on military subjects. I believe everyone in Canada accords him that respect. One of the odd things about this, and this is typical of what you
Supply-National Defence find in the Liberal party, is that only the other day the hon. member for Leeds was quoting from this same pamphlet in an attempt to show that General Foulkes was opposed to nuclear weapons. This is typical of the Liberal party, trying to go in two directions at once. The Leader of the Opposition quotes him as being strongly in favour of nuclear weapons, which he is. The hon. member for Leeds was quoting from this booklet, as a reference to page 8250 of Hansard will show, in an attempt to show that General Foulkes a great military leader in Canada, was against nuclear weapons.
This again is typical of what you get in the Liberal party. You find people going in opposite directions, so you have complete confusion in the party. I am afraid I often feel sorry for the Leader of the Opposition-
Don't feel sorry for him, feel sorry for yourself.
-as a result of the things the people in his own party do to him.
You should feel sorry for the Minister of Trade and Commerce, too.
You need the help of the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs; they should be here to help you.

I should like to draw attention to the long, sustained remarks which have been coming for some time from the hon. member for Essex East, who is deliberately breaking the rules by remaining in his seat when he makes these interruptions.
I apologize.

The Leader of the Opposition made a reference to the statement the Prime Minister made in regard to the acquisition of the three weapons systems to which I have referred, the Bomarc, the Honest John and the 104. He went into the question of lead times and then gave us his own interpretation of what I had said yesterday and on previous occasions in that regard. I should like to make it quite clear once more that you cannot decide today to arm your forces with nuclear weapons carriers and, having made that decision, expect to have the forces armed with these weapons within two or three years. It takes a considerable length of time after an order is placed to produce any one of these weapons systems, and it takes a considerable length of time to train people in their operation.
As I said in my speech when I opened this debate, and as I have said on numerous occasions, it has seemed the part of wisdom to acquire certain weapons systems which

Supply-National Defence are capable of carrying nuclear warheads. Then in the event a decision should be taken that nuclear warheads are required, we would be in a position to make use of them. It was in connection with this use of the analogy of the bear and the rifle that the Leader of the Opposition chose to object.
I did not object to it.

This is the situation. If you are going to take due precautions in the extremely troubled situation which has been existing for the last two years or more and you believe that there is any possibility that you might have to have nuclear weapons for your own defence, for defence of your own territory, then it was essential to secure the carriers, the systems which could use nuclear warheads and to put in orders for them some considerable time ahead. The Leader of the Opposition objected to the fact that we had placed orders for the Bomarc, the Honest John and the F-104, I submit that it was only the part of wisdom and prudence to have done so, whether or not they are ever actually armed with nuclear warheads.
In this connection I would just recall to the minds of hon. members that yesterday the hon. member for Trinity was comparing the Honest John unfavourably with the Little John, thus indicating how absolutely little he knows about this matter. The Honest John is a very much more effective weapon than is the Little John. The Little John is not yet even an approved weapon. It has a range of less than half of that of the Honest John and its punch is approximately one sixth less than that of the Honest John. Nevertheless the hon. member for Trinity rises in his place as though he knew all about it and says that the Honest John is an obsolete weapon and that the Americans are now producing the Little John, a very much better weapon. Once more he indicated his complete ignorance of these matters of a technical nature.
You are hiding behind your security curtain.
The hon. member for Trinity is an expert on curtains.

At this point the Leader of the Opposition made his great confession about changing his mind. I have no complaint about his changing his mind. The only thing about which I complain is that he does it so frequently that you never know where you are at with him. It is quite reasonable for a man to change his mind every two years, we will say, or every year or even oftener if conditions warrant it. But to do it every month or every week seems to be

a little bit beyond reason and leaves us in a complete state of mystery as to what his position really is on these subjects.
Following that, he went on to interceptors and in effect stated that they are no more of any use. He said that their only purpose was to protect S.A.C. bases and that they were no protection whatever for Canadian cities. I submit that if there were no defence at all in Canada or in the United States against manned bombers, the world would not be in its present situation. The Russians would probably have been in control of everything a considerable length of time ago. It is the fact that there is a defence against the manned bomber particularly, which makes it unlikely that manned bombers will come over here to drop bombs. This defence therefore constitutes a great protection for Canadian cities and for the entire population.
In addition to that, of course, in the event that a war started, while it is true they would not knock down all the bombers that come over, nevertheless they would knock down a considerable number of them; and every time you knock down a bomber carrying one or two atomic bombs, you have saved the lives of a large number of people and avoided a great deal of property damage. While these things, of course, are relative, to say that they are of no protection whatever to Canadian cities is to make a statement which is just not correct.
Next, the Leader of the Opposition proceeded to discuss the Arrow. I dealt with the Arrow the other day when the matter was raised by an other hon. member on his side, and I am not going to say much about it now. However, I will make one or two comments. This was when the Leader of the Opposition complained and asked why we changed our minds. He said, "Why did the government change its views on the bomber threat?" Again he asked, "Why did they say, when the Arrow was done away with, that there was not going to be a bomber threat any more?" Of course, that was never said to begin with. What was said at the time was that other means of defence against the bomber would be investigated. I have here the statement of the Prime Minister in connection with this matter made on Friday, February 20, 1959. He ended the statement with these words:
The government has taken no decision to acquire other aircraft to replace the CF-100, which is still an effective weapon in the defence of North America against the present bomber threat. The Minister of National Defence and the chiefs of staff are now engaged in further studies in the various alternatives for the improvement of our defences.

The then minister of national defence on May 17 last year in discussing the estimates had this to say:
Regarding the need for an interceptor, as seen at that time-
This is at the time of the cancellation of the Arrow.
-the chiefs of staff were instructed to investigate the possibility of obtaining another aircraft at a cheaper price to replace the CF-105.
We did not say that the bomber threat was gone. We did not at that time say that the CF-100 would not be replaced. In fact, we said just the opposite.
Selected scripture readings again.

To continue what the minister of national defence said on May 17, 1960:
That was stated in the House of Commons by the Prime Minister when he gave his statement, that the chiefs of staff were being instructed to investigate and see whether there was any other aircraft of proven design that was available.
As a matter of fact we have secured the F-101. As I stated here yesterday, contrary to the opinions of the hon. member for Trinity it is an exceptionally good aircraft and fills the needs.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I should like the minister to quote the opinion which I expressed, which is contrary to the one he just quoted.
I have the floor.
He is continually falsifying the record by misrepresenting the facts.

The hon. member cannot resist interrupting, Mr. Chairman. He is extremely sensitive. I suppose there is no one so sensitive as is the man who knows he is wrong. The hon. member for Trinity demonstrates that fact.
Let us keep our tempers down.
My temper is all right. It is the tempers on the hon. member's side that he needs to worry about. I refer to the hon. member for Trinity.
Don't be smart.

I think the hon. member for Essex East had better speak to his colleague. He is excited. As was stated by the then minister of national defence, the cancellation of the Arrow to a very great extent was due to the fact that it was just too costly a weapon for the Canadian economy and Canadian defence budget to be able to stand. The cost
Supply-National Defence of it would have been something in the neighbourhood of $2,250 million or about $12,500,000 a plane.
You are lying again.
Oh, oh.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Trinity has just said, "You are lying again". I would request that you ask him to withdraw that remark as any other gentleman would.
Mr. Chairman, the minister used that figure no less than a day ago-
Withdraw.
Will you allow me to make a statement, Mr. Chairman.
Withdraw.
On a point of order may I say that I asked for a withdrawal. If the hon. member is not sufficient of a gentleman to observe the rules of the house, then just let him sit quietly.
He can prove you were lying.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I can give the hon. member for Trinity some authority for acquiescing in the request of the minister and I would appreciate it if he would withdraw the remark.
I would like you to hear me out, Mr. Chairman.
No.
On a point of order-
He has the right of reply.
If I can prove the minister is lying, will you accept-
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member should withdraw. He has no right to make a speech. He must withdraw.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member withdraws that particular word I hope it will not be interpreted in the sense of the acceptance on this side of the chamber of facts which we know not to be accurate as stated by the minister.
That is different.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I think perhaps the Leader of the Opposition was speaking from the point of view of the group situation in bringing in that particular factor. In the matter before the committee, the allegation made by the hon. member for Trinity was direct and personal and was impugning the integrity and honour of the minister of the crown who had the floor.

Supply-National Defence
For that reason, without any preliminary explanation I would ask the hon. member for Trinity to kindly withdraw the remark.
The evidence of the defence expenditures special committee-
Withdraw.
-pages 146 and 147-
Withdraw.
Mr. Chairman, would you please ask the hon. member to resume his seat? I have the floor.
-the committee was advised by the-
Withdraw.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. I have the floor, as it turns out, and I do not think there is any need to exercise the temper of the committee, which has been on a fairly gentle level throughout this very serious and important debate on national defence.
I say again that there is no need for any preliminary explanation on the part of the hon. member for Trinity. I know him well enough personally, to know that he knows he should withdraw the remark so we may continue the debate that is before the committee.
I withdraw the phrase I used, in accordance with parliamentary practice, while reserving the right to vindicate the statement I made later in the debate.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Chairman, after this unseemly interruption I should like to resume what I was saying, which was that the cost of the Arrow, at $2,250 million-
You never learn. You are stupid-

-which would have been $12,500,000 per copy as the program was presented at that time and as was the estimate of the company, was just completely beyond the capability of the budget. When we told the company that and said we could not continue the program, they then made an alternative proposal of putting in, instead of a Canadian-manufactured weapons system, a United States-manufactured weapons system and said that under those conditions the cost of the airplane would be $7,800,000 per copy instead of $12,500,000 per copy.
That was the figure of the Department of National Defence.

However, this was still completely out of reason and, as the minister of national defence said on May 17, 1960:
[The Deputy Chairman.]
All I can say in conclusion is that the cost of $12J million for an aircraft, or even, if the alternative system of fire control had been introduced, of $7,800,000, was just a price tag which was too high to be included in the defence budget of those days.
That was the situation in regard to that.

And get back half of it in
taxes.

I should like to point out in this connection that we were not alone in cancelling one of these extremely high priced airplanes. The United States cancelled their 108 really for exactly the same reasons that we cancelled the 105, because they considered the cost of the airplane was too great for the return involved, and also because they considered their other airplanes, the F-101, the F-102 and the F-106 were adequate for the purpose of meeting the bomber threat as they saw it at that time.
Of these airplanes, of course the F-101 is one of those we are going to get, and it is the only two-seater airplane of the lot. Both the 102 and the 106 are single-seater airplanes and are not adapted for the job that is to be done here in Canada. The next thing-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the minister, but his time has expired.
Go ahead.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the committee give unanimous consent to the minister continuing?
Agreed.

The Leader of the Opposition went on to say that he thought the Bomarc was obsolete, that it is no good. Then of course the hon. member for Trinity made similar statements. If that is the case, here is a very peculiar thing which I would ask the committee to consider. There was a story written by Paul Dubois in the Ottawa Citizen of October 29, 1960. The dateline was "Thurso". It was about the speech of the Leader of the Opposition at a rally in support of Gaston Clermont, Liberal candidate in the by-election occurring at that time in Labelle riding.
And elected.

I would read the committee the direct quote. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition will say he was misquoted, but the direct quote of what he said was this:
A nuclear deterrent may be necessary for the U.S., but not for us and other countries. If Russia ever attacked North America and specifically Canada, Montpellier would be a prime target for the Russians, Montpellier and communities for hundreds of miles around would be reduced to ruins.

If Montpellier was going to be a prime target because it had the Bomarc base there, why does the Leader of the Opposition now say that the Bomarc is completely useless? If it is completely useless the Russians would not be wasting any bombs on it.
Oh, oh.

We find the Leader of the Opposition, for election purposes, going to this area and saying this terrible Conservative government had built a Bomarc station there and that was going to bring Russian bombers and these people would be wiped out if the balloon ever went up.
The balloon went up this last minute.

The Leader of the Opposition says the Bomarc is no good and nobody takes it seriously except this government. He says the Russians do not pay any attention to it. That is another example of the logic of the Leader of the Opposition in connection with these matters. Now-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Take a long breath.

He went on to say that the Liberals had put up a much better policy last year and he indicated much better roles that Canada might be following as far as defence is concerned.
What was this great policy they put up last year? As described by my predecessor, it was a policy of scrap, scrap, scrap. They wanted to scrap practically everything and what they did not want to scrap in this so-called policy consisted chiefly of advocating things which we had already done or were proposing to do. I have a list here and I could go over them in detail, but I hardly think it is worth while. I will just indicate that they urged the abandonment of the SAGE Bomarc system and recommended the purchase from the United States of a number of supersonic interceptor aircraft. They knew we were negotiating at that time for supersonic aircraft, so they recommended this and thought they would get on the bandwagon, I suppose.
There is one other thing I should like to mention. They advocated, really, that the navy should become a sort of glorified merchant marine.
Assault vessels for the troops.
Fortunately that policy is not supported by anybody except themselves. That so-called policy is so full of holes that it is much worse than one of those famous cheeses.

It smells worse, too.
Supply-National Defence

The Leader of the Opposition read some quotations from newspapers supporting the position that they take. I have a whole file here attacking the position they have taken, but I certainly have not time to read them. This sort of reading does not prove very much, of course.
After lunch-I think the Leader of the Opposition must have had a good lunch-he seemed to get onto a somewhat better tack. He got away from this attempt to justify the mistakes that he and his party had made in the past in regard to defence and he got on to a discussion of NATO, what its objective should be, how nuclear weapons might be controlled in it, and so on. The hon. gentleman said he did not object to NATO having nuclear weapons. As I indicated, I was very glad to have that definite statement from him and I hope he will stay with it. I think we all realize that the control of nuclear weapons is an extremely difficult problem, as the hon. gentleman himself admitted. It is, of course, one which has been exercising the attention of governments of the NATO countries for a very considerable time. To date, no generally acceptable solution has been reached. It is a problem which I certainly trust can be solved, just as the Leader of the Opposition does and as, I think, we all do, but it has not been solved to date.
There is another question which was raised by the Leader of the Oppositoin and with which I should like to deal briefly. He referred to 15 fingers on the trigger. Of course, it would be hardly a credible type of deterrent if we had to obtain the agreement of 15 countries before nuclear weapons might be used, in certain circumstances particularly. In this connection a great deal of thought has been given to whether what are known in the navy in particular as rules of engagement might not be worked out-whether all the 15 countries of NATO might not agree to those rules of engagement, as they are called, which would lay down the situation in which each country would agree that nuclear weapons might be used. There is, I think, hope of arriving at some type of what might be called full NATO control over the use of nuclear weapons by this means.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke of the necessity, in his view, of building up the conventional front line strength of NATO. I fully agree that not only the conventional front line strength of NATO but the conventional strength of the organization generally should be built up. I do not think anybody would quarrel with the hon. gentleman in this regard. Ever since the organization was established, one of the greatest difficulties as far as NATO is concerned has been the failure

Supply-National Defence of certain members of that organization to build up their conventional forces at a sufficiently rapid pace to the strength to which they themselves had agreed to bring them at some time in the future. Of course, the greater the degree to which each of the individual countries in NATO builds its conventional strength the stronger the force will be. I think the Leader of the Opposition and myself share common ground in that regard. As a matter of fact, the increase in the Canadian force which was announced here last week is an indication of Canada's willingness to build up her own NATO strength and increase her contribution to NATO.
I should like to say a word about one idea which the Leader of the Opposition put out- the idea that the Russians might launch a limited conventional war, and that we must have some means of dealing with it. I do not think that eventuality is very likely, though I do not say it is impossible; nothing is impossible. But I think it is very unlikely that the Russians would start a limited war in Europe which they would expect to keep as a conventional war. If they were to do so I think the chance of such a conflict developing into a nuclear war would be very great. For this reason I hope the Russians would not contemplate such action for a minute because it would be an extremely dangerous type of move.
As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, perhaps the greatest danger we face in the world today is that of a war started by accident. This is something which could happen, and it is a possibility which needs to be guarded against very carefully as far as the west is concerned'-and we trust the Russians will take equal precautions. However, as I say, the chance that they would start a fair sized conventional war in the expectation that it could be kept at that is, I think, very unlikely. The basic situation is that they have nuclear weapons in their force in eastern Europe, and if they started to move, Mr. Khrushchev himself has said they are going to use everything. That is why it is necessary to have sufficient strength to deter them from ever making such a move. I agree it is the most important thing in the world at the present time to try to ensure that peace continues. On that note I think I will end.

I apologize for taking up the time of the committee at this stage but it is most difficult to conduct a responsible examination of the estimates of the Department of National Defence when the committee cannot rely on information given it by the Minister of National Defence. The example we have had this afternoon is just one of


many. Either the minister's memory is incomparably bad or he gives us wrong information.
For example, in respect to the cost of the Avro Arrow, in May of this year, speaking on Vancouver island during the by-election, the minister is reported to have said, according to a newspaper which he indicated this morning was a good paper, that the planes would have cost $15 million each. The report in the Victoria daily Colonist reads in part:
Referring to the Liberal leader's remarks about the scrapping of the Avro Arrow jet interceptors the defence minister stated that the planes would have cost $15 million each and that the huge cost would have meant scrapping much of the army and navy strength.
This afternoon the minister must have decided in his imagination that it would be more credible if he reduced the figure to $12 million each. And then, when he was challenged, as he was yesterday when he pulled the same trick, he reduced the figure to $7.81 million each. Even that figure is too high, because that is the figure which was given to the special select committee on estimates a year ago as the cost of 108 operational aircraft plus 12 pre-production models. If hon. members do the arithmetic they will find that the cost per operational aircraft was $6.8 million each.
Still too much.

That is all in the evidence. The minister is aware of it, and for him to stand up and tell this committee that the cost would have been $12 million each is an insult to hon. members, particularly as the evidence given by the former deputy minister of national defence, now Air Chief Marshal Miller, was that the planes would cost $6.8 million each. How can we have any faith in anything the minister tells us if he uses a device of this kind to try to confuse and bewilder both the committee and the Canadian people?
This is a type of arithmetic which might be applied to a new situation. The minister has just worked out an arrangement under which the Canadian Department of National Defence is to receive 66 Voodoo aircraft in exchange for certain things. I have the agreement here. I shall not read it in detail, but in exchange for the 66 Voodoo aircraft the department agrees to take over from the United States the cost of maintaining Pinetree radar stations previously maintained by the United States air force. In addition, it is to contribute $50 million toward a program of military aid- toward the acquisition of F-104 aircraft to be built at Canadair in Montreal.
In addition, it will pay one third of the cost of spares and ground handling equipment for the Voodoo in the amount of $10.9 million.

Now, there is no cut-off date as to when Canada's responsibility ends in respect of maintaining the Pinetree line. The annual cost of maintaining the Pinetree line has been variously estimated. The then minister of national defence, the Hon. George Pearkes, V.C., advised the house on March 2, 1959, as reported on page 1518 of Hansard as follows:
Mr. Speaker, before the house rose for the dinner recess, the Leader of the Opposition had asked for information with regard to the cost of the Pinetree system. As I explained, the Pinetree system is shared by the United States and by Canada, some of the stations being operated by Canadians and some being operated by the Americans. The cost to Canada of operating each year is approximately $28 million; that is the cost of operating those Pinetree stations which were either built by Canada and manned by R.C.A.F. personnel or were built by the United States and manned by R.C.A.F. personnel. The cost to the United States is approximately $43 million for operating their stations. That figure of $43 million includes some $5 million which the United States are spending on purchasing equipment for those stations in Canada.
Hence if Canada were to take over the operation of the line in its entirety it would mean the addition of $43 million to our defence budget at the present time.
A United States congressional subcommittee was advised by the director general of the United States air force budget that the saving to the United States air force by Canada taking over the cost of the Pinetree line was $50 million a year. If this is so, Mr. Chairman, let us assume that we have to maintain this Pinetree line for ten years. The cost, even by using the lower figure recorded by the Minister of National Defence, would be $430 million. Add to this $50 million which is Canada's share of the purchase of F-104's, and $10.9 million which is our share of the spares for the Voodoo, and the total cost is $490.9 million for 66 aircraft or approximately $7.5 million per copy. If we had to maintain those stations for 15 years the cost would be a total of $705.9 million, or more than $10 million a copy, far more than it would have cost to carry on with the Avro Arrow program.
The Minister of National Defence told the people in Victoria that the commencement of the Avro Arrow program was the greatest mistake ever made by the Canadian government. Well, the deal he has just made with the United States government, which could result in the cost of $10 million each for aircraft which at the most are not worth more than $2 million each, is in my opinion one of the biggest boobs ever pulled by a minister of national defence.
In closing may I say I think the minister should apologize to the committee for using figures upon which it cannot rely.

Mr. Chairman, if these allegations came from some serious source I
Supply-National Defence would take them seriously. However, I consider the source from which they come and I will merely say that the figures the hon. gentleman is producing are probably comparable with the figures he was trying to produce yesterday as to what the cost would be for the 15,000 more troops we are going to raise, which he insisted was double what I had said they would be, although this was a figure arrived at by careful estimates of the departmental officials and officials of treasury board. As far as the actual cost of taking over these Pinetree lines, and so on, is concerned, if the cost went on for long enough, of course, it might be very considerable. But the main point is that we are taking over those radar stations in Canada, manning them by Canadian personnel and operating them with Canadian personnel rather than having them operated by United States personnel.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are always complaining about having United States personnel here stating that it is an infringement of our sovereignty. Therefore rather than complaining about it they should be happy to see Canadian personnel replacing United States personnel in manning those radar stations. The point is, if you take a long enough period you can arrive at any figures you like.
Members of the committee will recall an item which appeared in the paper the other day. There was a clergyman in Boston who sent a bill to the chancellor of the exchequer for $18 worth of damage done to the fence of his church back in 1770 something. He presented a bill for upwards of $750,000. If you take a long enough period you can come up with a terrific figure. In effect this is what the hon. member is doing.

Mr. Chairman, such indecision on the part of the government is not only disappointing but also detrimental to the interests of Canada, and as long as no clear and specific decision is arrived at on this most important matter, Canada will be incapable of playing the leading part that it should play.
I listened last Tuesday to the statement made by the minister. That statement can only lead to speculation. Here is what he said as recorded on page 8223 of Hansard:
It requires that they be equipped with weapons comparable to if not better than those of a potential adversary. It is the policy of the government that our forces should not be required to face a potential enemy with inferior weapons.
Mr. Chairman, most newspapers understood that the government had decided to acquire atomic weapons and to become a member of the nuclear club. But that statement is ambiguous and causes dissatisfaction everywhere among the public.
1 also listened to the remarks of the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny); he too avoided any definite statement on this capital matter. Indeed, he considered war in terms of the 1914 world war or the second world war because, according to page 8241 of Hansard, he stated:
If the worst should come, if we have to fight again, I do not hesitate to say that we shall once again win the battles of tomorrow just as we won the battles of yesteryear, and this for many reasons.
Well, the minister has forgotten, I think, that victory has no meaning at all in a nuclear war. However, he was a little more careful yesterday than he was when he addressed a rally in Mont Laurier during the last by-election campaign in the constituency of Labelle. minister will recall, I hope, that one of the reasons for his party's humiliating defeat in the riding of Labelle was precisely the stand taken by his government on this question of nuclear weapons.
Mr. Chairman, after three days of debate, it is obvious that the government's national defence policy is several years old, as the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) has shown, and that the government has not had the courage to adopt a definite position concerning the use of nuclear weapons in Canada. As long as this situation prevails, we cannot hope to play the part we could play, and we would be ill-advised to criticize today the other countries which belong to the nuclear club since our objections to nuclear tests would be weakened because of the position taken by the government.
That is a cause of great disappointment for all Canadians but they have one reason for keeping up their hopes, and that is the fact that there is one political party which has remained true to the policy it has always advocated with respect to nuclear weapons. Here I should like to quote from the newspaper Le Devoir of Tuesday, April 11, 1961. Here is what Paul Sauriol had to say in an editorial:
The Liberal party rally, last January, clearly declared itself against acquisition or use of nuclear weapons in Canada, under any form of control; Mr. Pearson said that such weapons were not required for the time being.
What position we took at the rally was our position before and it still is our position. That is something that one cannot say of this administration.
I do not want to be too critical of the C.C.F. members who have been wearing since last summer a new jacket which fits them about as well as a strait-jacket. As I say, I do not want to be too hard on them, because it is really pitiful to see them trying to take positions now to the left, now to the right, according to the instructions they get.
I simply say that the only encouraging sign for Canadians is the fact that at least there is in the Canadian political life one party with a clean cut position, with a clear stand, a constant stand, and I am proud to be a member of that party, the Liberal party.

We have had a rather lengthy and interesting discussion, Mr. Chairman, with respect to military hardware. It seems to me to be pretty well a stalemate, and at times the debate was difficult to follow. Of course, I would not suggest for a moment that I am capable of speaking with any knowledge or judgment on such a question. Now, Mr. Chairman, at the request of a number of people I again raise a matter that I raised yesterday, a matter that is of serious concern to a great number of Canadians. Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, I made certain statements with respect to General Heusinger and expressed strong opposition to his appointment as chairman of the military representatives committee of NATO. This means that he is one of those who plan the strategy and tactics of NATO and who, indirectly, would direct the activities and actions of Canadian troops. I want to say that my statements were not made lightly. They were not made just to create resentment or anything of that sort. I feel very keenly on this matter and I speak with conviction. I feel as keenly as a number of other persons do, a number of other groups in Canada and in the United States.
The Associate Minister of National Defence replied briefly to my arguments and at one point said that General Heusinger was a man who had served his country with distinction. I am quite sure that the Associate Minister of National Defence spoke according to the information he had available. I am confident also that, judging from his remarks,

Supply-National Defence he has not been completely informed on this matter. In order to put the record straight, and on behalf of a number of Canadian citizens, I want to place the facts on the record. The appeal urged the annulment of the appointment of General Adolf Heusinger, chairman of the military representatives committee in permanent session of NATO)
In his autobiography, "Befehl in Widersteit," published in West Germany in 1950, Heusinger wrote that he sympathized with the 1923 Hitler putsch in Munich, but did not participate because he was sure the attempt would fail.
In 1940, Heusinger became chief of operations on Hitler's general staff. Was responsible for the military planning of all Nazi invasions from then on.

In 1942 was made responsible lor all actions against partisans. In August 1942 this order, initiated by Heusinger, was sent to the army group centre on eastern front:
"The Fuehrer demands immediate retaliatory action for (partisan) attack on the railroad station in Slavnoye, with the use of the strongest measures of terror. Report what measures you take.'' Heusinger's order resulted in the following: In Slavnoye the Nazis threw several dozen live children into a deep well. None survived. In another village, Gayanka, Heusinger's troops exterminated the entire population of 115.
Heusinger, as chief of operations of the OKW (Oberkommando der Wehrmacht)-the high command of the Nazi forces, commanded the special extermination squads (Einsatzgruppen). These squads were given the task of exterminating all Jews and other groups. William L. Shirer describes some of the mass atrocities committed by Heu-singer's Einsatzgruppen (see pages 961 to 963 of "The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich.")
In "SS-Alibi of a Nation" Reitlinger says that Heusinger planned the levy en masse of the civilian population on the eastern front (page 386).
Heusinger was one of Hitler's most trusted generals. When a bomb planted by army officers exploded at Rastenburg. East Prussia, during a meeting of Hitler and his top generals, the following facts should be remembered:
After the bombing, Hitler said on the radio, "But you should know of a crime unparalleled in German history. The bomb seriously wounded a number of my true and loyal collaborators." (For Heusinger's role in the aftermath to the July 20, 1944, bombing see Shirer, pp. 1044 et seq : Reitlinger, "SS," pp. 386 et seq.).
The loyal Hitler general who was giving a detailed report on the Russian front at the precise time of the bombing was Gen. Adolf Heusinger.
That, though wounded, the general who led the vengeful hunt against other Nazi generals who had failed in their plan to kill Hitler so that they could negotiate a separate peace with the West was Gen. Adolf Heusinger.
That the top-ranking military figure who participated prominently in the mass executions that followed wherein the victims were slowly strangled
