Item agreed to.
236.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and major equipment, $71,823,500.
I should like to ask the minister if he would explain the reduction in expenditures for armament, equipment and electronic equipment. There is also a reduction in ammunition.
What was the first one?
Armament, electronics and ammunition.

Well, so far as armament equipment is concerned, the programs have been continuing programs. They are broken down and the first is guns, mountings and weather-shields. There were $2,328,000 spent in 1960-61 and this year there will be $1,100,000. The thing is that it was a continuing program and this is the amount that is estimated will be required to complete the program this year. There was the Sidewinder missile and facilities in 1960-61, and there are none for this year. Torpedoes and equipment, anti-submarine mortars, mines, et cetera, and there is to be more spent for those this year than last, $1,138,500. Then, there

is weapons control systems and facilities, $771,000 this year as against $1,678,000 last year. Again, this was a continuing program and less is required for it. Freight charges, customs, excise and so forth amounts to $90,500 this year as compared with $130,000 last year.
The next item was electronics. There are reductions in several places here but the biggest one is in radio communication equipment. Last year we spent $3,902,000 and this year it will be $1,935,000. There will be a somewhat smaller amount spent on Sonar equipment, about half as much, $845,000 as against $1,498,000, and for electronic equipment, power supply, navigational and internal communication equipment.
I wonder if the minister would give us a recapitulation of the new equipment supplied to the brigade group in the last 12 or 24 months?
We are on the navy at the present time, Mr. Chairman. This item does not come up until we get to the army.

Item agreed to.
Canadian Army-
237.	Operation and maintenance, $359,572,000.
I wonder if the minister would now give us the recapitulation of the new equipment supplied to the brigade group?

There is quite a long list, but I will keep on reading as long as the committee can bear with it. The list occupies two and one half of these big pages. Does the hon. member want all the items read out?
Perhaps the minister could just give us the principal ones at the start.

These are all listed as major items which have been received in stock since the second world war. There is the FN rifle and the automatic FN rifle to replace the 303 Bren gun. There is a submachine gun, 9 millimetre; there is a 106 millimetre recoilless and anti-tank rifle and ammunition; there is the 3.2 inch Heller anti-tank rocket launcher and ammunition; there is the S.S. 10 anti-tank missile for training purposes; medium mortars, 81 millimetres, and ammunition; field artillery, 105 millimetre howitzers and ammunition; surface to surface launchers and training ammunition for them; training missiles for the Honest John. There is communication equipment, including the United Kingdom family of very high frequency sets for the brigade group in Europe. There is the five-mile V.H.F. radio sets; the C-42 wireless sets to replace the No. 19. There are the cargo trailers in the one quarter ton-three quarters ton range. Then, there is the "Rat, a Canadian developed vehicle, the Ferret scout cars, standard

military pattern vehicles in the one quarter, three quarter and 2J-ton range. Partial requirements for a 5-ton cargo vehicle. There is the medium gun tank, Centurion, mark V; parachute stores and equipment; light aircraft-the L-19 for air op. flights; Bell helicopters and presently the Hiller helicopter which is now being secured, as well as two Sikorsky H-5 helicopters.
You have ammunition of various kinds. There are kits for up-gunning the Centurion tanks from 20 pounders to 105 millimetres to increase their hitting power, and associated ammunition; short range surveillance radar and counter mortar radar. Special equipment vehicle kits of all kinds; water tanks, light metal workshops, small arms repair and so on; vehicle navigational aids. Then, there is the armoured track vehicle the Bobcat which we have ordered; light reconnaissance helicopters; communications and engineering equipment of various kinds; the United Kingdom heavy ferry and heavy assault floating bridge. Then, there are various machine guns, general purpose machine guns and ammunition.
Those items are the ones that are now forecast for delivery, which have been ordered and so forth. I see these are marked "secret", so I will not go on with them. These are some of the major items of equipment which have been secured.
I thank the minister for the list. He went back quite far when he went back to world war II.
I said since world war II.
Am I wrong in saying back to world war II? Is that different from since world war II?
Yes; I think the implication was that it included some world war II equipment.
I am sure it does include some. Did I hear the minister correctly when he said that some of the 762 millimetre rocket launchers are already installed in Europe?

No, none of them is installed in Europe as I indicated in the house when I made the announcement in connection with this matter. I think we anticipate it will be along towards the end of the year before they will be sent to Europe.

The minister anticipates that some will be installed this year. I thought I heard him refer to some practice rounds or something. I refer to the previous minister's remarks as found at page 7556 of 1960 Hansard where he states as follows:
While there are no funds allocated in this year's estimates, it has also been announced that the Canadian army is to procure the Honest John
Supply-National Defence launcher and associated surface-to-surface missile, the 762 mm. rocket. This weapon, too, has a nuclear capability.
Then before the defence estimates committee last year at page 330:
We are acquiring the Honest John which is a ground to ground weapon and which, when we receive it, will be capable of firing a nuclear warhead. When we receive it next year-
That would be this year.
-it will be capable of doing so. We are training some of our staff and some of our personnel in the uses of that weapon now. The problem in respect of storage and so forth should be solved before we receive this weapon.
My question is this. Does the minister still expect to receive them before the end of this year? If so, will the problem of storage and so forth with respect to nuclear weapons have been solved by that time?

We have received the deliveries of these Honest John launchers. We have formed a battery to operate them-and it will be sent to Europe. We have it under training at the present time. We have secured some practice rockets for practice firing with the rocket launcher. I think that is the situation. As I said, towards the end of this year or early next year we shall have a battery in shape to send over to the brigade in Europe.

I wonder whether the minister can say whether, as reported in the congressional subcommittee on defence expenditures, the 762 mm. rocket launcher is not accurate enough to use with high explosive shells?

This is the first I have heard of anything along that line. I am informed that this statement is not correct and that the United States are developing a conventional warhead to use with this rocket launcher.

One item in the blue book indicated that one of the duties of the Canadian army was the ground defence of the Canada-United States region. Assuming an all-out nuclear war, just exactly what is included in this term, "ground defence of the Canada-United States region"? What plans are foreseen for the Canadian army in this particular situation? It would seem to me that it is rather unbelievable that the U.S.S.R. expects to invade Canada from the Arctic in this kind of war that I am assuming. I should like an explanation of this particular item, if the minister does not mind.

There is always the possibility of airborne landings in order to knock out particular installations, particularly some of the radar installations and things of that

Supply-National Defence sort, in order really to prepare the way perhaps for a large bomber attack. There is also always the possibility of a considerable amount of sabotage and things along that line. You therefore must have troops in order to guard against these possibilities. Some of our troops are trained for airborne operations, as parachutists and as airborne troops.

That statement is very interesting but I find it rather hard to believe that they would actually invade with paratroopers before they attacked the country with missiles. It just does not seem to hold water strategically. I find it to be part of this unreality which the hon. member for Trinity was talking about this afternoon. I just cannot see this as a rational phase of the program at all, in terms of the kind of war we seem to be hearing about.

As I explained to the hon. member, the possibility of attempting to seize certain installations and thus to disrupt the general defences of the continent is something which is quite likely to be attempted. If there were no defence against it and if there were no troops that were able to counter it, it is something that would then probably happen.

The minister mentioned that the brigade group was being supplied with some of the automatic FN rifles. I recently heard a report that these rifles are being withdrawn by virtue of the fact that an error has been made by Canadian Arsenals and in order that they may have the breech blocks modified. I wonder whether the minister can make any statement with respect to the alleged cost of more than $1 million in withdrawing these rifles in order to have modifications made.

The situation is that a modification is being made to the FN rifles owing to the fact that the ammunition made in some of the NATO countries and which we may have to use has a primer which does not work properly as it is pierced to too great an extent by the Canadian FN rifle. With the ammunition made in Canada there has been no difficulty whatever. However, with a very occasional round of ammunition from some of the other NATO countries there has been difficulty in that there has been a bit of a blow-back. Nobody has ever been seriously injured by this blow-back but there is the possibility that a man might lose an eye if this happened. Consequently we are modifying all these rifles in order to ensure that any country's ammunition of this calibre can be safely fired in it.

Can the minister assure the committee that the modifications now required are not the result of certain modifications made at Canadian Arsenals to the Belgian designed rifle, and were not made by any of the other NATO countries which accepted and took into use this rifle?

As far as I recall the matter, although I have not been able to get the specific information here, the Canadian manufactured rifles were made with a slightly heavier barrel in order to give a longer life and a longer range. As I say, the Canadian ammunition has never caused any trouble whatever but some of the European ammunition very occasionally has resulted in a bit of blow-back, as I stated.
Can the minister inform the committee what the estimated cost per rifle is for the modification?

I cannot break down what the cost is for this particular modification. Some other modifications are being made at the same time that the rifles are going in for this particular modification. They are really what you might call normal improvements and also include the replacement of damaged or worn out parts and a general clean-up of the weapon. The cost for the whole thing will run to approximately $16 per rifle.

I have one other question, Is it correct that the army has directed that the FN rifle be used with a weaker cartridge than that originally designed for it because of the fact that there is a gas leak around the breech block?

No, Mr. Chairman. As I indicated before, we have restricted the use of certain lots of ammunition which did not prove to work completely in all cases, in order to ensure there would be no danger to any of the personnel using it through blow-back.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to continue the questioning on the FN rifle. Could the minister please tell the committee when the last competition for the Hamilton Galt trophy took place, and how the scores compared since the Lee-Enfield rifle has been out of use during the last few years?
I have not that information here. I will have to send for it and give it to the hon. member later.

Mr. Chairman, on Thursday, September 7, the Prime Minister told us that the government, after consultation with allied governments in NATO, has come to the conclusion that certain measures

should be taken to strengthen Canada's preparedness for defence both at home and overseas.
I refer to a booklet called "The Record Speaks". On the cover there is this passage:
The government of Prime Minister John Diefen-baker has accomplished more for the ordinary man- and woman of Canada than any government in our history.
There is a very appealing chapter entitled "National Defence and Defence Production" over the signature of Hon. George Pearkes, former minister of national defence. The first sentence reads as follows:
Despite increased costs for new equipment in a new age, Canada is spending less dollars on defence.
In 1960-1961 defence expenditures are down 10 per cent from 1956-1957, the last year under the Liberals.
I do not wish to introduce a partisan note in this debate-
But you are going to anyway.

-but I am concerned about what appears to be a drop of approximately $145 million on over-all defence expenditures, if I read the estimates correctly, from the year 1956-57 to which Hon. George Pearkes referred. In particular I am interested in, not the equipment of the army but the personnel of the army.
There is one thing in which I think this committee is very interested. That is the Canadian services colleges. I am referring to an article written in the Royal Military College review of 1959 by the director of studies, Colonel W. R. Sawyer, who writes as follows:
When the college was reopened after the war, strong emphasis was put on the principle that the level of instruction should be equal to that of the universities. The minister of national defence, the Hon. Brooke Claxton, stressed this in his address at the official opening ceremonies on September 20, 1948:
Colonel Sawyer goes on to say in his article:
We have steadily held to the view that these qualities can be developed best by study of the three traditional branches of learning-the humanities, the social sciences, the physical sciences.
I think there is reference to the fact that the Royal Military College is the only military institution in the commonwealth which is degree-conferring. I have occasion from time to time to be in Kingston at a sister institution and I can speak most enthusiastically about what we see and hear of Royal Military College.
I think great heart has been given to people who care about our military affairs by the strong leadership in that school and the level of teaching that has prevailed. I know that the Hon. Ralph Campney has been extremely interested in the Royal Military College and
Supply-National Defence I know that General Pearkes maintains a close interest. We rejoice in the appointment of Brigadier W. A. B. Anderson, with his superlative background, the most honoured graduate of his year in R.M.C., a graduate of Queen's University with service in the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery. He has graduate training from nearly every important staff college in the world and has given our institution great dignity and strength.
We know, too, that Colonel Sawyer, with his almost 100 highly qualified teachers, nearly 40 of doctorate level, has done a great deal to lift military training in this country to an extent to which we are certainly proud. I have studied with some care the calendar offered by Royal Military College and it is amazing to see the strength of departments that are not really directly military in their nature.
Personally, I concur very much in the emphasis stressed by Colonel Sawyer of elevating Royal Military College and the sister colleges to the type of institutions that will make our cadets great service officers in due course by staffing R.M.C. with the best, most highly qualified people possible.
It seems to me that more than ever before the army needs flexibility, a fresh approach and the type of personnel who will be capable of dealing skilfully and well with many new situations, problems and people. I know how interested the minister is in these service colleges. I wish to ask him whether perhaps there has been too great a decrease in salary levels of the college. I may be misreading the estimates, but in referring to page 331 and looking at the items from director of studies down to instructor, class 1, I have formed the impression that there is approximately $100,000 less being paid in 1961-62 than there was the previous year. I know it was with great difficulty that this faculty was gathered together in Royal Military College in the first instance.
One of the persons very interested in R.M.C.'s growth and strength was W. A. Mackintosh, then principal of Queen's University. I believe he was at one time a member of the Canadian services colleges advisory board. We know that in other educational institutions of that level, generally speaking our teaching salaries are appreciating rather considerably. I think there are very few universities in Canada where in 1961-62 the salary level will be less than that of 1960-61. I am not informed or in a position to be critical, but I ask the minister whether this kind of reduction is justified.
I also wish to ask whether in our great national need for more troops, we are now bringing along enough graduates out of these schools. It is obvious that we have gathered

Supply-National Defence together an extremely able staff, gentlemen who could very easily be absorbed by other universities in Canada and the United States. As we look over the qualifications of these men we see that almost every lecturer has qualifications from several universities. I should think they would be highly mobile personnel and easily lost.
I wonder whether the minister would be kind enough to indicate what is developing at Royal Military College. I can say, from what we can see from where I live, close to Kingston, that we are extremely proud of this school. R.M.C., we think, has never stood so high, and I am one who has been in a position to form an exceptionally high opinion of R.M.C. graduates of the past.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the hon. member for his remarks about Brigadier Anderson and Colonel Sawyer. Brigadier Anderson was a good friend of mine whom I saw a good deal of during the war and since. Also, I am glad to note his interest in the Royal Military College. As far as the salaries of the professors are concerned, they have gone up, not down. I think that is clearly indicated in the details of services in the blue book at page 331. Hon. members will see that the director is getting $14,500 as against $12,000 last year. Fourteen professors are getting $168,000 as against $136,000-their salaries have gone up considerably. This has been necessary, as the hon. member pointed out, in order to retain the services of university professors of a high calibre since those men are in short supply at the present time and we at the military colleges are, of course, in competition with the universities and colleges throughout the continent. Hon. members will see that there are 23 lecturers provision for whom amounts to $136,000 this year compared with $129,000 last year. There are 14 instructors and they are receiving $73,000 this year compared with $67,000 last year. I think that is typical. The salaries have gone up and, as I say, this is necessary in order to retain the staff.
I am glad to say we have an excellent staff not only at the Royal Military College but also at the College Militaire Royale and at Royal Roads. We have on our staffs some extremely outstanding men in their particular lines. We are fortunate indeed that in many instances these men remain with us, although they have been offered higher salaries in other institutions, because they happen to like the type of work they are doing and, in particular, the type of young men with whom they are dealing, in addition to certain facilities for research which are given to them and which they might not have available in other places. As a
[Mr. Matheson.l
result we have been able to retain our staff in spite of the fact that the salaries they receive are not as high as those they have been offered in other places.

In respect to the program to replace the 20 pounders on Centurion tanks with 105 millimetre guns, I wonder if the minister would tell us what the projected program is. According to the white book of 1960, improvements to the fire power of the Centurion tanks are estimated to cost $6 million for which $482,000 is being provided in 1961-62. Then in 1962, according to the blue book:
The army major equipment program includes provision for improvements to the fire power of the Centurion tank. The estimated cost of this program is $6 million of which the estimated expenditure in 1961-62 is $587,000.
I should like the minister to tell the committee how many of the tanks overseas have been reconverted to date, and what the projected program is for the balance.

I am not in a position to say how many tanks have been converted up to the present time. This work is being carried on at the discretion of the brigade commanders so that he will not have very many tanks out of action at any one time. However, the whole program will be completed at the end of this year.

That is an amazing statement. The minister says the whole program is to be completed by the end of this year. How can that be accomplished when we are being asked to fund only about one sixth of the total, including last year's estimate? It will require 12 years to complete the program on the basis of the amount funded here.
The answer is that that includes the ammunition which will be secured in the future.
The $6 million figure includes the ammunition?
Yes.
Could the minister tell the committee what proportion of the $6 million is required for the installation of the guns and what proportion is being spent on ammunition? I must say this seems unusual.
I am sorry but we have not got that information here. We shall get it. It will come down shortly and I will give it to the hon. member.

I am sure all of us will be glad to see that the Bobcat light tracked vehicle is being produced in Canada. Could the minister indicate how many have already

been produced and how many foreign governments, if any, have bought them? Could he also tell us what the approximate cost per Bobcat will be, including development costs.

There were four of these vehicles, hand made, one might say, as a means of developing the vehicle and experimenting with it. There are 20 being produced on a production line at the present time to discover whether there are any difficulties in turning these vehicles out in quantity and, if so, to correct those difficulties. As soon as those 20 have been produced a further 480 will be secured.

Have any foreign governments signed contracts to accept the Bobcat? I understand there is a German carrier of the same type-if it is not of the same type perhaps the minister will tell us. But would the cost of producing that vehicle be comparable to the cost of producing ours?

A considerable number of countries have shown some interest in this vehicle but we have received no definite orders as yet. I should like to point out that a number of other personnel carriers, such as the German carrier to which the hon. member referred, are not amphibious vehicles such as this one is. They have no swimming ability, and as a carrier which can cross all types of country and which is, in addition, amphibious, we think this is the best one being developed. As a result we have hopes we shall be able to sell this vehicle to other countries.
Could the minister tell us how many of the Bobcats are now with the brigades in Europe?
That question indicates the naivete or the childishness of the hon. member. He has just heard me say that four handmade models have been produced and that 20 more are in production.

It is not childish. I was just reading the blue book and I find in it this statement:
A production run of 20 models of the Bobcat light armoured tractor carrier will be commenced in 1961-62.
What I want the minister to tell the committee is where the associate minister got the wild statement he made in this house when he told us that 500 Bobcats were on order.

When I made the announcement in connection with the Bobcat some considerable time ago I said that we were definitely securing 500 of these vehicles. I
Supply-National Defence explained that 20 of them were being produced as rapidly as they could be produced as a production line run and that as soon as they came through successfully the other 480 would immediately be secured.
On a question of privilege, may I say that if the hon. member would just read Hansard he would see that what I said last night was exactly what the Minister of National Defence has just said.

I assume it is too early to know what the production cost of the Bobcat, including development costs, will be. Perhaps I can reserve that question for later on.
There is one question about which I am particularly concerned and it relates to the fact that the army controls the warning system. Last Friday I asked the minister a question with reference to the fact that this had been reported as being inadequate as long ago as last January but nothing had been done about it. Second, it had been stated that the system was aimed for outside audibility but the minister suggested that such a statement had not been made.
I want to say it had been made in front of officials who I am sure are very good witnesses who said that that was the situation.
Last Tuesday two officers arrived from Picton. They came to Peterborough to carry out tests, the tests which were predicted by the Minister of National Defence. I am very happy to see that his department has gone on with this matter with the speed with which it has shown. When those two officers arrived they informed the officials in Peterborough that they were testing for outside audibility.
This afternoon the minister complained that the people on this side of the house had not been reading his speeches. It appears to me that some of the people in his own department have not been reading his speeches because they have been testing for outside audibility. When they were told what the minister had said in the house last Friday they said they had heard nothing about this. They got in touch with Ottawa and were told that no new orders had been issued and therefore they are now testing the sirens once again for outside audibility.
I wish this matter could be cleared up because it is of extreme concern. I am sure the minister realizes this because he had been made contact with in the area that I represent.

I said nothing about testing for inside audibility. What I did say was that the degree to which those sirens could be heard inside buildings depended on the type of construction of the building. For example, I used a bank vault down in the basement

Supply-National Defence of a building where you would not hear the siren at all. I used this as an extreme example.
The only way in which you can test and get a test which will be valid in Peterborough and in various parts of Peterborough or anywhere else is on outside audibility. Because, if you start testing on this structure, that structure and the other structure, you are going to get a little different result in each one, depending on the type of construction and the particular room in the building in which you carry on the test and, of course, how much the particular building happens to be shielded by other buildings from the site of the siren. The only way in which you get any sort of test which is standard or uniform is on outside audibility.

Can the minister tell the committee what are the Canadian army commitments at the present time to the United Nations or any other form of international service, and can he give us some details in regard to this service? I know figures were given some time ago but I was wondering what the figures are now.
My officials will turn up the exact figures.

While this is being done perhaps I might ask another question related to my previous one. To what extent are those Canadian contingents of United Nations forces or other international services maintained by Canadian air transport?

Well, as far as the location of the force is concerned, first there is the United Nations emergency force in the Suez. It consists of a total establishment of Canadian army units of 69 officers and 789 other ranks, for a total of 858 all ranks. There is a reconnaissance squadron in that, Lord Strathcona's Horse; a signal squadron, a transport company, and an infantry workshop as the main units making up that particular force.
The R.C.A.F. has 14 officers and 74 other ranks with that force, so that the total of all ranks in the force is 941.
In the Congo the army has 41 officers and 230 other ranks; the air force has six officers and two other ranks, making a total of 279.
In India and Pakistan in that truce observer role the army has eight officers. In Indochina the navy has two officers; the army has 28 officers and 24 other ranks; the R.C.A.F. has two officers, making a total of 56 all ranks.
In the United Nations truce teams in the Middle East there are 17 army officers. In other countries there are one naval officer

and seven army officers; three army other ranks; three R.C.A.F. officers; three other ranks; making a total of 17.
I am sorry, I have forgotten what the second question was.
To what extent are these Canadian forces maintained by Canadian transport?

There are five scheduled North Star flights per month from Trenton, Ontario, via Langar, England and Pisa, Italy to El Arish and return.
As far as the Suez forces are concerned, the total number of flights in support of those forces in the year ended September 30, 1960 was 66, or a total of 788,000 odd miles flown.
I do not suppose the hon. member wants the number of passengers and so forth. As far as the Congo is concerned, there are 15 R.C.A.F. personnel on the strength of the United Nations force there. That was as of June 1. There are two scheduled North Star flights per week to the Congo from Langar via Pisa, Italy to Leopoldville and return, and there are two scheduled North Star flights per month from Trenton, Ontario, down to the Congo and return.

Perhaps I may be permitted to pay my own humble tribute to the magnificent work that these men are doing on behalf of peace and for their country. I know we are all very grateful for the service they have rendered and are continuing to render under particularly difficult circumstances in the Congo at the present time.
I noticed from what the minister has said that the signals personnel in the Congo have been reduced somewhat, because in the blue book of May reference is made to the army signal unit comprising 280 all ranks. I think the figures the minister gave were a little less than that. May I ask the minister whether the transfer, if you would like to call it that, of those Canadian signallers to the Congo, when it took place, had any effect on the work of the Canadian army signals in Canada? Has the work of training the signallers been carried on in the normal way notwithstanding the transfer of so many of the signals unit to the Congo.

Well, the training at the signals school has been expanded considerably because of the number of signallers employed in the Congo and in the Suez, in order to increase the supply of signallers.
I should like to thank the Leader of the Opposition for the tribute he has paid to the men whom we have serving in those places in the cause of peace and particularly those in the Congo, who, as he has stated, have had an

extremely difficult time, particularly in certain spots. I know that the whole Canadian people are grateful to them for the job they have done there.
As to the difference in the numbers, originally there was a considerable contingent of Canadian officers and some other ranks on the United Nations headquarters staff in the Congo. That has gradually been cut down as other nations have made contributions to the United Nations headquarters staff and also there has been a redistribution of the signal personnel at various points in the Congo. The Leader of the Opposition will perhaps remember that fighting took place at Matadi, the seaport for Leopoldville, and that our signal detachment was under fire for some time. It was then withdrawn to Leopoldville and it has not been sent back because United Nations troops were not sent back to maintain the position there. As a result of some of these shifts of this kind, the number now is not as great as it was when the booklet was put out.

Do we pay the full expenses of all our contingents in these United Nations forces? I assume that we do and, if we do, do we get credit for that expenditure against the assessments which are levied by the United Nations to cover the expenses of United Nations activities, a credit which we will perhaps never be able to realize in cash?

Theoretically the way the matter is supposed to work so far as costs are concerned is that we pay the normal costs, pay and allowances, of our personnel who are there. The United Nations is supposed to pay the extra costs for accommodation and so forth. We bill them for these extra costs. In the case of the Suez force, it has been on a definite basis and these bills have been paid. As far as the Congo is concerned, the same system is supposed to work but there has never been any final determination of what the United Nations would pay and therefore the matter is still in abeyance.

Would the minister comment on this statement by the former minister as found on page 462 of the proceedings of the defence estimates committee? I quote:
You asked what weapons if any are replacing any of the Browning machine guns used by the Canadian army. It is planned to replace the .30 calibre Browning in due course by a machine gun of the 7.62 millimetre NATO standardized calibre. Preliminary studies are being carried out on some new machine guns which might meet the requirements. Consideration is being given to the replacement of the .5 calibre Browning in due course by the new heavy machine gun. As yet, no decision on the type of gun to adopt has been made, but various guns are being considered.
Can the minister indicate if either of these decisions has yet been made?
Supply-National Defence
No, Mr. Chairman, there has been no final decision taken on that particular matter yet.
Would the minister advise the committee as to how many of the new C-42 wireless sets have been delivered to the brigade group in Europe?

All units of the brigade in Europe are fully equipped now with this new wireless set as are the regular army units in Canada. I think some of them have also been delviered to militia units. If not, I think some will be delivered fairly soon for national survival purposes.
Would the minister indicate whether he has any plans to equip the Canadian army with light aircraft, more specifically of Otter, Beaver or Caribou class?

No, there are no definite plans. Various proposals along this line have been made and studied. No decision has been made to equip the Canadian army with any aircraft of this type. There is quite a considerable question involved. The particular proposition was, of course, to equip the brigade in Europe, but for a formation of that size it is a matter of considerable doubt whether it is a practical proposition to give it its own little air force, you might say. There is quite a body of opinion that this is not a practical way to solve the problem of the need for air transportability and for air transport. As far as Canada is concerned, of course, air transport requirements can be met by the R.C.A.F.

I am sure the minister would admit that the contrary opinion is held in some quarters. Would he also indicate whether he plans to obtain any heavy helicopters for the brigade group to be used for moving personnel and equipment?

I have had a considerable number of these plans and propositions put before me and have given them a good deal of study, both with respect to aircraft of the Otter or Beaver type and also heavy helicopters. I think there is a need for a certain number of heavy helicopters and I hope to be able to work out something definite in that regard in the very near future.
Would the minister advise the committee how many consultant architects and engineers were used in the last fiscal year and what was the total cost?

While that is being looked up, I might reply to a question that was asked about the Hamilton Galt trophy competition. I have the information here for the last three years only. In 1958 the trophy

Supply-National Defence was won by the second regiment, R.H.C., in 1959 it was won by the first Royal 22nd regiment and in 1960 it was won by the first P.P.C.L.I. regiment. The competition is between all regular infantry battalions and includes the scoring of all personnel of the battalion. A steady improvement in firing skill of the battalions as a whole has been experienced. The director of infantry is still searching for statistics on the actual results.

I thank the minister very much for that information. Could he tell us whether the scores indicated an improvement as a result of the use of the new rifle compared with the Lee-Enfield or whether the improvement resulted from greater accuracy in firing rather than the use of the FN rifle?

We have the percentage scores for these three years and they show an increase from 127 to 132 to 141. They do not show which rifles were being used which I think was the point the hon. member was getting at. I will have to send for that information. The last question was in connection with the number of architects and consultants. The amount of money which was budgeted for consultants fees in 1960-61 was $900,000 and in 1961-62 $500,000 or a decrease of $400,000. I have not got the actual number.
Is the minister giving the figures for those on the staff of national defence headquarters?
These are consultants' fees.
Consultants to the department?
Yes.

In his list of equipment for the brigade group the minister mentioned the S.S. anti-tank missile for training. Would he indicate his intentions with regard to an operational anti-tank missile for the brigade group?

Well, no final decision has been made as to what type of missile of this kind will finally be adopted as our regular equipment. We have been using the French wire-guided weapon, the S.S.-10 for practice purposes and for training. However, we have been evaluating other weapons of the same type and, as I say, no final decision has yet been made as to which one we will eventually adopt.

If the minister examines the box score he will see the basis for our suggestion that the brigade group is not as adequately equipped as it might be. We admit quite freely that some of these programs are


coming along in more or less orderly fashion. We strongly suspect, however, that some of them have been held back for budgetary reasons. This is the reason we charge that the brigade group has been starved for equipment at the same time rather heavy expenditures have been made for other equipment which, in our opinion, is not nearly so essential.
I might give a sort of running box score: No Honest John rocket launchers in Europe, and no decision as to how they will be equipped when they get there; the FN rifle being re-constructed; Centurion tanks are being re-equipped and so far we do not know how many. The ammuniton has not all been ordered, as yet. The Bobcat is not yet ready to go into production, let alone be delivered to the brigade group. The C-42 wireless set is apparently fully installed and in use. There are no light aircraft and the minister is not yet convinced they are a requirement. I would suggest he visit some of the installations of other armies that are equipped with light aircraft to see their capabilities and then, on that basis, perhaps he would be impressed with the advisability of providing some light transport companies for the brigade group. There are no heavy helicopters yet available or on order, although the minister is giving this some consideration. Finally, there is no final decision with respect to an anti-tank missile.
This box score, Mr. Chairman, is the basis for the charge we have made, and we believe the facts substantiate the position we have taken. I wonder if the minister would give the committee a list of the equipment which has been issued to the militia for national survival operations?

My officials will turn up that list, and while that is being done I should like to say that the Centurion tank, of course, is a heavy British post-war tank and an exceptionally good one. The up-gunning of it has been proceeding quite satisfactorily and, as I said will be finished by the end of the year. With 20-pounder guns, it is still a very effective tank.
In so far as some of the other criticisms are concerned and this so-called list the hon. member has read, I would ask him to compare that list with the partial list of just some of the major equipment to which I referred a while ago as being supplied not only to the brigade in Europe but also to the regular army troops in Canada and, in some cases, to the militia. It is very easy to pick out four or five items and say that these are not yet complete. The basic fact is, however, that we have, by and large, completely reequipped the brigade in Europe and the other army units since the second world war with vehicles, weapons and what-not. This has

been a very considerable undertaking. So far as the anti-tank wire missile is concerned, to which reference was made, there are probably a half a dozen of those which have been produced in various countries. It takes a considerable length of time to evaluate all these. We also hope there will be some standardization so far as the NATO countries are concerned in putting them into their armies. In the meantime, as I say, we are using the French type.
There is a list here of the major items of survival equipment which have been issued to both the Canadian regular army and to the militia units. There are rescue kits on an operational scale for the two types of units, regular and militia. There is radiac equipment for the re-entry forces and fall-out reporting posts. There is a limited quantity of gamma survey meters, and the models of low range survey meters are the CDV-710 contamination meter and the CDV-700 in quantities sufficient to permit training and limited operations; approximately 30 per cent of the requirement of tactical dosimeters and dosimeters chargers; over 50 per cent of the requirement of personal dosimeters and approximately 40 per cent of the requirements of readers for these dosimeters; full requirements for training kits and training devices; communications equipment, including the United Kingdom C-42 wireless set, which is a 15-mile very high frequency set.
The major items of equipment which are on order and of which we hope to get deliveries fairly rapidly and regularly are the additional requirements of radiac equipment of various kinds and these dosimeter chargers for them; remote reading gamma survey meters for fall-out reporting posts; nuclear burst position indicators; communication equipment including telephone cable and public address sets, miscellaneous radio sets; portable heaters; decontamination apparatus; mobile laundry equipment; mobile bath equipment; gasoline driven saws; centrifugal pumps; torch cutting equipment; water purification equipment; various generating and lighting sets; some winter footwear; food cooking equipment; various items of crowd control equipment.
Planned for procurement are additional radiac equipment above what is already ordered; decontamination vacuum cleaners, collapsible tanks for water storage and additional lighting equipment. As I indicated last week, we have taken a considerable number of measures to speed up the securing of a considerable quantity of equipment needed for national survival purposes. We are securing all of this just as rapidly as it can be produced for us.
Supply-National Defence

I am very pleased to learn of' this speed-up. I understand, indirectly, that to a large extent it results from the attention drawn to the need for it last year when the estimates were before the committee. At the same time, I know the minister would not wish to take credit for all the reequipment which has been given the brigade group over the years, most of which was ordered away back and then subsequently delivered to the brigade group long before the minister had any responsibility for the provision of equipment.
I wonder if the minister would give the number of resignations from the militia for the years 1959, 1960 and 1961 respectively and perhaps the rate of enlistments for the same periods?

Well, I would have to get the number of withdrawals from the militia. I think perhaps we could get the information best by giving the strengths at various times. The strengths going back to, we will say, March 31, 1958-this is the total strength, officers and other ranks-41,000. I will leave off the odd hundreds. December 31, 1958, 41,400.
March, 1959, 40,900; December, 1959, 40,700; March, 1960, 40,000; October 31, 41,000; December 31, 42,600; March 31, 1961, 43,200; June 30, 1961, 44,000. It will therefore be seen that during that period there has been a gradual increase of upwards of 4,000 in the numbers. We will try to get the number of the people who enlisted and the number who withdrew for the past year. I think that was what was asked for.
I should like to have the rate of enlistment or the turnover in that period if you have it handy.	.
No. We have not it at hand but we will get it. It may take some time to get it.

I wonder whether the minister would bring us up to date in relation to Maple Leaf services being supplied to the armed personnel overseas? Has he received any complaints recently, particularly with respect to the range of goods being carried and the fact that allegedly there is not a sufficient range of Canadian products?

There are, of course, complaints. There are always complaints over the operations of anything along these lines. The complaints are chiefly of two kinds. One is on the part of troops who have newly gone over to Germany. There are complaints that there is not the same variety of goods as that to which they have been accustomed at home. I think this situation can readily be understood. It is just not possible to carry

Supply-National Defence the great variety of goods, such as canned goods and so on, of all kinds which you find in a supermarket here in Canada.
The other type of complaint that I have received is with regard to the prices in the Maple Leaf services. This has been based chiefly on a belief-which is some cases is correct and in some cases is quite wrong- that the United States PX's are selling the same goods more cheaply. If you examine into this matter you find that some goods are certainly sold more cheaply in United States PX's. However, on the other hand certain goods are sold more cheaply in the Canadian Maple Leaf stores. Of course you never hear any complaint about that matter. It is taken for granted. But if there is found an item the price of which is cheaper in the United States PX's you get the complaint that it should be sold at that price in the Canadian Maple Leaf services. Of course, one of the reasons that there is a difference in prices is that the United States PX's are securing goods in very much greater quantities than we are and on a direct supply line, and thus their costs of acquisition and their transportation costs in the case of many items are less than ours. In the case of certain other items, as a matter of fact, as I say we can produce at a better price. This is the general situation with regard to complaints with respect to Maple Leaf services. However, I have never received very serious complaints in this regard.

I wish to read a rather incredible letter addressed to the Hon. Lester B. Pearson, House of Commons, Ottawa, Ontario or a copy of it. It reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am a retired Canadian army officer and veteran of world war II. I take the liberty of addressing this letter to you in order to place at your disposal certain facts gained from personal experience concerning Canadian complicity in the recent military action against Cuba organized by the government of the United States. It is my present conviction that the matter must be thoroughly exposed in order that proper measures be taken to prevent our further entanglement in the disastrous consequences of American policy toward Cuba.
Six months ago I was hired by the C.I.A. as an instructor and detailed to a camp where anti-Castro units were trained in landing operations. Through my close association with C.I.A. officials and participation in the camp activities, I was in a position to obtain some knowledge of the extent of Canadian involvement, as the following list of particulars will indicate:
1.	From information secured through C.I.A. channels, it is clear to me that Messrs. Diefenbaker and Harkness had full knowledge of, and indeed encouraged, the recruitment of Canadian citizens on Canadian soil by the C.I.A. for service in units being prepared for the invasion of Cuba. The same evidence indicates that R.C.M.P. officials co-operated with the C.I.A. in this activity.
2.	My estimate is that from 200 to 300 Canadians were recruited. In the main they were unemployed

persons and ex-servicemen. Practically all of them joined up because of the high rate of pay.
3.	In addition, several regular army officers took part in the training and actual landing operations in Cuba. Presumably their participation was approved by their superiors.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. Will the hon. member who is reading this document kindly identify its source?
I will give it later.
I should like him to identify it now, Mr. Chairman.
The initials of the gentleman are "D. J. S." I wish to finish reading it.
What is his name?
It is just initialled.
It is an anonymous letter.
If it is an anonymous letter, it is out of order to read it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Is the hon. member adopting it?
No. Some rather unusual statements are given here. He is willing to come forward. I will carry on and paraphrase it.
Name him.
He goes on to say this-
Mr. Chairman, will you kindly rule on that point of order.

I was
wondering whether the hon. member who was reading the letter was giving me his own abbreviated version of the person who signed the letter or is the letter actually signed by initials as indicated?
No. It is initialed but not signed. I can paraphrase the contents of it.
Just a minute, please.
While you are ruling on this important point, Mr. Chairman, I should like to make it quite clear that I did not refer the copy of this letter to the hon. gentleman.

The
ruling I had in mind is to be found in Beauchesne's fourth edition, paragraph 158, subsection 3, page 134, which states:
(3) An unsigned letter should not be read in the house. On the 16th May 1928, a member stated during debate that a letter which he had been quoting was not signed. The Speaker said: "Such a letter should not be read into Hansard.', all letters when read must be signed and they become part of the documents of the house".

I think the point is well taken by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, in view of the apparent length of the letter and also in view of the fact that it is for all practical purposes an anonymous letter. I would suggest that a free paraphrasing of it would be more in order.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and I shall paraphrase it. I raise the matter because he sent this letter to the Leader of the Opposition and to five members of parliament. He goes on to say this.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Does the hon. member take these remarks as his own as well as paraphrasing the letter? Is he taking responsibility for them?
I am not obliged to take responsibility for paraphrasing information.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Oh, yes, you are obliged to take responsibility for an anonymous letter.
I am not reading the letter. I want the minister to answer this.
Disregard the rules.
He goes on to indicate that the invasion collapsed and he mentions money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The point I raise is that the hon. member is purporting to read an anonymous letter and he says, "He says". I suggest that the hon. member either accept these remarks as his own, a procedure which is in accordance with the rules of the house, or accept responsibility for them.
Mr. Chairman, I can overcome that quite easily according to the rules by saying I have been informed. That is quite correct.
No, you cannot.
Oh, no.

On the
point of order that has been raised, I would appreciate it very much if the hon. member for Peel would direct the attention of the Chair specifically to the rule which covers this particular point. In my humble opinion, if this rule does exist, it has been honoured in the breach.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, no.

I say
that from my experience, and in my opinion. I would appreciate some guidance as to the specific precedents in this matter. The point I have in mind has occurred frequently in debates and discussions in the house when in quite recent times hon. members on both sides of a particular argument have quoted
Supply-National Defence from the same editorial. Clearly hon. members on both sides of the argument cannot be assuming responsibility for the same editorial which in part seems to support both sides of the argument.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Surely that would be out of order, Mr. Chairman, because it is specifically governed by citation 157, subcitation 5. That citation is perhaps not relevant to our particular discussion, but the reading of editorials in support of argument has been frequently ruled to be out of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I would refer you, Mr. Chairman, to citation 159, subparagraph 3, which by an analogy covers this situation. The citation reads:
It has been admitted that a document which has been cited ought to be laid upon the table of the house, if it can be done without injury to the public interest. The same rule, however, cannot be held to apply to private letters or memoranda. On the 18th May, 1865, the attorney general, on being asked by Mr. Ferrard if he would lay upon the table a written statement and a letter to which he had referred on a previous day, in answering a question relative to the Leeds bankruptcy court, replied that he had made a statement to the house upon his own responsibility, and that the documents he had referred to being private, he could not lay them upon the table.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is another sentence which you did not read.

The
citation goes on to say:
-the documents he had referred to being private, he could not lay them upon the table. Lord Robert Cecil contended that the papers, having been cited, should be produced; but the Speaker declared that this rule applied to public documents only.
I think, with the lack of some immediate direction and instruction from precedents, we should proceed on a common sense basis. I think perhaps we are all of a mind in this particular instance. Without attempting to establish a precedent and-
Mr. Pallet!: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member does not accept responsibility for the statements he makes. This is fundamental to the practice of the House of Commons. It is such a fundamental rule that it is basic to the whole proceedings.

Mr. Chairman, possibly
through a lapse of memory or oversight I did transgress the rules of the house in this instance. But I will not transgress the rules of the house further. All hon. members know that I try to keep them as much as possible.
Do you, or do you not, take responsibility?

Having had certain information which now seems very unusual, I would ask the minister two or three questions which will be quite in order.

Supply-National Defence
First, does the minister know of any Canadians being recruited to serve in forces that were used in the invasion of Cuba?
Second, does the minister know of any Canadian army personnel being directly or indirectly involved in such an arrangement?
Third, in view of certain persons making these most unusual statements, and a certain person being willing to come forward to give information in detail, if requested, will the minister give any person who is willing to come forward and present evidence to the defence committee an opportunity to substantiate any statements they have made in correspondence, conversation or otherwise?

I shall be very glad to have anybody come forward with anything that he can substantiate in regard to any matter along this line. As far as any Canadian army personnel having had any part directly or indirectly in the Cuban affair is concerned, I know definitely that none of them had. In other words, these various statements in this anonymous letter are just completely false. There is the statement that the Prime Minister and I had full knowledge of the matter. I know that I had absolutely no knowledge of the matter in any way, shape or form. As I say, I also know that the Canadian army had no part of any kind in training people or anything else along that line.
I suspect this is the same man, as a matter of fact, who made an appearance on a television show here in Ottawa some months ago and claimed that he had been in Cuba and that there were a lot of other Canadian soldiers in Cuba. He claimed they were using Canadian army rifles, and things of this sort. I answered a question or two in the house on it. He said they had been using .303 rifles which were stolen from a certain camp. I have forgotten the name of the camp now, but on investigation it happened to be a camp where there never had been any .303 rifles because it had come into operation after the FN rifle had been issued. This showed a palpable falsehood in these claims.
As a matter of fact, the man claimed that he served in certain Canadian army units, and so forth. We looked the matter up and found he had enlisted, under his brother's name as I recall it, and had been discharged because he was found to be mentally unstable.
He then threatened me, and the R.C.M.P. were actually looking after him for a while. He was going to do away with me because of the answers I had given. But subsequently somehow or other, I think Liberty magazine printed an article for him and showed pictures of him, presumably in Cuba. It turned out on investigation that

these pictures had actually been taken by a Toronto photographer-his name was right on the back of the pictures-
Did he have a beard?
-and they were taken in the botanical gardens at Toronto. I suspect that the fellow who wrote this letter is the same man.
In order to clear up the matter-
Tear the letter up.
-would the minister say whether he invites this person to come forward and sustantiate his claims?

I invite him to come forward and substantiate his claims, but if it is the same man as I suspect it is, he is just looking for more notoriety and I am not going to give it to him.
The Acling Chairman (Mr. McGee): Shall vote 337 carry?

Mr. Chairman, would the minister tell the committee to what extent the standardization of arms and ground equipment has proceeded in NATO? I know that there has been a standardization of the FN rifle. I am not sure how far that has been carried out. Has there been some backsliding from that example of standardization? What else has been done to standardize arms and equipment in the NATO forces?

This is one of the areas in which there has been disappointingly slow progress. The amount of standardization outside of the FN rifle has been disappointingly little. It arises to a large extent, I think, because each country, for purposes of maintaining employment in its own industries, and so on, always attempts to manufacture everything it possibly can in that particular country. I believe this is the main reason why it is so difficult to get standardization of these different pieces of equipment.
Mr. Chairman, a question was asked about the up-gunning of the Centurions. The hon. member for Trinity asked for the division of the $6 million which was put into this program. Six hundred thousand dollars of that amount is for the modifications to the guns, and $5,400,000 is for ammunition.

I thank the minister for that information. I wonder if the hon. gentleman has the information to enable him to answer this inquiry. I shall read it for the benefit of the minister. Without going into voluminous detail, suffice it to state that under order in council, PC 1959-1/1297 northern allowance

at $87.50 per month was converted to isolation allowance and reduced to the sum of $70 per month with effect from October 1, 1959, this new allowance to be reduced by 20 per cent each year for a period of five years, to the end that at the conclusion of this period no special allowance would be paid to personnel posted to Dawson Creek, British Columbia. However, a discrepancy arises from the fact that even at the reduced rates isolation allowance is awarded only to personnel who were posted to Dawson Creek prior to the order in council coming into effect. Personnel posted subsequent to that date receive no consideration. Therefore, a number of personnel posted prior to the order in council being passed receive $52.50 per month even after the 20 per cent reduction which became effective on October 1, 1960, in addition to normal pay and allowances, while those posted subsequent to the order in council receive only normal pay and allowances. Yet all live under the same circumstances and conditions.
I wonder if the minister would indicate, if these facts are correct, whether or not he thinks this situation is equitable and whether he proposes alleviating the discrepancy in the treatment of personnel at Dawson Creek.

I am told there was a complete study made of these isolation allowances and northern allowances. In some cases they were increased as a result of this study, while in others they were decreased. In the cases where they were decreased the decrease was to be effected over a five year period. I have here a list of the areas in which allowances were decreased and of those in which they were not. I presume that if increases were paid with respect to the northwest highway system it was because a considerable number of other places such as Dawson Creek certainly cannot be looked upon any longer as isolated posts.

Does the minister not feel that even if the allowance is reduced over a five year period the amount paid should apply to all personnel at a particular station rather than be applied to some and not to others?
I must say frankly that I am not familiar with the situation, and therefore I am not in a position to answer that question.
Would the minister take it into consideration and let me know the results of his inquiries either privately or otherwise?
Yes, I shall be glad to have this looked into and if I cannot give an answer before the estimates are completed I shall write to the hon. member.

I should like to direct to the minister one or two questions about the public
Supply-National Defence relations staff. Can the minister say how many such personnel the army has engaged in this work and how that number compares proportionately with the numbers employed in the other services? This is one item of expenditure in connection with which I sometimes wonder whether the taxpayer is getting good value for his dollar. I have not had much opportunity to observe the work of the P.R.O.'s. I did have one opportunity to do so in July and I cannot say I was much impressed by what I saw on that occasion. However, I should not like to draw any conclusion from a single observation.
I should like also to find out on what basis these P.R.O. people are allocated to units and formations and whether any thought has been given to unifying the work of this department in the three services.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The public relations directorates of the services and defence research board have three main functions:
1.	To facilitate a flow of unclassified information about the armed services and defence research board to the public.
2.	To provide counsel to their respective services, to ensure that each service is, in fact, serving the public interest to the best of its abilities, in closest possible harmony with other national interests, and that its plans, policies, programs and activities are presented or performed in such a way as to reflect the high standards of the service concerned, and its dedication to public interest.
3.	To advise upon and implement planned community relations programs, particularly at overseas establishments.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo will realize that wherever there is a service establishment, particularly overseas but here in Canada also, the relationship between the civilian population and the service population can sometimes cause difficulties. One of the ways in which this situation can be helped is through good public relations. I was asked to give some figures, and I can tell the committee that at national defence headquarters there are two civilian public relations officers. The navy has a total of 14 officers and ten civilians. The army has 28 officers and 34 other ranks, besides 30 civilians, for a grand total of 92. The R.C.A.F. has a total of 29 officers, 35 other ranks and nine civilians for a total of 73. The defence research board has two civilians engaged in this work.
Could we have any indication of the total cost? Is that figure available?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: It is not broken down-

Could we not have some indication of the cost? I understand the navy has 14 officers, the army 28 officers and the
