Item agreed to.
23S. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and major equipment, $60,556,000.

I should like to take this opportunity to raise a question which is of interest to my own constituency. There was an artillery armoury there called the General Brock armoury which was purchased by the department a few years ago. An anti-aircraft battery was stationed there. In June of this year the armoury was sold on tender having been declared surplus and the artillery battery was required to move into the Victoria Avenue armoury which has been the home of a company of the Lincoln regiment. Could the minister say why the General Brock armoury was declared surplus and sold? It was about three times the physical size of the armoury which remains and it was a more modern building although not so well designed as an armoury.
Consequently, we think it will now be necessary to rent space to train individuals of the militia in the Niagara area for civil defence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we will have to send for this information for the hon. member.
The minister might now answer the question I asked earlier.
Well, I am informed that the question of a Newfoundland armoury is awaiting the decision on the ownership of the Pepperrell air base, and that some accommodation in it might be used as an armoury.

I am going to ask my annual question of the minister concerning the proposed Sudbury armoury. The hon. lady from Niagara Falls gave me the idea when she was talking about the armouries. Has any progress been made with the construction of this building? I am advised that army construction experts have been in Sudbury recently looking over the situation and have made a report to the department. A new arrangement has been suggested concerning the construction of this building. I am advised that local money can be obtained for its erection on a lease back contract. It is suggested, of course, that the department oversee the construction of this building according to army regulations, and rent it for a


period of 20 to 25 years, with the purchase of same to be arranged at that time, if they so wish.
Is there any money in this year's estimates earmarked for this purpose? Of course, you realize, that the property for this armoury has already been donated to the crown and has been lying idle there. The deed is still held by the Department of National Defence.
I am asking this question to see whether the department has taken any serious thought of the construction of this building under other arrangements.

This is one of the armoury projects with which it happens I am thoroughly familiar. I went into it in considerable detail as the hon. member knows, with the delegation from Sudbury and I am doing my best to get the things approved and get construction started as soon as possible. It is at the head of our priority list for armouries in Ontario. I have not yet managed to get it approved by treasury board, but I hope to be able to do that in the very near future.
Thank you.

I should like to direct a question to the minister with regard to the armoury situation in Fort William. It has being brought to his attention on several occasions. I wonder whether the city of Fort William is on a basis similar to that mentioned by the hon. member for Sudbury. The Department of National Defence is well aware of the need for an armoury at Fort William. Will the minister give some assurance that consideration will be given to this matter in the near future?

Mr. Chairman, I dealt with this question, I think it was the day before yesterday, as a result of the speech which the hon. member made on item No. 1. I really have nothing to add to that. I said at that time we have to make arrangements to rent a hall in Fort William to accommodate a company of the Lake Superior Scottish and this will go some small way at least to meet the need there. I regret to inform the hon. member that, unlike the situation in Sudbury, the actual building of an armoury at Fort William is not close to the top of the priority list and therefore I can give no indication as to when the construction might be started on an armoury in Fort William.

I am in a position almost similar to that of the two previous speakers, but my proposal to the minister is a little different. At the present time we have a militia unit in the city of Kimberley in British Columbia and we have endeavoured to carry on over a period of years, handling

part of the program in one building, part in another building and part in schools, keeping the equipment wherever cover is available. I have worked on this for some time. The last letter I had from the minister stated that the information had been requested from departmental officials and would be available at an early date. I sincerely hope it will not be very long before I will be able to obtain that material.
A brief has been submitted to the department concerning the necessity for the armouries at Kimberley. The submission is as follows:
That Kimberley Armouries limited erect a building acceptable to the Department of National Defence standards for a militia armoury.
That this building be rented to the Department of National Defence for a period of 20 years, at rates sufficient to write off the cost of construction and such other charges as may be deemed necessary.
That at the end of the contract period, the building be sold to the crown for a nominal sum agreed in the contract.
That the building be erected on the 2.25 acres of crown land held in the name of the Department of National Defence in the city of Kimberley.
Financial backing for Kimberley Armouries limited has been obtained from the Royal Trust Company, Vancouver, B.C., through the bank of Montreal, Kimberley, B.C.
The land was given to the Department of National Defence by the city of Kimberley so that an armouries could be built. It constituted the last suitable site in the community when the gift was made. The city had itself received the land as a contribution from the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada limited as park land, with a clause defining an armouries as an acceptable improvement.
There are several other items in this brief. They have enclosed the signatures of very responsible men in the community and also of members of the opposition party. In addition to that, they have given us a brief summary of the militia activities in Kimberley over the past few years. It is now known as the 17th field squadron R.C.E. at Kimberley, at Creston and at Cranbrook. During the years they have been in operation they have trained 33 officers and 525 men. In addition they have 65 cadets in the city of Cranbrook and 35 in the Creston area.
Also attached to this brief, Mr. Chairman, is the engineering project of the building as it will look when completed, in addition to the site plan which has been laid out on the property concerned; and also tentative estimates of the amount required for the construction of this building, with an approximate cost of $150,000.
In view of the fact that we feel this project is an essential in the area, I should like to give the committee a slight resume of the geographical location of Kimberley. It is situated very close to my own town, within 20
Supply-National Defence miles to be exact, in the heart of the Rocky mountains. It is my understanding that in case of an emergency the militia would be called upon to undertake a great deal of the work necessary at such a time. I took up this matter with the department and they came back with the reply that in the case of an emergency help would be forthcoming from Calgary and Kamloops where units are already established.
One look at the map, Mr. Chairman, would bring to your attention the problem that would exist in moving equipment and personnel from either of the two points mentioned. The Rocky mountains and the lakes and rivers in the area forestall any quick movement of troops and equipment. I would appreciate it if this matter could be given consideration at an early date. The Kimberley group has gone to a lot of trouble in preparing plans and data, and in the event of the citizens signing a letter of intent that they are prepared to proceed as a private group should approval be obtained within a reasonable time construction of the Kimberley armouries could also be a winter works project. We are very anxious to proceed with construction and if a prompt reply could be given by the minister or the department within the next few days or weeks we could possibly arrange for some construction this winter.

I happen to know this unit at Kimberley. It is a very excellent engineering unit and they are to be highly commended on the work they have done. I also have an additional interest in the unit. It was formerly an artillery unit and was part of the regiment that I commanded as a militia commander in the years immediately after the war. It was later converted to an engineering unit. I know what the need is for an armoury there. It has been on a priority basis for some considerable length of time. At the present time it is in the same situation in western command as Sudbury is in central command. It is at the top of the priority list so far as the construction of armouries in western command is concerned and I trust we can get some action on it fairly soon.

On the subject of armouries, Mr. Chairman, about a year and a half ago a brief was presented by some gentlemen in Kitchener with regard to the need for a new armoury. We have five or six units in Kitchener and Waterloo which are scattered all over the place and I am quite sure that the rent paid on the buildings now occupied would pay for a new building in about ten years time. Accommodation could also be

Supply-National Defence provided for the navy and civil defence personnel in such a building. I would appreciate it if the minister would look at that brief again.

This is another case where we realize that an armoury is very badly needed. As a matter of fact, it is fourth on the priority list of central command. I can assure the hon. member that we have it very much in mind and it is really a matter of when we can get sufficient funds to construct it, as well as a number of other armouries.
Can the minister tell us the ultimate decision with respect to the University avenue armouries in Toronto?

The city of Toronto and the metropolitan district have both indicated that they wish to have this site for a new law courts building and that they wish to proceed with the agreement entered into some years ago under which we are to turn over that site to them. We have built one other armoury, the Dennison armoury, which I believe will be officially opened next month or perhaps even this month. It has been taken over and will be officially opened very soon. There is a need for two more armouries of the same size.
The metropolitan district was supposed to assist us in securing land sites to build the two additional armouries but unfortunately nothing has been produced yet. One site was put forward but the expropriation which the metropolitan district sought to put through was cancelled when the matter was taken to the courts and therefore we lost that site. We do not have definite sites for these other two armouries. I hope we will be able to get them very shortly so that construction can be started.
Can the minister say when the department will have to give up the University avenue site and will the two other armouries be ready by that time or will there be a hiatus?

The original agreement was that we would give it up by December 31 of this year, but in view of the fact that sites have not been provided and therefore it has been impossible to proceed with construction I have informed the city officials that we cannot give up the armouries at this time and will not be able to do so until we have been able to provide alternative accommodation.
Is it true that that very famous regiment, the 48th Highlanders, does not wish to carry on if it has to leave the University avenue armouries and is that situation being resolved?

I do not think there is any question of that. Some people may have made statements along that line. I do not know. If so, they have not come to my attention. I have had no indication whatever that the 48th Highlanders will not continue and I would be very surprised, in fact, if they are not anxious to continue.
Can the minister say whether any decision has been taken with regard to a new armouries for the city of Vancouver?

The Vancouver armouries would have been started before now except for some difficulties there over the site and the objection on the part of some people to having it built on a piece of crown owned property where we originally intended to put it. I think that the matter of the site is being straightened out now. As far as western command is concerned, the Vancouver armouries is the second one on the list and comes immediately after Kimberley as a priority project.
Could the minister say who is responsible for the establishment of these priorities?

After carefully considering the situation in the light of the needs of the militia and the accommodation at present being used, each command recommends a list of armouries in the area which they think should be constructed. This list is reviewed at army headquarters and then reviewed again by myself. The list is established on that basis.

With respect to North Bay, in view of the developments that are taking place from a military standpoint, can the minister say whether he sees any reason to believe that the priority rating for the project there might be raised? I know it is well down the list.

North Bay is not nearly as much a priority project as some of the others that have been mentioned. The list is changed from time to time depending on changes in conditions. At the present time North Bay is in seventh priority position on the central command list which would mean that there is not much hope of getting it built in the immediate future.

Perhaps the minister missed my question. In view of the fact that it has that rating and in view of the developments in the military field that are taking place across the country, I wonder whether there is any reason to believe that North Bay's priority might be raised in the reasonably near future.

As I said, the matter of armoury construction and the priority list are under review continuously and there are changes made from time to time depending on changed situations. I do not know enough about the situation with respect to this armoury compared with others to be able to give a definitive answer to the hon. member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I wonder if the minister would inform me whether or not the department is holding land on Rainnie drive in Halifax for army building use?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the department does hold this land for possible future army development.

Item agreed to.
Royal Canadian Air Force-
239. Operation and maintenance. $536,666,000.

I should like to ask some questions on item 239 which concerns R.C.A.F. operations. I was very interested in the announcement by the minister on September 11 in connection with the replacement by 1963 of the Harvard trainer with the CL-41 jet trainer as the basic R.C.A.F. training aircraft. There is a very fine R.C.A.F. station in my home city of Moose Jaw. The minister's announcement has aroused great interest there. I was present during graduation ceremonies for the last class of student pilots, and I saw how eagerly they looked forward to their jet training after flying Harvards, although they were also very proud of the Harvards. By 1963, student pilots will be training on these jet trainers.
Could the minister tell the committee what changes may have to be made at R.C.A.F. stations to accommodate the jet trainer, particularly in so far as personnel, maintenance and repair hangars and runways. Will the runways which have accommodated the Harvards have to be lengthened or strengthened to accommodate the CL-41? I am not sure of the exact length of the runways at the Moose Jaw R.C.A.F. station, but I know that jets do not normally land there. If it is necessary to lengthen the runways, and I imagine it will be, could some of this work be done this fall and perhaps during the winter to provide winter employment?

There will be no changes required in the hangars. There will be >a very small increase in maintenance personnel. There are only two of the stations in which there needs to be an increase in the length of the runways, one is at Penhold, Alberta and the other is at Moose Jaw. The runway at Moose Jaw is only 3,700 feet long and it will need to be extended to 6,000 feet. The
Supply-National Defence work will not be undertaken this year because of the date of delivery of the new trainer, which will not be until 1963. It is not a priority matter to lengthen the runways at the present time or in the next few months.

I listened to the minister yesterday when he said that our troops were splendid and their equipment was excellent. I agree with the minister 100 per cent in his reference to our troops, but I have grave doubts about his description of their equipment. After listening to the debate in the committee yesterday and today, I have grave doubts about the equipment provided for the three services. At this particular time, I want to refer to the equipment of the air service.
Now, the Voodoo airplane which is being purchased is a second hand plane. It is being purchased from the United States. The CF-104 is being made in Montreal. These two airplanes will not be effective operationally with the R.C.A.F. for some time. Certainly, there are none of these planes in Europe. I do not see how the minister can say that the equipment of the air wings in Europe is excellent, particularly when they are equipped with airplanes that cannot intercept some of the commercial jet aircraft. They certainly would not be fast enough to intercept enemy fighters or fast enemy bombers.
I have read several times in the press, and the truth is, that since the cancellation of the Avro Arrow program this government has had no definite defence policy at all. It is two and a half years since the Avro Arrow program was cancelled, at which time five airplanes were nearing completion. Only now are we starting to replace them, and with slower aircraft. It is true that the government proceeded with the construction of two Bomarc bases, one in northern Ontario and the other north of Montreal, but these will not be in operation for some months yet. After two and a half years, and when we have a crisis on our hands, we find we have no adequate air defence in Canada. We have outmoded fighter planes in Europe and we have two Bomarc bases that are non-operational.
I do not pretend to know anything about the Bomarc B, but I have read articles in the press, as I know other members have, emanating from the United States and dealing with tests that were made. These tests are certainly not very reassuring. At the time the decision was taken by this government to go ahead with the Bomarc B missile bases, I read one article concerning tests made in the United States. These tests would lead one to believe the Bomarc interceptor missile was of very dubious value. This article stated at that time that in 12 tests the missile

Supply-National Defence got off the ground on only four occasions and only hit a slow moving target on one of the four occasions. There was a later article that appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on December 29, last and I have it here, concerning tests made of the Bomarc B missile at the Elgin air base in Florida. The article stated that the series of tests at that time were a success.
The article went on to say that eight of the tests were complete failures, and that 14 of the next 15 tests were successful. I suppose that means that in the next 15 tests the missile got off the ground 14 times, so that 14 successful tests out of 23 could not be described as great success. During these tests there was a near miss on a jet drone travelling at subsonic speed over the gulf of Mexico. The article only describes this one test, and I do not know whether or not more tests were made on a target. If the missile only made one near hit in the whole 23 tests, that is not very good.
I hope the minister can give us some information as to subsequent tests, and I hope the results were better than that. I have read some derogatory remarks from defence people in the United States concerning the Bomarc B. In view of this, I think the minister should allay some of our fears about the usefulness of the Bomarc B. As I said before, I hope he will give us some results of later tests, as these articles have appeared in the press. As I said earlier, I do not know anything about the Bomarc B. I think the minister owes it to the members of this committee and to the people of Canada generally to give some information as to the results of the latest tests made on the Bomarc B missile.
It is generally agreed that the Bomarc B missile is useless without an atomic warhead. The Prime Minister himself said this in effect two and a half years ago. He at least said that it could not reach its full potential use without an atomic warhead. I have the quotation here but I do not propose to give the quotation from page 1223 of Hansard. I heard the hon. member for Quebec East and the Leader of the Opposition quote from that speech today.
The Bomarc B will have atomic capability but the government will not announce whether or not an atomic warhead will be used. To me it looks as though United States personnel will be stationed at our two Bomarc bases and will have control of these Bomarc warheads and that we shall be able to use them only when they give us permission to do so.
After reading what the Prime Minister said over two and a half years ago about the Bomarc B and about its reaching its maximum

potential only when it is equipped with an atomic warhead, I would conclude that the decision was made by the government at that time that when the Bomarc B missiles are completed they would be equipped with atomic warheads or that at least they would be available for use. As I said before, it is over two and a half years since the Prime Minister said that the government was examining various questions with the government of the United States in connection with the acquisition and storage of Bomarc B missiles. It has taken a long time to get an answer. One can only conclude that the examination is still in progress. Even though we assume that the Bomarc B is equipped with atomic warheads, that it can get off the ground and that it can hit the target more than once in 23 times, as was reported in earlier tests, the Bomarc B missile base is still itself a target. That fact has been brought out here today by the hon. member for Trinity and the Leader of the Opposition. It is a target for the intercontinental missile. It is also a target for an air to ground missile from a bomber. If these bases are put out of commission, these bombers can just roam at will as far as the Bomarc B missiles are concerned and certainly as far as our slower aircraft are concerned at the present time.
Yesterday the minister said that Russia had comparatively few intercontinental missiles. He said that the chief means of the delivery of atomic bombs by Russia was by bombers and that we need something to stop the bombers. This is a far cry from the words of the Prime Minister when he cancelled the Avro Arrow contract two and a half years ago. I also have here the words of the Prime Minister but I do not propose to quote them now. The reason given by the Prime Minister at that time was not that the Avro Arrow was not a good machine but rather that new projects were overtaking the aeroplane. Indeed, the main reason for cancelling that contract was that we would not need interceptor planes as they would be of no use against intercontinental missiles. The minister now tells us that we need interceptor planes almost more than we need anything else.
The minister says that the Liberals have no defence policy. After all, the Liberals were developing the fastest interceptor plane in the world. By now the R.C.A.F. would have been equipped with fast interceptor planes. The government scuttled the Arrow program, yet the minister says that our party has no defence policy. After killing the ace in our defence, they say that we have nothing left. I say that they have nothing left. They certainly have nothing left at this time with which to defend us here at home. As I said

before, they have no interceptor planes that can take their part against enemy planes in Europe.
One or two of the Avro aircraft were flown with engines not adapted to them. I met a number of officers of the R.C.A.F. and I may say that they were greatly impressed by the speed of this aircraft, its manoeuvrability and its great climbing power. In any case, five of these planes at or nearing completion at the time were cut up by the blow torch and the opportunity was lost to test them further. There is no question about their being cut up by the blow torch. In an answer to a question by the hon. member for Trinity, as found at page 5683 of Hansard of July 8, 1959, the Minister of Defence Production stated as follows:
The fact is that the ministry of national defence gave orders to my department, and my department to crown assets that all equipment should be taken out of these aircraft and that they should be reduced to scrap. Those were the orders received from national defence.
I have heard hon. members on the other side of the house disparage the Avro aircraft. If the performance of this aircraft was so poor, why did the government cut them up? Why did they not save them so that the R.C.A.F. might test them and prove to their own satisfaction whether or not they were good or whether they did not come up to the required specifications. I met many officers in the R.C.A.F. who had the impression that it would still be the fastest military plane in the world.
I heard some reference to the cost. I think the minister said this plane would cost $12.5 million. I read a speech of the Prime Minister in which he said that, with certain modifications, it would cost $7.8 million. Today the hon. member for Trinity mentioned a figure of $6.8 million. The hon. member for Trinity, in giving the offset cost against the Avro Arrow, did not mention the Bomarc B bases. These cost well over $100 million, and as far as we have been able to find out they are not much use. Certainly if this were put as an offset against the cost of the Avro Arrow, the government is spending just about as much money.
The government started out on this Bomarc B program and these cheaper and slower airplanes because they did not have the money. Why did they not have the money? The weird financing of this government, the promotion of higher interest rates by the conversion loan and other fiscal procedures have certainly saddled us with a great deal of debt. Already the extra interest aggregates over $800 million. I think this, and this alone, is the main factor why we have no defence policy; why we are accepting
90205-6-530
Supply-National Defence slower airplanes than the Avro. This is the main reason why our airmen in Europe and here in Canada would be sitting ducks for faster airplanes.
If our equipment is as excellent as the minister says it is, why is he now buying secondhand airplanes from the United States? I think the government has given greater priority to the payment of higher interest rates than they have to an adequate national defence. Unfortunately for us the government has been more solicitous of the money changers of our defence and the personnel manning that defence.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words in connection with the rather extraordinary statements which have just been made. In the first place, the hon. member said the F-101B is a secondhand airplane. This is not so. This is the latest two-engined interceptor that the United States have in their system. The airplanes that were secured from them are not secondhand airplanes; they are airplanes that came off the assembly line just a few months ago. Of course they have been tested, and so forth, but this has to be done with every airplane. Therefore any allegation that these are secondhand airplanes is just not correct.
The hon. member is under a complete misapprehension about the Arrow. It would not have been in service had the program been completed. The Arrow would not have been in service until late in 1962. We will have the F-lOlB's in service more rapidly than we would have had the Arrows in service had the program been continued. I should like to correct that misapprehension.
You only say that now because you cannot be disproved.

I am not going into this Arrow matter again. I spoke on it two days ago and I spoke on it at some length this afternoon. I simply repeat the fact that it would have been an extraordinarily expensive program which the defence budget just could not stand and which the Canadian taxpayer could not stand. It was a terrible mistake that the program was ever initiated, and I think we have to accept that this was the case. The result was that a good deal of money was wasted on it. The hon. member says the Bomarc B is no good and he talks about some of its-
I did not say that.

-early failures. This is what the hon. member said, as I wrote it down. The hon. member said there had only been one successful bid out of 23 tries, and so on.

Supply-National Defence

I read that from the press.
I did not say that was true.
If you did not believe it to be the case, you should not have put it on the record of the House of Commons. You should take the responsibility for what you say.

On a point of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I did not say that was the case.
I said I did not know anything about the Bomarc B; that I had read this in the press.
I hoped this was not the case, and I asked the minister to give us the results of some further tests.

As a matter of fact, last year and the year before in the early testing and the development of the Bomarc B which was then going on, every time a failure of a Bomarc firing was announced the hon. gentleman opposite rose and hailed it with the greatest of glee. They made as much out of it as they could. They asked all kinds of questions and made all kinds of jibes at the then minister of national defence.
Of course, when there began a series of reports of successful firings of the Bomarc B they stopped that tactic. This is the first time for some time that anything has been said about the firing ability of the weapon, its accuracy, and so forth.
A few months ago I was down at Elgin field. I saw a firing of this weapon. It was a highly successful firing. I talked to the people in charge of the program. I spent over a day there. We have two R.C.A.F. officers attached to the field. They have been there a considerable length of time. I saw records of the firings of this weapon, which are very extensive now. The weapon is well proved and is highly successful.
Reference to early failures when the weapon was being developed are of course not applicable at the present time. The hon. member said the Arrow was the ace in the defence policy. He seems to think the Arrow was the chief piece of equipment and the cornerstone of our whole defence policy. This was never the case. Then he went on to say that now we have no Arrow, we have nothing.
That is also completely contradictory of the policy adopted by the Liberal party in January and the policy they have been stating since, that we do not need interceptors; we should have only a few airplanes for reconnaissance and identification purposes, but they should not shoot.
The hon. member is now stating a proposition completely contrary to that when he says the Arrow was the ace in the defence policy. It was, of course, nothing of the kind. It was one piece of hardware. It proved to

be much too expensive a piece of hardware, and if we had gone ahead with it, it would have resulted in a completely unwarranted proportion of the defence dollar going into one particular piece of equipment.
The hon. member then went on to say the Bomarc bases cost over $100 million. As far as Canada is concerned, this is just fantasy. The actual estimated cost to Canada of these two Bomarc bases has been put on the record previously. The total cost of the two bases, the one at North Bay and the one at La Macaza, will be $13,993,560. Over half of that amount has been spent up to date. The annual cost to us of maintaining these two bases will be about $1 million.
Too much.

It will be just over $1 million a year. As a result, the Bomarcs are actually the greatest defence bargain I think Canada has ever secured. We are getting a greater amount of protection and value from these two Bomarc bases, per dollar invested in them, than from any other kind of equipment that we have ever secured in recent years. That is the actual story in connection with this.
I have read in newspapers the statements which have been made by members of the Liberal party. They have said these Bomarc bases are terrificly expensive and are costing Canada $50 million or $100 million a year.
We did not say "in Canada"; we said "total cost".
They said the bases were costing $100 million each, and so on and so forth. As I say these are the actual figures. They are, from the national defence point of view, a very great bargain indeed.

Before we leave the subject of the Bomarc I wonder if the minister will explain how the Bomarc operates against ballistic missiles launched from beneath the wings of aircraft. This is really the central argument.

I have mentioned several times in this debate that the Bomarc is designed against the manned bomber. It does not deal with intercontinental ballistic missiles, and any mention of it in connection with those missiles is, unless it springs entirely from ignorance, designed only to confuse the issue. It has been stated time and time again that the Bomarc has no connection with intercontinental ballistic missiles- stated so often that I do not know why this question continues to be brought up. The hon. member referred to intercontinental ballistic missiles but he was, I think, referring to air surface missiles launched from aircraft.
That is what I said. The minister was not listening.

I was listening carefully. Perhaps the hon. member made a slip of the tongue. However, this has been asked so frequently-the hon. member asked it the other day. He asked whether the Bomarc was any good against intercontinental ballistic missiles.
I said: stand off bombs from bombers.

He said that the other day when he was speaking. Attempts to confuse the issue in this way will get nobody any place.
As far as the stand off bomber is concerned, how many stand off bombers there are or will be, and at what range they will be able to fire their missiles is something that we at present do not know. The Americans have such missiles. The weapon is still in the development stage but I think it has been developed to the point where the range runs up to 300 or 350 miles. They expect that in future it will have a range of a thousand miles. Whether or not the Russians have any of these weapons yet we do not know, but we must assume that if they have not got them they will probably get them shortly. But if they have anything like the range that they have at the present time the Bomarc is going to be effective against them long before the bombers can get off their missiles against the Bomarc bases. In any event, we are dealing here with what the possibilities are likely to be in the future. It is a matter of speculation, not a matter of fact.

Before we leave this point may I say that this is the type of information which the minister gives the committee-information which misleads both the committee and the Canadian public. The minister knows that the range of the Hound Dog missile is greater than the range he has just given. He also knows, or should know-we presume he has some of these facts at hand since he is minister of defence-that the range of the ballistic missile which will be carried by the B-52 bomber and the British V-bombers is considerably greater than that range. The figure used by the President of the United States in his message to congress was 1,000 miles. That is a far cry from 300 miles, and it does not help the discussion here for the minister to pick the figure of 300 miles in an sndeavour to convince us that since 300 is Less than 400 his Bomarc will be effective, still less that it will be effective in the future.
The Bomarc stations are not yet operational. The minister has not yet made up his mind
90205-6-530i
Business of the House as to whether they are to have atomic warheads or not. By the time he does the Russians will certainly have this type of ballistic missile with a range far greater than the range of the Bomarc. The minister cannot continue to mislead the public and the committee any longer in this regard. He has got to admit that as far as the future is concerned the Bomarc is useless because the carriers against which it is designed will never come within range of it.

I have had about enough of this constant harping about my misleading the committee. I state in the most definite and categorical terms that I have given no information to this committee in which I do not firmly believe and for which I have not got a basis of expert opinion behind me. As to misleading the committee, may I say that the hon. member for Trinity gives figures which he pulls out of his imagination and out of the air. He says: these are the correct figures; all the figures produced by the defence departments of the whole western world are wrong. I have had enough nonsense of that kind. The hon. member is completely childish in making these repeated statements along that line and I think he should get wise to himself.

And I think we have had enough of these childish interruptions by the minister. I think he often gives to this committee information which is not accurate, and he must know it. He then takes the liberty of hiding behind security regulations-he cannot disclose the true figures to the house, he says, because it would not be in the national interest for us to be told the facts. He can then get up and use any figures he likes; we do not know what is going on, but he does. Figures printed in the Congressional Record are not accurate, but his are; figures printed in the message sent by the President of the United States to congress are not accurate, but his are; figures shown to other hon. members in private by representatives of the armed forces of the western world are not accurate but his are. He is the only source of wisdom, the only source of accurate figures. He suggests if we had to rely on the minister's figures we would be in a sad state indeed and I deplore the type of accusation he has just made.
Progress reported.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORTED STATE- MENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Prime Minister would care to comment on a statement made in Ghana yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, presumably on behalf of the government, to the effect that the United Kingdom now had to choose between the European common market and the commonwealth.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED STATE- MENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I saw that report. It is a news report and I am sure it does not represent what was said. I have made it very clear on a number of occasions that we in Canada have made representations to the United Kingdom and have pointed out the potential effects of its joining under the treaty of Rome unless provision is made at the time of joining the Six for an exception in respect of those things upon which Canada and thte other parts of the commonwealth depend. No such alternative as that suggested by the question of the Leader of the Opposition has been advanced at any time by the government.
The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, following the discussions that took place when Mr. Sandys visited various parts of the commonwealth, stated in the House of Commons that an application to join the common market would be made-I am paraphrasing what he said in that connection-but that commonwealth relationships would not be thereby weakened economically or otherwise.

subtopic: REPORTED STATE- MENT BY MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Would it be possible for the Prime Minister to secure for the information of members of the house the text of what appears to have been a very important statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce?

Mr. Chairman, at the adjournment last night, following my remarks the Minister of National Defence quite properly said that he did not intend to take any direction from me as to what he should or should not say in this debate. But I am sure that on reflection the Minister of National Defence will agree that at this critical time it is essential for the government to state its position with regard to the question of the acquisition of nuclear weapons. The government can state that it has no intention at the present time of acquiring these weapons, or it can take the position that it proposes to acquire them, but it must not leave the house in the position where it is denied an opportunity of debating this matter at the earliest possible moment when the government has made its decision.
I expressed the view yesterday, bearing in mind the well known device employed by this administration, that we might well find that the government will make a decision after adjournment and before we come back to this house. The country is now asking this government to declare its policy with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons. The government, before this debate concludes, if it wishes to discharge its responsibility, should face this question and tell us precisely where it stands.

We are entitled to know what is the government's policy about Canada accepting nuclear warheads. We know the position of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and we have very much suspected, from pronouncements of the Minister of National Defence, that he and his colleague are not in agreement on this subject. Indeed the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the former minister of national defence did not on this question seem to be in full accord. What conclusion are we to draw from the remarks of the Prime Minister in his speech the other day, when he paid to his colleague a tribute which he felt was deserved? He said idealism was something that was essential, but we had to recognize that opinions had to be changed from time to time, particularly in the discharge of responsibilities in this difficult and complicated period.
Are we to conclude from this that the government is about to make a decision with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons? Was this statement by the Prime Minister a forerunner of the government's intention? Was this a way of making easier the load of the Secretary of State for External Affairs? If that is the situation, then we certainly are warranted in asking the Minister of National Defence to say forthrightly where this government stands at this time with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons in Canada. We certainly cannot tell from the statement made by the minister on September 12, as reported at page 8223 of Hansard. The minister said, among other things, beginning in the second last paragraph:
Defensive weapons with a nuclear capability may be required to maintain the credibility of the deterrent, and in the event that the worst happened would be required to provide an effective defence against Soviet aggression.
Then he said:
The situation is much the same as that of a man living in a lonely cabin in the woods who fears he may be attacked by a bear. He does not wait until the bear actually attacks him to buy a rifle, but secures it beforehand and has it ready in the event of need.
One might well ask, with regard to that statement, does it mean-does the minister intend-that there shall be no ammunition for the rifle? What does the statement mean? Then he said:
The Bomarc will form part of the defences we must maintain against the manned bomber as long as there are potentially hostile aircraft in existence that can be used against us.
These statements are the closest indication the minister has given of what the intentions of the government are, but they do not tell us what, in fact, the government really intends to do in this matter. This question is of vital importance. On February 20, 1959

the Prime Minister announced the government's policy. He announced that it was the government's intention to acquire nuclear warheads. I refer to volume 2 of Hansard for 1959, and the words of the Prime Minister as reported at page 1223 are as follows:
The full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved only when they are armed with nuclear warheads. The government is, therefore, examining with the United States government questions connected with the acquisition of nuclear warheads for Bomarc and other defensive weapons for use by the Canadian forces in Canada, and the storage of warheads in Canada.
Then he went on to say that problems connected with the arming of the Canadian brigade in Europe with short range nuclear weapons for NATO defence tasks were also being studied. Then, in volume 1 of Hansard of last year, the Prime Minister said at page 73-
On what date?

On January 18, 1960. He said:
We pointed out in detail that careful thought is being given to the principles that in our opinion are applicable to the acquisition and control of nuclear weapons. I proceeded to deal with our views in that connection and summarized those views by saying that the full potential of the Bomarc could be achieved only when they are armed with nuclear warheads.
He commented on the retention by the United States of ownership and custody of nuclear weapons and then, because he properly wanted to guard against the diffusion of nuclear weapons, he said that whatever was done, once the weapons were acquired we could be sure that they would be used only on conditions agreed to by the Canadian government. But later the government changed its mind. The Prime Minister said later that we would accept nuclear weapons from the United States only if there was joint control. The Prime Minister said he wanted the kind of joint control which prevails in the United Kingdom. Then on November 24, 1960 the Prime Minister added a new reservation, which was that no decision with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons would be taken as long as any progress was being made in the matter of disarmament.
The Prime Minister made it clear in his foreign policy statement on Monday that there was, indeed, no progress being made in the matter of disarmament. I agree with the right hon. gentleman that it is regrettable that notwithstanding the efforts of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and others, no progress in disarmament is being made. The test talks have been halted. The Soviet union now wants to integrate those talks with general discussions on disarmament. The Prime Minister is right in saying no progress

is being made in disarmament. But because no progress is being made in this direction are we to conclude, in the light of the statement made by the right hon. gentleman on November 24, 1960, that the government is now about to acquire nuclear weapons?
However, the Secretary of State for External Affairs does not share the Prime Minister's views as to whether or not progress is being made in this field. He said the other day in answer to what I had said that he was still optimistic about the possibility of progress in disarmament being made at the forthcoming session of the general assembly of the United Nations.
Who is right, the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs? If the Prime Minister is right, then the Minister of National Defence owes it to the country to tell us now what are the government's intentions in this matter, and not to clothe its intentions in words incapable of interpretation. Not to do so suggests that the government at this moment has not a clear and unambiguous policy.
As a matter of fact, the only definite statement we have had with regard to this matter is the statement of the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. When he spoke in the foreign affairs debate he said, as reported at page 8162 of Hansard:
The government's stand on this matter has been made quite clear. At the present time we say no, but if events should take place in the world that might require these weapons then the government would have to give reconsideration to that position.
The parliamentary secretary of course is not a member of the government, but he does hold an important post in the administration at the present time. He said that the present policy with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons is "No". This is the only forthright statement on this subject that we have had from this government in this debate. Is this the policy of the government? I ask the minister of defence now, is it a fact that the parliamentary secretary, unwittingly perhaps, has stated the real position of the government with regard to this matter? In any event, the ambiguity and the lack of clarity in the declarations of the minister deserve to be compared with what he is reported to have said in May of this year outside of this house. He is reported in the Toronto Star of May 20, 1961 as having said-
I would be very careful with regard to anything they report.

My hon. friend can correct me. If he thinks the Toronto Star has misreported him, let him so state. I do not want the minister to be misquoted. What

Surely that is the position. If the government takes the position at this time that it cannot state its position in any other way than it has done, let the minister give us the reason for this. We are entitled to know precisely what is the government's view and policy.
I mentioned yesterday the way the government treated parliament with regard to amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Two days before parliament adjourned the government, through the Minister of Labour, said it was still considering amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, and within four or five days after parliament adjourned the government announced a royal commission to inquire into the whole question of unemployment insurance. We want to make sure at this critical time in human history that after the house adjourns this government does not make an announcement, when the house is not in session, on a matter of such vital concern to the people of Canada.
Our position is that we should not acquire nuclear weapons. The Leader of the Opposition has stated our reasons on other occasions.
I went over some of them again the other day. Our reason is not that we do not want Canadians to be as efficiently endowed with the necessary instruments to provide for effective defence as others, but we recognize that the deterrent now exists in a primary way through the United States.

Supply-National Defence
We want to discourage the diffusion of nuclear weapons. We share the government's view that we do not want war. We certainly do not want to see nuclear war. We do not agree with the Associate Minister of National Defence that we can now speak of war in terms of victory. If a nuclear war develops there will be no victor. Anyone who takes a contrary view is simply not conscious of the terrible, cataclysmic consequences which would result from the modern instruments of war. This is the situation, and so we want to discourage the diffusion of nuclear weapons. They now exist in the hands of a limited group. If we acquire nuclear weapons, how can we complain about other countries acquiring them?
We do not intend to become a nuclear power because we believe this is really beyond our resources. We believe that the fulfilment of our duty to our allies in NATO does not depend on the acquisition of nuclear weapons by Canada at this time. As I say, the deterrent now rests with the United States, and certainly if we were to acquire nuclear weapons in Canada-I am sure the Secretary of State for External AfEairs has argued this to his colleagues-this would not help him in his negotiations and consultations with other countries at the United Nations. Therefore we are entitled to ask, what is the government's position in this vital matter?
I have asked the minister, as have other members on this side, for a clear and unequivocal statement of policy. Surely this house is entitled to that at this time. I will say that I agree fully with what the minister said yesterday on another subject. I refer to the criticism he levelled at the position taken by the hon. member for Kootenay West regarding his party's position on NATO. I agree with him that the reservation which binds the new party with regard to NATO is one which is contrary to the very constitutional set-up of NATO now. It ignores the fact that the nuclear possession of weapons, which forms part of that reservation, is an already existent fact. The only reason we have NATO is the failure of the Soviet union to implement article 43 of the charter of the United Nations, which would render unnecessary the existence of any alliance such as NATO itself.
I would recall to the hon. member for Kootenay West and others the words of their former leader, Mr. Coldwell, who on March 28, 1949, used these words with regard to NATO, as reported on page 2073 of Hansard:
Contrary to the propaganda against the proposed North Atlantic treaty, the proposal is not an attempt on the part of so-called American imperialism to bring western European democracies

into an alliance for the purpose of destroying the Soviet union. It originates in the anxiety of western European democracies to persuade North America to support them in a defensive union. They believed this would halt a threat of aggression and provide the necessary defensive strength so that if the Soviet union has aggressive plans against them she will be turned from that course and thus make possible the peaceful solution of existing difficulties and problems.
Those words of Mr. Coldwell reflect what has happened. I agree with the Minister of National Defence that if it had not been for NATO we might have found ourselves the victims of aggression. In any event, as Mr. Coldwell has said and as we know and as the hon. gentleman knows, our membership in NATO has to do with its defensive purposes. We complain, of course, and no one has done more in that regard than the Leader of the Opposition, about its failure to live up to the economic objectives of article II of the treaty. Of course. But at this time when individual countries vis-a-vis the Soviet union would be outnumbered, what is there for like-minded nations of the free world to do other than combine in a defensive alliance?
There may be difficulties. My hon. friend has difficulties about West Germany. That is understandable because of his participation in the first world war. But the fact is that a realistic examination of the situation suggests that there was nothing else for Canada to do in 1949 but to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, so strongly supported by the leader of the C.C.F. at that time, and a year ago violently opposed in this house by the present leader of the C.C.F., now constituting itself into a new political group that now, under duress by its existing leader, gives support to NATO on terms that would render impractical the operation of that body. That is a fact that hon. gentlemen must not overlook.
I agree with the Minister of National Defence with regard to his complete answer yesterday, in which he pointed out that NATO is now a nuclear power. He forgot to mention the declaration made by General Gruenther in 1957, I believe, with regard to the intentions of NATO in that respect. On this point I am in full accord with the minister. We have given indication in this house that we appreciate the problems facing the administration at this time with regard to the current crisis in Berlin.
But having said that, I repeat to the Minister of National Defence my view that when we are discussing these estimates, estimates involving so much of the treasure of this nation; at a time when we are all concerned about the dangers that lurk ahead, dangers that have been characterized by the Secretary of State for External Affairs as indicating that we are on the brink of war,

the refusal of the Minister of National Defence in the face of that situation to state clearly what is the government's position with regard to the acquisition of nuclear weapons is in my judgment, I say respectfully, a misreading by the minister and the government of their obligations to the house and to the people of Canada at this critical time.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East, and I have read as carefully as I could the speeches made in this debate by members of the Liberal party, of the government party and of this party. It seems to me that what must logically follow from those things advocated by the hon. member for Essex East, and I am sure other members of that party are associated with him in this regard, is that he is advocating that Canada should become a full-fledged nuclear power in possession of all these hellish weapons that now exist. I think that is the government's attitude too, even though it has not yet had the courage to make such an announcement.
I should like to make a few comments about NATO and the remarks of the hon. member for Essex East in that regard, because he had such an intense interest in certain political developments about a month ago indicating that he perhaps wished that he belonged to a party that had such enthusiasm and such feeling. He says-so does
the government, and I think we all agree____
that NATO is a defensive military alliance and that its purpose primarily is that of defence. However, I think what we are doing is placing an awkward interpretation on the question of defence and trying to show that the organization is different from an offensive or aggressive military organization; because to my knowledge it was stated for the first time yesterday by the Minister of National

Supply-National Defence Defence that NATO has had a nuclear strategy, as I believe he put it, since 1954, and therefore is a nuclear power to a certain extent.
I think we must say that the type of defence that NATO has is one based on offence, just as the type of defence that the Soviet union has is one based on offence. The United States also agrees, as I understand it, that the type of defence which is based on nuclear weapons is not primarily the type of defence which means that you try to shoot down and destroy all or as many of the invading forces' equipment as you can, but one which rests upon the threat of retaliation and the threat of wreaking nuclear damage upon the invading country to as great an extent as possible. This is a type of defence which is really offensive, and offensive in two senses of the word.
The hon. member for Essex East made reference to some speeches by Mr. Coldwell in 1949, during which he made some comments about NATO itself. In this regard, I think we must remember that 1949 is not 1961, and the attitudes and concepts that were originally conceived for NATO are entirely different from those which exist today. The Leader of the Opposition, a very close friend of the hon. member for Essex East and a former secretary of state for external affairs, had a hand in the development of NATO, the use of the forces, and is given the credit for the inclusion of article 2 in the NATO agreement; at least, that is my understanding. I understand also that had it not been for the insistence of the then secretary of state for external affairs, perhaps the agreement would not have contained any reference to economic co-operation, as it does at the moment.
This was one of the primary thoughts Mr. Coldwell had, and it was one of the primary thoughts the Leader of the Opposition had then, I am sure; that we need to develop economic co-operation amongst these nations, and this would be a good means of competition, as it were, with the Soviet union's economic offensive in which she is engaged and has been engaged for some time in various parts of the world. In 1949, at the time Mr. Coldwell made his comments, NATO was not a nuclear power and did not have nuclear weapons. It was conceived as an organization which would be economic, and in the military field would be dealing with conventional weapons. It was not until 1954, as the Minister of National Defence revealed for the first time yesterday, that NATO became a nuclear power or accepted, as the minister put it, nuclear strategy. I will use his words so that I may not be accused of transforming what he said into something else.

These conditions did not exist in 1949. The concepts and ideas that Mr. Coldwell had when he endorsed the plan, and which the then secretary of state for external affairs expressed, are different from those which exist at the moment. In 1949 West Germany was not rearmed. This event took place at the insistence of the Leader of the Opposition when he was in office. Former nazi generals, as has been mentioned so adequately and no doubt will be repeated by the hon. member for Kootenay West, were not in control of and exercising influence over NATO affairs. These are factors which make the situation entirely different. When the hon. member for Essex East cites what Mr. Coldwell said in 1949 and says this is inconsistent with the attitude that exists today, he might as well go back to some of the comments of Julius Caesar and say they apply equally well today.
We support and have always supported the ideals and attitudes for which the present Secretary of State for External Affairs has worked, mainly the promotion of disarmament discussions leading to a disarmament agreement. All the other connected attitudes, ideals and concepts of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs receive our whole support. We are just as sorry as he is that the Soviet union saw fit to destroy what little faith may have existed in its present administration in any part of the world by the resumption of nuclear tests in the atmosphere. We regret also, along with the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the fact that the United States has been placed in a position of again participating in nuclear bomb tests.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, it will be necessary to make some reference to external affairs because, in my opinion, the attitudes of the Department of National Defence in relation to other countries are interwoven with the attitudes of the Department of External Affairs. We feel that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is one of the most sincere, dedicated and humble persons within the present cabinet. We wish him well in his endeavours along the lines upon which he has been working ever since he took over that particular office. We would like to see the Soviet union discontinue this bomb testing. Quite frankly, however, I do not know how this end could be accomplished except by expressing pious hopes, because this is something that is within the ambit of the Soviet government. I do not know how outside influence can be brought to bear on the Soviet union to cease and desist.
Send them a telegram.

Well, I think that sort of communication would have more effect if it

came from the Department of National Defence than if it came from me. However, that is about the extent of this government's effectiveness in the world today. A telegram would be about as effective as anything else.
We wish there would be a resumption of disarmament discussions. We wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs would find that the countries would come to an agreement on the ideas which he has been propounding for a number of years. Unfortunately, though, I think he is whistling in the dark, and for a variety of reasons. The first reason is the attitude of his own government, because it is inconsistent with his ideas. We have heard references to the so-called troika principle being advocated by the Soviet union. I think we realize, too, that we have a troika principle involved in the present cabinet. We have the triumvirate of the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, all engaged in the same general activity-
What about the Minister of Trade and Commerce?

Well, the Minister of Trade and Commerce was unofficially rebuked today for something he may have said in Ghana. Perhaps there will be a revision of the text by the time it gets back to Canada and everything will be straightened out. However, we find that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in a minority within this triumvirate. We find that the Minister of National Defence does not agree, and never has agreed, with the promotional work done by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The other day we heard the Prime Minister practically cut the feet from under the Secretary of State for External Affairs on this question of promoting disarmament.
We do not wish to see those ideas of the Secretary of State for External Affairs sacrificed for the ideas of retired colonels who still wish they were in the armed forces and able to direct people around the country in somewhat the same manner as they did before. I say that almost as soon as this government took the decision-and this matter was brought to a head in some decisions the Prime Minister had made-to scrap the Arrow and buy or obtain the Bomarc, at that time the government in its own mind made the decision that it was going to have nuclear weapons, tactical or otherwise, in the hands of Canadian troops on Canadian soil. However, it has not yet the courage to stand up and say that this is its attitude. It is waiting for a propitious moment. It is waiting for public opinion to be built up slowly by these

However, I venture to say that we shall have them on Canadian soil. I venture to say that we shall have them attached to the Bomarc missile when and if we get it and when and if it is operated. I venture to say that we shall have it attached to the Honest John or the Dishonest John-whatever way you want to put it-type of missile, and that we shall have it on the Voodoo aircraft. As to this attitude that the Minister of National Defence is taking, as I say he has not the courage to say so in so many words. This is a disgraceful state of affairs and in my opinion it is not too helpful in promoting any sort of war for peace on the international level.
I believe Canada has had a certain degree of respect among the other nations of the world for a number of years. However, we are gradually losing that admiration and that degree of respect which previously existed because we are becoming more and more closely allied and, to a large degree, subservient to the United States military machine. This fact is becoming recognized throughout other countries of the world. It is not our participation in NATO from which this development has arisen. As soon as the NORAD treaty was signed-and I might say that it was endorsed by both the government and the Liberal forces in this House of Commons-this was another indication that our military welfare or our so-called defence welfare and our economic welfare rested in the hands of these people in the United States.
During the course of this debate it has been stated that this is a time of crisis, a crucial moment, when we should have cool heads, logical thoughts and a non-partisan attitude in order that we may show a united front to the enemy whoever he may happen to be. By those hon. members who spoke earlier the feeling was also expressed that differing ideas were welcome, because we wanted to develop a policy that would be effective in promoting peace. One hon. member-I shall not make reference to him personally-spoke about there being a bipartisan foreign policy in Canada, and said it was too bad there was not a tripartisan foreign policy in Canada. Then he engaged in what I thought was a most unwarranted and uncalled for condemnation of the hon. member for Peterborough with respect to the remarks that hon. member had made in this house on the estimates of the Department of External Affairs, and on defence also.
That sort of thing does not add in any way to a unified feeling or unified desire to

If, as there have been in this house, accusations of treason, treachery and selling out to the Soviet union are going to be made by members on the government side against members who may have different points of view, I submit that this does nothing to develop any conscious, sensible, unified approach to these particular questions. It is true that the hon. member for Peterborough has ideas which are different from those of the government. The hon. member for Essex East has different ideas, or so he said a moment ago.
Very different ideas.

The hon. member for Trinity has different ideas. However, there is no desire to label these hon. gentlemen as treacherous souls or treasonable types because they expressed different points of view. I do not understand why members in this House of Commons will say on the one hand, "We want to develop a non-partisan attitude on defence policy matters", and then will turn around, for political reasons, and get involved in the accusations that were levelled against the hon. member for Peterborough and the hon. member for Kootenay West. As I say, I think it is regrettable that there does not exist in this house at the moment a degree of respect for differing views.
Before I conclude my remarks I should like to make a comment or two about the question of disarmament. As I have mentioned on a number of earlier occasions, it is an objective toward which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has been working for a number of years but which, of course, has been fairly well scuttled for the time being. I submit again, as I have stated earlier, that all the negotiations and discussions that have been going on throughout the approximately 340 meetings that were held, to a certain extent could not hope to come to fruition. They were not in themselves pointless, as they laid the groundwork for certain areas of agreement to be developed; but as I have said on a number of occasions, there is not going to be any disarmament unilaterally by either the United States or the Soviet union. I also submit that there is not going to be any disarmament by those two powers by agreement. Hence all these speeches and wishes about a disarmament agreement being reached between the United States on the one hand and the Soviet union on the other hand were just pious hopes. They were about something that was not going to happen.
Neither the United States nor the Soviet union was going to enter into such an agreement for disarmament, regardless of the con-

ditions about inspection and the like, because there is in the world today a third growing military power, which was recognized by the Secretary of State for External Affairs as a necessary part of the discussions. I refer to China. So long as China is a growing military power and if, as we are led to believe if we can accept the reports that emanate from various government sources, China will be a nuclear power perhaps within a period of five years or less, you are not going to see the Soviet disarm with China building up, and neither are you going to see the United States disarm. What I think will happen if these disarmament discussions are resumed-and I think it should have happened previously-is that China will become a part of them. Without China becoming a part of them they are not going to end up in any agreement one way or the other. All we shall be doing is meeting, talking and building up our nuclear forces. Without China in these discussions I think they are to a great degree, although not entirely, a waste of time.

Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago the Minister of National Defence told us that he was not going to be bludgeoned into making any further statements with regard to government policy on the use of nuclear weapons. May I say that nobody wishes to bludgeon him. However, we still hope that he will be able to make a statement in order to clarify a most important matter which we think is not clear.
His attitude reminds me of a story which perhaps I may tell the committee. It is the story of a young subaltern who had just received his commission in the army and was taking his platoon out for a march for the first time. He was leading the platoon up a hill, and at the top of the hill there was a precipice. As his platoon got closer to the precipice the young officer became a little panicky because he could not remember the order to change direction. I know how he must have felt. As they got closer and closer to the brink-and we are told, in another context, that we are on the brink now, in a more serious way- he became less and less able to think of the proper order, until finally on the very edge of the brink his sergeant turned to him and said, "For heaven's sake, sir, say something, if only good-bye".
We do not want the minister to say goodbye, at least not in this sense, but we do hope he will give us a clearer statement on this vital issue-and I will deal with this later in my remarks-than we have received over the years from any member of the government, though we have received a fairly clear statement, I admit, from one of the parliamentary secretaries.

This discussion of defence is being held in a world situation, the critical nature of which has been emphasized to us by the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and other leaders of western governments. It is impossible, of course, to think of a more serious subject at a more serious time than what we should do to defend the peace, which is the only secure defence of our country, in this situation. While, of course, we do differ very strongly with government attitudes and government policies in the implementation of government objectives which we share, we do not disagree-and this has been pointed out by other hon. members of this committee-with what those objectives should be; security, defence through peace, and preparations to that end.
The Associate Minister of National Defence had this to say in his contribution to this debate on September 12. I quote from page 8241 of Hansard. Reference was made to this statement by my hon. friend from Essex East this morning:
Ii the worst should come, and if we have to fight again, I do not hesitate to say that we shall once again win the battles of tomorrow just as we won the battles of yesteryear, and this for many reasons.
Mr. Chairman, if the worst comes-and there is no reason why it should come-we will not win the battles of tomorrow in a nuclear war, because not only is it impossible to win a nuclear war but it is impossible, we are told by experts, even to wage one. So I think no one can get any comfort out of the fact that we will win the battles of tomorrow, if these battles are permitted to occur, by a breakdown in the sanity of man.
That does not mean, of course, that in the face of this situation we should just give up, sit back, wring our hands and say "Nothing can be done about it", and look around for an escape to some other planet. Perhaps that will be within the bounds of possibility in a few years. But it does mean that before we act and before we decide on policies we should be aware of not only the problems of defence but of the shifting and changing nature of those problems and what we in Canada can do to help solve them, not merely as a nation laying down policies for national defence-up to a point that is still required- but far more important, what we can do as a participant in collective defence, which is the only way we can develop enough strength to constitute a deterrent to aggression.
I have no quarrel of any kind with the minister in his emphasis on the necessity of collective action or indeed on the necessity
Supply-National Defence at times of subordinating the requirements of independence, in the pursuit of national defence policies, to those of interdependence.
This defence debate is the first we have had since this parliament met last November. In the first part of the session there was practically no discussion of defence problems. There was no defence committee discussion; there was not even a committee to discuss defence expenditures. In the face of the absence of earlier consideration of this vital matter, I think we had the right to expect from the minister and the government a report which would have gone into some of the essential problems of national defence, and a statement from the minister at this time which would have dealt with this matter in a fundamental way. We should have the kind of statement the United States congress gets periodically from the leaders of the government, the kind of statement the United Kingdom parliament gets from its minister of national defence. Instead of that kind of white paper we got this blue book which was issued a few months ago, which in a very inadequate way told this house of the problems with which we are faced in this country in defence strategy, defence planning and defence policy at this particular time. It is similar to the minister's statement the other day which was inadequate and uninformative on these basic questions of defence policy.
So far as I can gather, the minister's position is that the plans and policies we have been pursuing for the last four years are still valid; they still stand up. In spite of what may have happened in the world, we continue along those lines. If you like, we continue in this particular rut, that everything is fine and unchanged and no new policy is required, except perhaps to substitute some United States equipment for Canadian equipment, especially in the air. Apparently we must not keep changing our minds. The minister makes great play over the fact, as he puts it, that we on this side of the chamber, and I in particular, have changed our minds over recent years with regard to defence matters.
Believe me, Mr. Chairman, that is true, because the situation has changed greatly in the last four years and a person would be foolish not to alter his own views in the light of these changing situations. But the

Supply-National Defence minister says that no change, as far as he is concerned, should be made. That seems to be the policy of the government, except perhaps with regard to a change in the attitude of the Secretary of State for External Affairs which is now being forecast by the Prime Minister.

The director of this institute-and I heartily agree with what he says-said a few months ago:
