The Leader of the Opposition went on to say that he thought the Bomarc was obsolete, that it is no good. Then of course the hon. member for Trinity made similar statements. If that is the case, here is a very peculiar thing which I would ask the committee to consider. There was a story written by Paul Dubois in the Ottawa Citizen of October 29, 1960. The dateline was "Thurso". It was about the speech of the Leader of the Opposition at a rally in support of Gaston Clermont, Liberal candidate in the by-election occurring at that time in Labelle riding.
And elected.

I would read the committee the direct quote. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition will say he was misquoted, but the direct quote of what he said was this:
A nuclear deterrent may be necessary for the U.S., but not for us and other countries. If Russia ever attacked North America and specifically Canada, Montpellier would be a prime target for the Russians, Montpellier and communities for hundreds of miles around would be reduced to ruins.

If Montpellier was going to be a prime target because it had the Bomarc base there, why does the Leader of the Opposition now say that the Bomarc is completely useless? If it is completely useless the Russians would not be wasting any bombs on it.
Oh, oh.

We find the Leader of the Opposition, for election purposes, going to this area and saying this terrible Conservative government had built a Bomarc station there and that was going to bring Russian bombers and these people would be wiped out if the balloon ever went up.
The balloon went up this last minute.

The Leader of the Opposition says the Bomarc is no good and nobody takes it seriously except this government. He says the Russians do not pay any attention to it. That is another example of the logic of the Leader of the Opposition in connection with these matters. Now-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Take a long breath.

He went on to say that the Liberals had put up a much better policy last year and he indicated much better roles that Canada might be following as far as defence is concerned.
What was this great policy they put up last year? As described by my predecessor, it was a policy of scrap, scrap, scrap. They wanted to scrap practically everything and what they did not want to scrap in this so-called policy consisted chiefly of advocating things which we had already done or were proposing to do. I have a list here and I could go over them in detail, but I hardly think it is worth while. I will just indicate that they urged the abandonment of the SAGE Bomarc system and recommended the purchase from the United States of a number of supersonic interceptor aircraft. They knew we were negotiating at that time for supersonic aircraft, so they recommended this and thought they would get on the bandwagon, I suppose.
There is one other thing I should like to mention. They advocated, really, that the navy should become a sort of glorified merchant marine.
Assault vessels for the troops.
Fortunately that policy is not supported by anybody except themselves. That so-called policy is so full of holes that it is much worse than one of those famous cheeses.

It smells worse, too.
Supply-National Defence

The Leader of the Opposition read some quotations from newspapers supporting the position that they take. I have a whole file here attacking the position they have taken, but I certainly have not time to read them. This sort of reading does not prove very much, of course.
After lunch-I think the Leader of the Opposition must have had a good lunch-he seemed to get onto a somewhat better tack. He got away from this attempt to justify the mistakes that he and his party had made in the past in regard to defence and he got on to a discussion of NATO, what its objective should be, how nuclear weapons might be controlled in it, and so on. The hon. gentleman said he did not object to NATO having nuclear weapons. As I indicated, I was very glad to have that definite statement from him and I hope he will stay with it. I think we all realize that the control of nuclear weapons is an extremely difficult problem, as the hon. gentleman himself admitted. It is, of course, one which has been exercising the attention of governments of the NATO countries for a very considerable time. To date, no generally acceptable solution has been reached. It is a problem which I certainly trust can be solved, just as the Leader of the Opposition does and as, I think, we all do, but it has not been solved to date.
There is another question which was raised by the Leader of the Oppositoin and with which I should like to deal briefly. He referred to 15 fingers on the trigger. Of course, it would be hardly a credible type of deterrent if we had to obtain the agreement of 15 countries before nuclear weapons might be used, in certain circumstances particularly. In this connection a great deal of thought has been given to whether what are known in the navy in particular as rules of engagement might not be worked out-whether all the 15 countries of NATO might not agree to those rules of engagement, as they are called, which would lay down the situation in which each country would agree that nuclear weapons might be used. There is, I think, hope of arriving at some type of what might be called full NATO control over the use of nuclear weapons by this means.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke of the necessity, in his view, of building up the conventional front line strength of NATO. I fully agree that not only the conventional front line strength of NATO but the conventional strength of the organization generally should be built up. I do not think anybody would quarrel with the hon. gentleman in this regard. Ever since the organization was established, one of the greatest difficulties as far as NATO is concerned has been the failure

Supply-National Defence of certain members of that organization to build up their conventional forces at a sufficiently rapid pace to the strength to which they themselves had agreed to bring them at some time in the future. Of course, the greater the degree to which each of the individual countries in NATO builds its conventional strength the stronger the force will be. I think the Leader of the Opposition and myself share common ground in that regard. As a matter of fact, the increase in the Canadian force which was announced here last week is an indication of Canada's willingness to build up her own NATO strength and increase her contribution to NATO.
I should like to say a word about one idea which the Leader of the Opposition put out- the idea that the Russians might launch a limited conventional war, and that we must have some means of dealing with it. I do not think that eventuality is very likely, though I do not say it is impossible; nothing is impossible. But I think it is very unlikely that the Russians would start a limited war in Europe which they would expect to keep as a conventional war. If they were to do so I think the chance of such a conflict developing into a nuclear war would be very great. For this reason I hope the Russians would not contemplate such action for a minute because it would be an extremely dangerous type of move.
As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, perhaps the greatest danger we face in the world today is that of a war started by accident. This is something which could happen, and it is a possibility which needs to be guarded against very carefully as far as the west is concerned'-and we trust the Russians will take equal precautions. However, as I say, the chance that they would start a fair sized conventional war in the expectation that it could be kept at that is, I think, very unlikely. The basic situation is that they have nuclear weapons in their force in eastern Europe, and if they started to move, Mr. Khrushchev himself has said they are going to use everything. That is why it is necessary to have sufficient strength to deter them from ever making such a move. I agree it is the most important thing in the world at the present time to try to ensure that peace continues. On that note I think I will end.

I apologize for taking up the time of the committee at this stage but it is most difficult to conduct a responsible examination of the estimates of the Department of National Defence when the committee cannot rely on information given it by the Minister of National Defence. The example we have had this afternoon is just one of


many. Either the minister's memory is incomparably bad or he gives us wrong information.
For example, in respect to the cost of the Avro Arrow, in May of this year, speaking on Vancouver island during the by-election, the minister is reported to have said, according to a newspaper which he indicated this morning was a good paper, that the planes would have cost $15 million each. The report in the Victoria daily Colonist reads in part:
Referring to the Liberal leader's remarks about the scrapping of the Avro Arrow jet interceptors the defence minister stated that the planes would have cost $15 million each and that the huge cost would have meant scrapping much of the army and navy strength.
This afternoon the minister must have decided in his imagination that it would be more credible if he reduced the figure to $12 million each. And then, when he was challenged, as he was yesterday when he pulled the same trick, he reduced the figure to $7.81 million each. Even that figure is too high, because that is the figure which was given to the special select committee on estimates a year ago as the cost of 108 operational aircraft plus 12 pre-production models. If hon. members do the arithmetic they will find that the cost per operational aircraft was $6.8 million each.
Still too much.

That is all in the evidence. The minister is aware of it, and for him to stand up and tell this committee that the cost would have been $12 million each is an insult to hon. members, particularly as the evidence given by the former deputy minister of national defence, now Air Chief Marshal Miller, was that the planes would cost $6.8 million each. How can we have any faith in anything the minister tells us if he uses a device of this kind to try to confuse and bewilder both the committee and the Canadian people?
This is a type of arithmetic which might be applied to a new situation. The minister has just worked out an arrangement under which the Canadian Department of National Defence is to receive 66 Voodoo aircraft in exchange for certain things. I have the agreement here. I shall not read it in detail, but in exchange for the 66 Voodoo aircraft the department agrees to take over from the United States the cost of maintaining Pinetree radar stations previously maintained by the United States air force. In addition, it is to contribute $50 million toward a program of military aid- toward the acquisition of F-104 aircraft to be built at Canadair in Montreal.
In addition, it will pay one third of the cost of spares and ground handling equipment for the Voodoo in the amount of $10.9 million.

Now, there is no cut-off date as to when Canada's responsibility ends in respect of maintaining the Pinetree line. The annual cost of maintaining the Pinetree line has been variously estimated. The then minister of national defence, the Hon. George Pearkes, V.C., advised the house on March 2, 1959, as reported on page 1518 of Hansard as follows:
Mr. Speaker, before the house rose for the dinner recess, the Leader of the Opposition had asked for information with regard to the cost of the Pinetree system. As I explained, the Pinetree system is shared by the United States and by Canada, some of the stations being operated by Canadians and some being operated by the Americans. The cost to Canada of operating each year is approximately $28 million; that is the cost of operating those Pinetree stations which were either built by Canada and manned by R.C.A.F. personnel or were built by the United States and manned by R.C.A.F. personnel. The cost to the United States is approximately $43 million for operating their stations. That figure of $43 million includes some $5 million which the United States are spending on purchasing equipment for those stations in Canada.
Hence if Canada were to take over the operation of the line in its entirety it would mean the addition of $43 million to our defence budget at the present time.
A United States congressional subcommittee was advised by the director general of the United States air force budget that the saving to the United States air force by Canada taking over the cost of the Pinetree line was $50 million a year. If this is so, Mr. Chairman, let us assume that we have to maintain this Pinetree line for ten years. The cost, even by using the lower figure recorded by the Minister of National Defence, would be $430 million. Add to this $50 million which is Canada's share of the purchase of F-104's, and $10.9 million which is our share of the spares for the Voodoo, and the total cost is $490.9 million for 66 aircraft or approximately $7.5 million per copy. If we had to maintain those stations for 15 years the cost would be a total of $705.9 million, or more than $10 million a copy, far more than it would have cost to carry on with the Avro Arrow program.
The Minister of National Defence told the people in Victoria that the commencement of the Avro Arrow program was the greatest mistake ever made by the Canadian government. Well, the deal he has just made with the United States government, which could result in the cost of $10 million each for aircraft which at the most are not worth more than $2 million each, is in my opinion one of the biggest boobs ever pulled by a minister of national defence.
In closing may I say I think the minister should apologize to the committee for using figures upon which it cannot rely.

Mr. Chairman, if these allegations came from some serious source I
Supply-National Defence would take them seriously. However, I consider the source from which they come and I will merely say that the figures the hon. gentleman is producing are probably comparable with the figures he was trying to produce yesterday as to what the cost would be for the 15,000 more troops we are going to raise, which he insisted was double what I had said they would be, although this was a figure arrived at by careful estimates of the departmental officials and officials of treasury board. But he produces any figures that his imagination suggests to him and I suggest that the committee should not take him to seriously-I certainly do not take him too seriously-in regard to these matters.
As far as the actual cost of taking over these Pinetree lines, and so on, is concerned, if the cost went on for long enough, of course, it might be very considerable. But the main point is that we are taking over those radar stations in Canada, manning them by Canadian personnel and operating them with Canadian personnel rather than having them operated by United States personnel.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are always complaining about having United States personnel here stating that it is an infringement of our sovereignty. Therefore rather than complaining about it they should be happy to see Canadian personnel replacing United States personnel in manning those radar stations. The point is, if you take a long enough period you can arrive at any figures you like.
Members of the committee will recall an item which appeared in the paper the other day. There was a clergyman in Boston who sent a bill to the chancellor of the exchequer for $18 worth of damage done to the fence of his church back in 1770 something. He presented a bill for upwards of $750,000. If you take a long enough period you can come up with a terrific figure. In effect this is what the hon. member is doing.

Could I ask the minister a question arising out of the article by Mr. John Gellner which he quoted a few minutes ago. The article criticized the Liberal party. Does the minister agree with this statement in the article:
The country certainly needs a Minister of National Defence who can overcome public apathy and suspicion, and restore confidence in Canadian military policy.
Where did the hon. member find that? The reason I ask the question is that as I recall this particular statement by Mr. Gellner, he went on to say, "It looks as if Canada has secured one."

No, Mr. Chairman. I will send the article over. It went on to say:
Let us hope Harkness is the man.

Supply-National Defence
But I am sure his hopes are not realized now.

He suggests strongly that I am the man, as I recall it.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, this debate, which is of such great significance to all Canadians, has now reached its third day, and we just heard from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) a masterful statement on all aspects of the national defence policy Canada should follow, a statement which the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) was unable to refute. We therefore have the proof that in this field as in all others, the Canadians who are looking for guidance and leadership must turn to the Liberal party and not to the government which persists in taking a confused and ambiguous position in this and every other matter.
Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak very briefly on this question which seems to me a capital one at this time and which is a subject of interest and concern for the Canadian people. The present situation may be summed up in the following question. What is the policy of this government with regard to the use of nuclear arms in Canada?
Mr. Chairman, I think that the discussion of the estimates of the Department of National Defence, which takes place this year in the midst of an international crisis, would have been a very appropriate moment for the government to state a definite policy and tell us clearly whether or not it had come to a decision with regard to the number one problem, the use of nuclear arms in Canada.
It is inconceivable that the government after three days of debate should leave us in an ambiguous position. The situation is becoming more and more confused. Only yesterday, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) when concluding his speech called upon the government and the Minister of National Defence clearly to state their policy in respect of nuclear arms in Canada. As a matter of fact, the hon. member for Essex East said this, and I quote from page 8330 of Hansard: (Text):
We are entitled to know, before parliament adjourns, with respect to this very vital matter of whether or not the government has a policy; and if it has, the government should state it in a forthright and unambiguous way.
(Translation):
Here is the answer given by the Minister of National Defence, as recorded in Hansard on page 8330.


(Text):

In reply to that, Mr. Chairman, I would say that I do not propose to accept the directions of the hon. member for Essex East as to what I should or should not say in this debate.
I contend that this is an extraordinary statement on the part of the minister and I hope that this observation of the minister will receive wide publicity because he has overlooked a very important fact. When the hon. member for Essex East asked the government to tell us what their policy is he was not speaking on behalf of the Liberal party only but also on behalf of the Canadian people who would like to know what the decision of the government is on this important question.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, such indecision on the part of the government is not only disappointing but also detrimental to the interests of Canada, and as long as no clear and specific decision is arrived at on this most important matter, Canada will be incapable of playing the leading part that it should play.
I listened last Tuesday to the statement made by the minister. That statement can only lead to speculation. Here is what he said as recorded on page 8223 of Hansard:
It requires that they be equipped with weapons comparable to if not better than those of a potential adversary. It is the policy of the government that our forces should not be required to face a potential enemy with inferior weapons.
Mr. Chairman, most newspapers understood that the government had decided to acquire atomic weapons and to become a member of the nuclear club. But that statement is ambiguous and causes dissatisfaction everywhere among the public.
1 also listened to the remarks of the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny); he too avoided any definite statement on this capital matter. Indeed, he considered war in terms of the 1914 world war or the second world war because, according to page 8241 of Hansard, he stated:
If the worst should come, if we have to fight again, I do not hesitate to say that we shall once again win the battles of tomorrow just as we won the battles of yesteryear, and this for many reasons.
Well, the minister has forgotten, I think, that victory has no meaning at all in a nuclear war. However, he was a little more careful yesterday than he was when he addressed a rally in Mont Laurier during the last by-election campaign in the constituency of Labelle. I should tell him that I was not far from the place where he was speaking and that I heard him enumerate the advantages of the La Macaza launching base. The

minister will recall, I hope, that one of the reasons for his party's humiliating defeat in the riding of Labelle was precisely the stand taken by his government on this question of nuclear weapons.
Mr. Chairman, after three days of debate, it is obvious that the government's national defence policy is several years old, as the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) has shown, and that the government has not had the courage to adopt a definite position concerning the use of nuclear weapons in Canada. As long as this situation prevails, we cannot hope to play the part we could play, and we would be ill-advised to criticize today the other countries which belong to the nuclear club since our objections to nuclear tests would be weakened because of the position taken by the government.
That is a cause of great disappointment for all Canadians but they have one reason for keeping up their hopes, and that is the fact that there is one political party which has remained true to the policy it has always advocated with respect to nuclear weapons. Here I should like to quote from the newspaper Le Devoir of Tuesday, April 11, 1961. Here is what Paul Sauriol had to say in an editorial:
The Liberal party rally, last January, clearly declared itself against acquisition or use of nuclear weapons in Canada, under any form of control; Mr. Pearson said that such weapons were not required for the time being.
What position we took at the rally was our position before and it still is our position. That is something that one cannot say of this administration.
I do not want to be too critical of the C.C.F. members who have been wearing since last summer a new jacket which fits them about as well as a strait-jacket. As I say, I do not want to be too hard on them, because it is really pitiful to see them trying to take positions now to the left, now to the right, according to the instructions they get.
I simply say that the only encouraging sign for Canadians is the fact that at least there is in the Canadian political life one party with a clean cut position, with a clear stand, a constant stand, and I am proud to be a member of that party, the Liberal party.

Mr. Chairman, regardless of the sombre nature of this debate, I for one am very pleased to note two cheering news items in the afternoon paper. The first in the Citizen, is headed, "U.S. Ready for Serious U.N. Talks With Russia". It is a Reuters dispatch from London and reads as follows:

We have had a rather lengthy and interesting discussion, Mr. Chairman, with respect to military hardware. It seems to me to be pretty well a stalemate, and at times the debate was difficult to follow. Of course, I would not suggest for a moment that I am capable of speaking with any knowledge or judgment on such a question. As a member of the working class I am more acquainted with the saw, the axe, the pick and shovel. I could pass some opinion as to the quality of those tools, but not those that have been mentioned previously in the debate.
Now, Mr. Chairman, at the request of a number of people I again raise a matter that I raised yesterday, a matter that is of serious concern to a great number of Canadians. Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, I made certain statements with respect to General Heusinger and expressed strong opposition to his appointment as chairman of the military representatives committee of NATO. This means that he is one of those who plan the strategy and tactics of NATO and who, indirectly, would direct the activities and actions of Canadian troops. I want to say that my statements were not made lightly. They were not made just to create resentment or anything of that sort. I feel very keenly on this matter and I speak with conviction. I feel as keenly as a number of other persons do, a number of other groups in Canada and in the United States.
The Associate Minister of National Defence replied briefly to my arguments and at one point said that General Heusinger was a man who had served his country with distinction. He then went on to defend the appointment of this general to this very important position. I am quite sure that the Associate Minister of National Defence spoke according to the information he had available. I am confident also that, judging from his remarks,

Supply-National Defence he has not been completely informed on this matter. In order to put the record straight, and on behalf of a number of Canadian citizens, I want to place the facts on the record. This appointment offends a good many Canadians in various groups, including religious, ethnic and other groups.
In order that there will be no misunderstanding, and for the sake of accuracy, I am going to read at some length. I trust the committee will bear with me so that the facts will be on the record. I have read a number of books and documents that have been brought to my office by people interested in this problem, including one lady of German descent. I have the Congressional Record.

In his autobiography, "Befehl in Widersteit," published in West Germany in 1950, Heusinger wrote that he sympathized with the 1923 Hitler putsch in Munich, but did not participate because he was sure the attempt would fail.
In 1940, Heusinger became chief of operations on Hitler's general staff. Was responsible for the military planning of all Nazi invasions from then on.

In 1942 was made responsible lor all actions against partisans. In August 1942 this order, initiated by Heusinger, was sent to the army group centre on eastern front:
"The Fuehrer demands immediate retaliatory action for (partisan) attack on the railroad station in Slavnoye, with the use of the strongest measures of terror. Report what measures you take.'' Heusinger's order resulted in the following: In Slavnoye the Nazis threw several dozen live children into a deep well. None survived. In another village, Gayanka, Heusinger's troops exterminated the entire population of 115.
Heusinger, as chief of operations of the OKW (Oberkommando der Wehrmacht)-the high command of the Nazi forces, commanded the special extermination squads (Einsatzgruppen). These squads were given the task of exterminating all Jews and other groups. William L. Shirer describes some of the mass atrocities committed by Heu-singer's Einsatzgruppen (see pages 961 to 963 of "The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich.")

After the bombing, Hitler said on the radio, "But you should know of a crime unparalleled in German history. The bomb seriously wounded a number of my true and loyal collaborators." The loyal Hitler general who was giving a detailed report on the Russian front at the precise time of the bombing was Gen. Adolf Heusinger.

Supply-National Defence today. In my opinion this type of appointment creates unnecessary suspicion so far as the Soviet and other countries behind the iron curtain are concerned. Place yourself in their position, Mr. Chairman, knowing that the chairman of the top planning body of NATO was a general who was merciless in the destruction of their civilian population.
I therefore say that in the first instance it is unsound from our point of view to create this -unnecessary irritation and to arouse suspicion on the part of behind the iron curtain countries as to our motives and as to our principles in which we profess we believe. I think it causes unnecessary distress to many people as for instance to the unhappy relatives who suffered from this sort of thing. I think it causes suspicion even among Canadians who are given cause to wonder, when we talk about our being a Christian democracy and use language of that type, how we can justify Canadian troops in reality, if not in effect, actually marching under the leadership of a general with a record such as this. It may create in young people a feeling of cynicism and a lack of belief in the things for which we profess to stand. I know that it creates a great deal of resentment among former veterans of the first and second world wars. Just imagine the feelings of relatives of veterans who sacrificed their lives in the first and second world wars in the defence of principles in which we in Canada believe. With all my heart I believe that an appointment of this type does our cause harm. I feel deeply on this question. I do not think we can justify this appointment. There are a good many other people in our country who feel keenly and sincerely with respect to a question of this type.
The hon. member for Essex East for whom I have great respect made some reference to my remarks yesterday and said that he could understand them as possibly they were somewhat motivated by my experience in the first world war. That is not the situation at all. No one can accuse me of being in any sense a person who has any antagonism towards any race. Anyone who has known of my life throughout the years and my activities in the district in which I live knows that is not true, and that on behalf of even German citizens during the war, I sought to make sure they obtained justice during those difficult times. I do not express these views because of antipathy to any race. I recognize the position of the ordinary soldier who served his country in time of war whether he was on our side or the enemy side. I refer to the ordinary soldier recruited to serve in what he considered to be his country's defence. However,


Mr. Chairman, we must remember that people like General Heusinger were the leaders. These were the people who decided policy. They were the ones who gave expression to nazi ideology, nazi ethics in battle, and who transgressed all the known ethics of modern warfare, in so far as one can term war as having any ethics at all.
A good deal of my information comes from friends of mine of German ancestry. A German lady visited my office just a few nights ago. She came from New York to visit me. I have also had Germans working for me in my constituency on many occasions and I know the contribution they make to society. They are the type of Germans who opposed nazism and left Germany because of it in the first place. They oppose nazism and I respect those people.
I am speaking of those who supported this nazi ideology which we, at great cost, defeated in world war II. I and others oppose this appointment because we believe, in the light of all the circumstances of what the western world suffered in world war II and because of our professed principles, that such an appointment is strictly immoral and, as I said before, weakens our cause.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in conclusion I urge the government to consider the feelings of the people who feel keenly about this; to obtain the facts and to do what they can to see that this general is replaced by someone with a clean military record, someone who cannot stir up the feelings of many in our country and other countries by creating unnecessary suspicion as to our methods.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to enter into any argument with the hon. member for Kootenay West as to the antecedents of General Heusinger. I merely wish to say that the hon. member has given the opinions of one or two men and perhaps somebody else in connection with this matter. My information is that it was precisely because Dr. Adenauer was convinced of the anti-nazi antecedents of General Heusinger that he appointed him as his chief military adviser in, I believe, 1950. I do not think the hon. member doubts the anti-nazi character of Dr. Adenauer or his general attitude.

Mr. Chairman, I have just this to say regarding what the hon. member for Kootenay West has said. I have no means of knowing the validity of the evidence he has produced, but it seems to me that to leave this matter open, with the possibility that this kind of thing will be disseminated in Russia, with no valid answer to it except that apparently Dr. Adenauer was satisfied, would be a very dangerous thing.

I hope we will pursue this matter further. It seems to me that if there were not an adequate answer to the evidence produced by the hon. member the Russians would be able to disseminate this opinion which we have received from a reputable source. The hon. member is known to us and his own war record is known. He knows of responsible people feeling as he does in connection with this matter and I hope the matter will not be allowed to drop here.
Shall vote 232 carry?

That is the Prime Minister:

The Prime Minister said in reply:
What I said was this. If perchance, and all of us hope to the contrary, war came, we would become a participant because of our relationship, our undertakings and our pledges in NATO.
I simply wish to say for the record that, while it is true that under article VI of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization we would be involved, we have constitutional processes in this country which, subject of course to the exigencies of nuclear war, we must observe. That is, before there is any declaration of war by the executive arm of the government or by circumstances such as I have envisaged, such as a nuclear war, parliament must authorize a declaration of war. There is no automatic involvement. This is our constitutional position. I am sure it was inadvertently left out by the Prime Minister.

Is this decision subject to the troika principle?
I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by that. However, I think he is aware that all three departments are concerned in this matter.

The study on manpower requirements at the national headquarters is related to this very question. If we find we can cut down the number of personnel at the headquarters it would, of course, mean we could construct a smaller building than would otherwise be the case. 233.	Operation and maintenance, $7,224,436.

I understand that the inspection services include the inspection of the quality of purchases of material and equipment and that they also cover the quality of performance. Will the minister say who carries out the inspection of the fixed assets and stores which are kept over a period of years? Will he also tell us whether the inspection services have anything to do with the inspection of the efficiency of administration or the efficiency of training?

The inspection services have nothing to do with those two latter matters. Once goods have been purchased and delivered to the respective services each service is responsible for the inspection of those stores in its own quartermaster's stores and so forth. Essentially the inspection services inspect articles which are being delivered to the Department of National Defence to ensure they are up to specification.
Who is responsible after that? Does the responsibility for continuous inspection rest with the commanders?

Once the stores are delivered -we will take boots as an example-they are delivered to the ordnance depot and the ordnance depot is responsible for seeing that they are kept there under proper condition and in good shape. Then, when they are delivered to a unit, say an infantry battalion, that battalion is responsible for their proper storage and to see that they are kept in proper condition there.

I was thinking of stores that might deteriorate over a period of years. Who would carry out any tests on goods that might deteriorate? Is that done by the ordnance department, or is there some machinery within the command for that?

It depends on what type of stores they are. If they are medical stores, the medical service would declare them unserviceable when they considered that they had reached that stage, we will say. With respect to dental stores, the dental people would do it. With respect to general stores, the ordnance people would do it. If a unit has some stores that it thinks are unserviceable it declares them unserviceable and the ordnance people inspect them, and if they agree they are unserviceable they take them to the ordnance stores for disposal.

Royal Canadian Navy-

I should like to ask the minister a question in respect of the navy. If he will consult page 1 of his blue book, the preamble, under the heading "Royal Canadian Navy" he will see listed there four roles for the Canadian Navy in support of Canadian defence policy. This numbering is mine. The roles are: (1) maintenance of sea communications; (2) the defence of Canada against attack from the sea; (3) to contribute to the collective defence of the NATO area from attack from the sea; (4) to contribute naval forces to the United Nations as may be required. Can the minister indicate which of these four roles is the most important role of the Royal Canadian Navy?

These roles are so interconnected that I do not think I can pick out one and say it is the most important. As I think is quite clear, they are not set out 1, 2, 3, 4, as the hon. member has just put them; they are put in as a sentence. As I say they are pretty closely interconnected. Therefore, I do not think you can pick out one and say it is the most important role.
Would the minister care to tell the committee what in his opinion is the principal threat against which the Canadian navy is to operate?

Of course, the principal threat is the submarine threat and, as is indicated here-it has been indicated on numerous other occasions-our navy is basically an anti-submarine navy consisting principally of destroyer escorts and frigates. The destroyer escorts particularly are specialized anti-submarine ships. The carrier and the tracker aircraft and the interceptor aircraft that it carries really for protection from the air, and the helicopters which are now being added to the destroyer escorts-the whole thing is designed to be a well co-ordinated anti-submarine force. It also, of course, has a capability for general sea warfare.

As the minister knows, the Russians are reported now to be producing atomic powered submarines, and concentrating on the production of atomic powered submarines from which nuclear missiles would be launched. Presumably, in an attack against the North American continent the Rusians would use their present supply, or the supply existing at that time, of nuclear powered missile launching submarines. If the minister is concerned about protecting the deterrent as well as providing such protection as he can to the Canadian civilian population, what provision is he making through the Canadian navy to cope with the threat from the atomic powered nuclear submarine?

Mr. Chairman, as I have just indicated, the navy is essentially an antisubmarine navy. It is designed to be able to hunt out and destroy enemy submarines. Part of the strategy at the present time is to do that as far away from the coasts of North America as possible. The fact that nuclear submarines may be in possession of the Russians as they are in the possession of the United States and that these nuclear submarines are faster is precisely the reason why we are equipping the destroyer escorts with helicopters. We are doing so in order that they will have the capability of tracking, and discovering and finding these submarines and destroying them at a considerable distance from the destroyer escort from which the helicopter operates and also at a considerable distance from our coasts.

Is the minister contending that Canadian destroyer escorts with helicopters would be capable of seeking out and destroying nuclear-powered submarines at some distance from our shores in either the Atlantic or Pacific oceans?
The answer is certainly yes. That is the basic purpose of the destroyer escort, particularly equipped, as I say, with a helicopter.

Perhaps the minister will let me make this comment. Here again I think that we are left in a most unfortunate position. The minister has stated, and he has been very careful with his language, that that is the purpose. We all know that is the purpose of the destroyer escort. We know that is the purpose of an anti-submarine force, but the minister did not say that we have that capability and he knows that we have not. What is more, the minister knows that we are not getting that capability.
Let me say for the minister's benefit that I have seen an atomic submarine in action and it can swim circles around our destroyer escorts or anything like them. The minister

knows this, and these submarines cannot be detected and destroyed with the type of naval vessel that we have. What is the minister contemplating that will cope with this threat? Is he contemplating the construction of anti-nuclear submarine submarines or anything of that nature with the speed, range and capacity to be able to deal with that type of threat?

All I am saying is that our competent naval officers inform me that the sort of statement the hon. member has just made is completely erroneous, that our antisubmarine vessels, particularly when they are completely equipped with helicopters using sonobuoys and so on, have the capability of destroying submarines at any time. Certainly you are not going to destroy every submarine. It was not done during the last war and it was not done during the first war. However, a very considerable number of submarines were destroyed in both of those wars and the submarine threat was eventually beaten.
There is also no question that the faster the submarine the more difficult it is to detect and thus to destroy, but nevertheless we have a very considerable capacity to destroy submarines at any time. Therefore I deplore the hon. member stating as though it were a definite fact that we have no such capacity. He has no means of knowing that. What he is really doing is making such statements in direct contradiction of the opinions of all those people who have devoted their lives to naval service, not only the senior naval officers in our service but in the British, United States and other navies.

I should like to follow up the comments of the hon. member for Trinity because I think it is the duty of hon. members in spite of the opinions of the experts to find out as much as we can about the defence of the people whom we represent. I think we are getting right down to the bottom of this whole thing right now as to just exactly what the value of our defence is.
The minister said yesterday afternoon that the enemy can have enough power to blow up the whole world but as long as they cannot deliver this power we seem to be fairly safe. 1 think that is a very good point but there seems to be quite a difference of opinion as to just what the capability of the enemy is. Perhaps we can assume that the enemy is only going to start a limited nuclear war and will only use a few submarines, a few I.C.B.M.'s and so on, but I think this is a fantastic concept and that the war will be an all-out one from the very beginning. Surely common sense would lead to this conclusion. Certainly
Supply-National Defence a submarine war would be the most potent method having in mind their mobility and so on. I would hope that we would realize the danger of the situation. I do not think we are deploring the opinions of the experts or in any way trying to bring strategic concepts into question. If the strategic concepts of the government hold water then we have no criticism; but I wonder.
We understand, for example, that the Russians have 500 submarines. I was very happy to hear the minister say that the major role of our navy is anti-submarine activity, but do we have in mind dealing with submarines that are out to sink shipping or is it a case of dealing with submarines the purpose of which is to strike at our cities, each submarine having far more power than all the bombs dropped in the last war?
In the blue book it is stated that we are responsible for the collective defence of the NATO area. That is a very large area involving the Atlantic, the Pacific, the North sea, the Mediterranean and so on. Can the minister tell us what particular areas Canada is responsible for and can he possibly tell us how many submarines might be likely to move into this area on the basis of the studies that are being made by the experts?
The minister said that the Russian power to deliver is limited. Everything is limited. Nothing is unlimited, but to what extent is their power to deliver limited? How many of the submarines moving into the areas for which our navy is responsible would actually be nuclear submarines? We cannot tell, of course, which are and which are not. What is the speed of the aircraft carrier, the destroyer escorts and frigates which are being equipped for anti-submarine activity? What are the detection capabilities? I think the Canadian people should know to what extent they are paying for defence, or to what extent they are simply paying for activities which will show that the government is doing something in the naval field but which activities are not really very important.
I should like to remind hon. members that we are not trying in any way to add to the terrorizing effect of the U.S.S.R., as the minister seemed to suggest. Before the last war Churchill was accused of trying to terrorize the British people when over a period of four or five years he was merely trying to put before them the realities of the situation in Europe which he felt had to be met. I think the Canadian people should know what the reality is on the basis of the knowledge that is available to the Minister of National Defence. Can the minister answer any of my questions?

I think that I had better explain first of all that the defence of the north Atlantic comes under SACLANT, the supreme allied commander Atlantic, who occupies the same sort of position as General Norstad does in SACEUR so far as NATO defence of the European land area is concerned. In the event of war he would have under his command not only the Canadian Atlantic fleet but also the United States and British Atlantic fleets, all of the other NATO naval forces in the north Atlantic. To begin with, he would dispose of all those naval forces in such a way as to form an antisubmarine screen. The purpose of the screen would be to try to destroy Russian submarines trying to get through the comparatively narrow waters leading from the Arctic ocean and between Iceland and Norway and also to prevent them from getting out of the Baltic. The purpose would be to contain as many as possible in those areas and also, of course, to destroy any that were already loose in or that got through into the Atlantic. In other words, the first function of the north Atlantic naval forces would be to destroy as many enemy submarines as possible and to keep them as far away as possible from the shores of the NATO countries. Subsequently, it may well be that Canadian naval forces would be employed in the convoying of merchant vessels in order to attempt to defend them from possible attack by submarines. I do not know whether or not this answers the question of the hon. gentleman, but broadly speaking that is the concept.

The situation is even more serious than I suspected, Mr. Chairman. You are assuming that the Russians, if they start a war, will have all their submarines in the Baltic and the Arctic and would not have them deployed throughout the world. It appears that there is no particular duty for the Canadian navy except to act as convoy for ships. This is not facing up to the reality of the situation in which Canada would be placed if war came. The minister said himself this afternoon that the Russians would not likely engage in a limited war, and there was no sense talking about giving the forces nonnuclear weapons because there would be an all-out nuclear war.
What we are doing in connection with naval defence there has no relationship whatever to what the minister said this afternoon about the kind of war which every military expert I have read suggests is going to take place. It will be a war which will take place in 30 minutes and the destruction will be so fantastic that I doubt very much whether there will be any convoying of troops from one place to another afterwards.

I think the hon. gentleman completely misapprehended the remarks I made. I said the first purpose of the North Atlantic naval forces would be to destroy Russian submarines and to contain them in their home ports in so far as possible. I said that one of the purposes would be to hunt out and destroy Russian submarines that may be loose in the Atlantic. Now, this is so far as the Atlantic is concerned. Then I said that subsequently maybe Canadian naval forces might be used in convoy work. This would only come later if a protracted struggle developed. This may not happen at all. In any event the primary purpose, and I should like to emphasize this, is to hunt out and destroy enemy submarines.
This applies also, of course, to the Pacific coast. On that coast this is a matter for cooperation between the United States Pacific naval forces and the Canadian naval forces. In the Atlantic area, the war plans are made by the supreme allied commander, Atlantic. He has specified the forces he would like from Canada and there are defence plans drawn up as to how those forces would be employed. I am not, of course, at liberty to state what those plans are.

I agree with the hon. member for Peterborough that we are carrying on here with this air of unreality which has seemed to weave in and out of the minister's remarks during the last two days. The minister deplores any statement which is made from this side of the house which is not in agreement with the statements he makes. However, this afternoon we had an example in clear terms of the fact this committee cannot rely on the information given to it by the minister. He said, in effect, you must not challenge the word of senior naval officers. I have here some opinions from a senior naval officer which are not in accordance with what the minister said. Now obviously, there is a difference of opinion.

-when U.S. submarines, presumably playing the role of missile-firing "enemy" submarines, provided "realistic and elusive targets". I'll bet they were elusive. Our naval forces today are not designed to deal with these sorts of things at all unless the "enemy" submarine purposely presents himself for sacrifice as a part of the war "game" just to make the "friendly forces" feel better. I continue the quotation:
The entire scheme of things is to my mind quite unrealistic and don't think the men in the Canadian navy don't think so too. They are, however, bound hand and foot to this concept agreed to by the government some years ago... when it was still valid... and somehow never changed since to meet the conditions of today.
As long as our navy is obliged to play this "head in the sand" game and obliged to provide forces to deal with this out of date concept, I suppose there is little wrong with the way they propose to spend our defence dollars this year... it will provide work for our shipyards and it will fill the pay envelopes of our sailors and shipbuilders. But don't let us be fooled into thinking it will provide us with any maritime defence. It won't.
Later on, he says:
Is it a valid concept in the present age? Of course not. We must come up with a "new look" in operational forces to deal with the new but very real threat from missile launching nuclear submarines. These are the real threat to this country and we must get the government to admit it. In these new forces Canadian nuclear-driven submarines designed to seek out and destroy other submarines, especially these missile-launching submarines, will undoubtedly play a major role. They are well known to be far and away the best, in fact they are the only effective type of anti-submarine vessel there is and they can be built in Canada in Canadian shipyards by Canadian workers.

The answer to that question is no. This is a responsible statement by an interested Canadian citizen trying to make a contribution to national affairs, and a very real contribution. This article points out in clear terms that in respect of naval policy, as in respect of most of its policies, this government has no conception whatever of what is going on in the world of military technology today. The minister told us earlier in the debate that two or three years lead time is required in the development of nuclear vehicles. During a recent trip to the United States in discussion with naval officers there, they indicated that, in their opinion, the only possible way that nuclear submarines could be dealt with would be by an atomic device. I should like to know if the minister concurs with this opinion or whether he does not. If he does, has he any plans to obtain atomic devices for the navy? If not, does he contemplate giving the matter any study because, as the minister can well appreciate, by the time he adds two or three years lead time to the end of his survey, any potential all-out war might be over.

I should like to deal with several of the comments that were made. I will deal with the last one first. There has been a good deal of study given to this matter. In fact, the means of killing submarines is one of the most intensive and continuing studies carried on by the navy. There is no question that the use of a reasonably small yield nuclear weapon would be more effective in destroying a submarine than would a conventional bomb or torpedo. I think there is no question about that fact because you get a much bigger explosion. However, there are plenty of conventional bombs and torpedoes which are also effective in destroying submarines. As to the matter that he mentioned first, namely some notes by Captain Groos, with regard to opinions as to strategy I would merely say this. I prefer to take the advice of the senior

Supply-National Defence serving officers in the Canadian navy, the British navy and the United States navy rather than the opinions of a retired naval officer who has just recently been standing as a Liberal candidate in a by-election and whose opinions on this matter might therefore be looked upon as being somewhat biased, having regard to the fact that they were supplied to the hon. member for use in this debate.

All I can say is that the minister's policy in respect of preferring the advice of serving officers over that of recently retired officers must have changed in the last three years or so. He used to take quite a different attitude. I can assure him that there is no bias whatever in the argument presented by Captain Groos. This was put forward in all sincerity in order to help bring to the attention of the nation the head-insand attitude of the minister in the hope that at some time in the not too distant future he will pull it out.

I think we are living in some kind of fairyland here. It just does not seem to me that the kind of war that is going to be carried on, if one takes place has come to the realization of this government. It would seem we are being told that it is going to be a much different kind of war than any in the past. Everywhere I look, in the magazines and in the latest books, it seems to be indicated that it is going to be a nuclear war and an all out war.
Show us your crystal ball.

The minister says, and probably quite rightly, that our naval forces are involved in SACLANT and so on. We are dealing with the estimates of our naval forces. We have not yet found out where those naval forces might be deployed, to what extent they can handle this area, or to what extent they can actually defend Canadian shores. In other words, we cannot find out and give the information to the Canadian people. I am sorry but I do not think I can go back to my constituency and say that the naval experts say thus and thus but that our Minister of National Defence simply says this is what he believes or this is what the naval experts believe. I want to hear on the floor of this House of Commons the extent to which this defence is actually possible. I asked the question as to the area our navy can be expected to look after in such a nuclear war and I have been told that they will be deployed in a certain area. The minister did not say that for security reasons this could not be stated. He has not said that the number of our submarines could not be stated.


I should like to know to what extent these ships have detection capable of picking up these submarines. It seems to me there are a great many questions which I should like the Canadian people to have answered. If there is no defence we have got to start working somewhere else. Perhaps this will affect our emergency measures organization too. I think it is an extremely disconcerting aspect of the whole picture.

I do not think the hon. member took in what I said a short time ago. The defence on the north Atlantic is a combined fleet of the NATO countries which have NATO forces bordering on the north Atlantic. All the naval forces of all of these NATO countries in the event of war come under the command of the supreme allied commander, Atlantic. It is then up to him to deploy those forces in the places where the Russian submarines are found to be. You cannot say that the Canadian navy is going to be used from point A to point B and point C and point D. It may be used any place on the north Atlantic where needed to hunt down and destroy enemy submarines. The same thing applies as far as the Pacific fleet is concerned. As I said, in the event of war it is a combined command between the United States and Canada. Also the naval forces of the United States and Canada in the Pacific would be used as one co-ordinated weapon to destroy enemy submarines and to protect the sea lanes leading in there.
I think that statement is clear enough and I think the hon. member's constituents will be able to understand it quite readily. In the case of ships you do not say that they will work in this particular area and this particular area only. Under modern conditions, the whole concept of naval defence is to have a co-ordinated command which will employ all of the naval resources available in the whole North Atlantic in the place where they are most needed at that particular time. The same thing applies as far as the Pacific forces are concerned. We had the same thing, of course, during the second world war. Canadian naval vessels were employed in all sorts of places throughout the Atlantic ocean, in the Mediterranean and so on.

I wish to remind the minister that it took five years to destroy the submarine menace in the second world war. The German submarines nearly brought Britain to her knees at that time. If an attack took place tomorrow, how long would it take before Canadian ships could occupy the areas they are expected to defend as part of this whole over-all strategy in SACLANT?

The best answer to that question I think is this. Except for the limited number that happen to be in dock refitting at any particular time, our ships are in a state of immediate readiness. At practically all times some of them are at sea. They are therefore available immediately to counter enemy submarines. This is one of the reasons why we are increasing the complement up to full strength, from an average of 86 per cent to 100 per cent. We are doing this so that they will be capable of going out and maintaining patrols for long periods. With 85 per cent manning they are able to go out and manage full operational duties for a few days but you have not enough men to keep them on three hour shifts. They therefore have to work overtime, as you might say, and they eventually become tired. That is the reason v/hy we are increasing the complement up to full strength. We are doing that in order to enable them to operate over long periods of time at full efficiency.
The minister has said that most of the Canadian navy is assigned to SACLANT.
I did not say that, Mr. Chairman. I said the Atlantic forces are assigned to SACLANT in the event of war and come under his command.

The minister says the Atlantic forces are assigned to SACLANT in the event of war. He gives the impression that, because they are part of the whole, we do not need to concern ourselves whether they do not have a particular capacity. However, two or three questions immediately come to mind. First of all, may I say this. Surely the Canadian ships have an area of responsibility. Surely there is a function they have to perform. It is an allied command. In addition to that, one of the roles which was put in the blue book-and perhaps it should not have been in the blue book-is the second one, namely the defence of Canada against attack from the sea. The question that arises is this. Are we incapable of protecting Canada against attack from the sea? Must we rely on the ships of other nationals who are also assigned to the supreme allied command, Atlantic, to protect Canadian shores from attack? Is it necessary that the submarines our navy has to cope with should be of the oldest possible vintage, nearest the surface and close in, where they can be easily spotted? I think the minister should give us some more assurance about this, because from what he has said so far I must agree with my hon. friend that there is a terrific air of unreality about this whole thing. We have no feeling of comfort 90205-6-529

Surely if the minister is going to be consistent at all-and perhaps he is not going to be, which would not be too surprising- he should concern himself with the reality of attack from the sea just as he told the committee he is concerned with the reality of attack by air.
May we please have a further explanation from the minister as to just how we are going to cope with an attack from the sea, and how Canada can play an effective role under the supreme commander of the Atlantic, when our ships are not capable of performing some of those functions they would be called upon to carry out if they were assigned a specific task?

Mr. Chairman, the unreality which the hon. gentleman speaks about exists in his own mind rather than in the mind of the Department of National Defence or in the mind of the navy. He is engaging here again in what seems to be the general activity of trying to run down the defence forces of this country by saying they are obsolete, their equipment is no good and they cannot do their job.
He has been doing this regularly. This is his stock-in-trade. Once more I can only say that I deplore an attack of this kind, particularly when it has been pointed out to the hon. member on numerous occasions that the allegations he is making are completely incorrect.
As far as our Atlantic fleet is concerned, as I have already stated, in the event of war it comes under the command of SACLANT and is used in accordance with his orders anywhere in the Atlantic where it can best be used and for which he is responsible.
At the present time, of course, one of the sub-commands in SACLANT is the commander, Canadian Atlantic sub-area. Our admiral at Halifax is the commander of that sub-area. He is responsible for the command and the defence of that area. In the event of enemy forces being in there, forces might be sent by Great Britain, the United States or other NATO people. He would take command of them and would carry on the operations.
In peacetime there is a considerable area off our coasts which the Canadian navy keeps under surveillance. It does this by means of its tracker aircraft and its various ships, and also with the maritime command of the R.C.A.F., which is constantly flying various routes over those waters in order to detect any submarine or other activity of that kind.
This is the way the operation is carried on in peacetime. As I say, in wartime you have

Supply-National Defence a unified command and all the naval forces of the NATO alliance in the North Atlantic would be used to the best advantage as one striking force.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has said I am trying to run down the Canadian forces. That, of course, is not true. First of all, to distinguish between the forces and the equipment, I think the Canadian forces are of the finest in the world, but I think they are handicapped by having some of the most obsolete equipment.
The hon. member for Peterborough and myself are trying, like Winston Churchill did in the late 1930's, to shake a complacent government out of its complacency. We are trying to get it to admit the facts of the world about it, and that is a most difficult task apparently.
I wonder whether the minister would indicate to the committee when the first keel of the destroyer escorts was laid, and would he also indicate how many are still under construction.

First of all I wish to state in the most definite terms that our destroyer escorts are considered, not only by our own naval authorities but by those of other countries, as the most modern and up-to-date destroyer escorts possessed by any navy. The number under construction at the present time is six. They are of the latest class. The first of the modern destroyer escorts, the St. Laurent, was commissioned in October, 1955.

No, not then.

Not then. I wonder whether the minister would indicate to the committee why, in view of the tremendous technological changes which have since taken place, and more particularly the fact that since then the first atomic submarines and the first atomic missiles carried by submarines have been put into operational use, he continues to build destroyer escorts which were then incomparable and which may still be the best destroyer escorts in their class, but which today are no match for the potential enemy. That is the point we are trying to get across to the minister. We would like the minister to tell us what plans he has to meet the threat of the future?

The destroyer escorts which have been built have been subsequently improved. Improvements have been added to them constantly and their anti-submarine

capability has been constantly improved, particularly through the development of the variable depth sonar, which is an invention of the Canadian defence research people.
We are now commencing to modify the existing destroyer escorts so they can carry a helicopter each, in order to greatly extend their range of operations, and thus their ability to both detect and destroy enemy submarines.
The hon. member seems to have the naive idea that if conditions change a bit, immediately you must scrap everything you have. This is the general line he was following last year-scrap this, scrap that, scrap the other and get a complete new line of equipment. You just cannot do that, particularly as far as naval vessels are concerned. The construction of a naval vessel is a long business. The design particularly, of a new naval vessel is a long business. As I have said, our destroyer escorts are as good as any that exist in any navy in the world. I do not know how the hon. member can expect us to do better than that.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has just underlined the problem. He has said that the designing of a naval vessel is a long business and that the construction of a naval vessel is a long business.
Is the minister telling the committee, in conclusion, so we will understand his position very clearly, that he has no plans for more modern ships than those presently under construction, and that he has no plans for the introduction of atomic weapons into the Royal Canadian Navy? Is that the present position of the minister and of the department?

We have all kinds of plans. There are no plans which have been definitely decided upon, approved and funded which I can announce at this time. The navy has a very considerable number of plans for ships of different kinds and a naval construction program upon which they would like to embark. There are quite a number of variations of their projected naval construction program, but I am not in a position to announce any of these at this time because they have not been definitely approved and there has been no arrangement made as yet with regard to their financing.

Before this vote carries I should like the minister to clarify this subject further. We have some 40 anti-submarine vessels. Can we really convince the Canadian people that if the U.S.S.R. should decide to attack Canada these vessels which are the sole defence of the Canadian area would have any hope whatsoever of destroying nuclear submarines armed with nuclear weapons? Can the minister give the Canadian people any indication or hope whatsoever that this naval contingent for which, as the hon. member for Trinity has said, we have nothing but the greatest respect, is equal to such a task? Would our forces be able to make any impact upon them whatsoever in the first few hours of attack in the kind of war which would take place in 1961?

I have tried on several occasions already to make the situation clear to the hon. member but he seems to have the notion fixed in his mind that Canada is going to fight Russia by herself. This is not the situation. He asks whether the Canadian navy can protect Canada against Russian submarines. Well, the Canadian navy is not going to protect Canada by itself. As I have told the hon. member on three or four occasions already, the protection of Canada and of the other NATO countries will be the responsibility of the navies of all the North Atlantic treaty countries which have navies in the north Atlantic. It is a combined affair. In the same way, the R.C.A.F. is not expected to defend all of Canada by itself against the Russian attack; it is part of the continental defence of this whole continent. It is a co-ordinated defence shared by our own R.C.A.F. planes, Bomarcs, the radar lines and the forces of the United States. In the same way the sea approaches would be defended by the navies of all the North Atlantic countries. I think we have to look upon the resources of the alliance as a whole and not have it fixed in our minds, as seems to be the case with the hon. member for Peterborough, that the 43 Canadian navy vessels are going to be the sole defence of the Canadian sea approaches against a Russian submarine attack or threat.

Perhaps the committee would permit a layman to make a comment on this question. As I listened to the discussion it seemed to me that what we have here is the minister trying to deal with a real situation-with the facts as they are- while the hon. member for Peterborough-I say this with deference-appears to be talking as if this was merely a war game or, to change the figure, a game of chess. With the greatest respect to the hon. gentleman, may I say that if there is an air of unreality here it is not present on this side of the chamber. This is not a game of chess. The submarine we got up from the United States so that our chasers would have something real to chase is a vessel that they had kept in mothballs. It is not reality to chase a submarine which has been kept in mothballs and which no one in his right mind would send out to sea in the event of war. That is not reality. It is putting the clock back at the very time when we should be projecting our imagination into the future. It is the hon. gentleman himself who is turning the clock back. I know he has many fine reminiscences of days gone by and he is entitled to them, but the time has come when men in responsible positions have to cease looking to the past. They have to look ahead and use imagination concerning the situation they will have to face in the future. That is what the minister has not done up to the present time, and I urge the hon. member for Greenwood to join with those of us who suggest that the minister should bring himself up to date and stop playing chess with mothball submarines and second world war equipment. He should project himself into the future so as to be aware of the real situation, not of make-believe situations.
